title: 起初，神创造
verse: 创世记一章廿七节
content:
书卷背景

《创世记》是圣经正典的第一卷，传统上认为出自摩西之手，是摩西五经之首。书名原意即「起源」——记载宇宙、人类、婚姻、罪、审判、列国，直到那蒙拣选、要使万国因之得福的家族之起源。全书以反复出现的家谱套语为骨架，例如「亚当的后代记在下面」（创5:1），大致分为两大部分：一至十一章的「原史」，记载神与全人类的关系，涵盖创造、堕落、洪水、巴别塔；十二至五十章的「族长故事」，记载神拣选亚伯拉罕、以撒、雅各、约瑟一个家族，要藉着这家族赐福万国。今天所读的一、二章，正是这整卷书、也是整本圣经故事的起点。

在全书结构中的位置

一、二章给出两幅互补的创造图景：一章按七日次序，由宏观到微观、由无到有，展示神以话语创造万有、井然有序，一步步迈向创造的高峰——人；二章则聚焦第六日，细看神怎样安置人在伊甸园中，为他造配偶。这两章为后面十一章的堕落、洪水，以至全卷、全经的故事，立下了「起初本该如此」的标准，也是往后一切败坏必将被拿来对照的尺度。

主题与神学重点
  • 一章：神藉着话语，用六日次序渐进创造天地万物，每一日的工作神都看为好的；第六日，神「就照着自己的形象造人，乃是照着他的形象造男造女」（创1:27），又赐福给他们，交托治理全地、管理海里的鱼、空中的鸟、地上活物之责；六日的工作完成后，「神看着一切所造的都甚好」（创1:31）。
  • 二章：细看第六日：耶和华神用地上的尘土造人，将生气吹进他的鼻孔，安置他在伊甸园中，使他修理看守；神说「那人独居不好，我要为他造一个配偶帮助他」（创2:18），便使他沉睡，取他的肋骨造了女人；圣经在此第一次为婚姻下定义：「人要离开父母，与妻子连合，二人成为一体」（创2:24）。到第七日，「神赐福给第七日，定为圣日」（创2:3），歇了他一切创造的工，安息了。
救赎历史脉络

「起初，神创造天地」（创1:1）——整本圣经的故事从这里出发：一个由神以话语创造、按祂形象安置人、并以安息为高潮的美好世界。神的话语、人按神形象受造的身分、工作与安息的次序，这三样将贯穿全部六十六卷书，反复被破坏，又反复被神信实地挽回。三章要记载这美好次序如何破裂，而整本圣经此后要走的路径，正是要藉着一位真正、完全活出人本该是的样子的那一位，领一群本已破碎的人进入那第七日所预表、却始终未曾真正得着的安息。今天所读的，是这条漫长救赎故事最初、也是最稳固的起点。

回应

你今天的身分和价值，不是从你的成就、你治理生活的能力而来，而是从神在创造之初已经宣告的事实而来：你是照着神的形象被造的（创1:27）。这形象后来因人的悖逆蒙尘破损，但神并未任凭它彻底失落——祂差遣祂儿子成为那位完全、毫无破损地活出神形象的人，替你我担当我们本该担当的一切亏欠，又亲自成就了那第七日所预表、我们靠自己永远达不到的安息。所以你今天不必靠着劳碌来赚取安息；因基督已经做成了得安息所需要的一切工作，你只管坦然进入祂已经完成的安息中。
content_en:
Book Background

Genesis is the first book of the biblical canon, traditionally attributed to Moses and standing at the head of the Pentateuch. Its name means “origin” — it records the origins of the universe, humanity, marriage, sin, judgment, and the nations, tracing history down to the chosen family through whom all nations would be blessed. The whole book is structured around a recurring genealogical formula — for example, “This is the book of the generations of Adam” (Gen. 5:1) — and falls broadly into two parts: chapters 1–11, the “primeval history,” recounting God’s dealings with humanity as a whole, covering creation, the fall, the flood, and Babel; and chapters 12–50, the “patriarchal narratives,” recounting God’s choosing of one family — Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph — through whom he would bless all nations. Today’s reading, chapters 1 and 2, is the starting point of this entire book, and of the whole biblical story.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 1 and 2 present two complementary pictures of creation. Chapter 1 moves in seven-day sequence from the macro to the micro, from nothing to everything, showing God creating all things by his word, in ordered sequence, building toward the pinnacle of creation — mankind. Chapter 2 then focuses in on day six, looking closely at how God placed the man in the garden of Eden and made a companion for him. These two chapters set the standard of “how it was meant to be from the beginning” against which the fall, the flood, and indeed the whole unfolding story of Scripture will be measured, and against which all later corruption will be judged.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 1: By his word, God creates heaven and earth in a six-day sequence, and each day’s work he calls good. On the sixth day, God “created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them” (Gen. 1:27), and blessed them, entrusting them with dominion over the earth, the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, and every living creature. When the six days’ work was finished, “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Gen. 1:31).
  • Chapter 2: A closer look at day six — the LORD God formed the man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, placing him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it. God said, “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him” (Gen. 2:18), so he caused a deep sleep to fall on the man and built a woman from his rib. Here Scripture gives its first definition of marriage: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh” (Gen. 2:24). Then on the seventh day, “God blessed the seventh day and made it holy” (Gen. 2:3), resting from all his work of creation.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

“In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth” (Gen. 1:1) — the whole story of Scripture begins here: a good world, created by God’s word, in which mankind is placed in his image, crowned by rest. God’s word, mankind’s identity as image-bearers, and the sequence of work followed by rest — these three threads run through all sixty-six books, repeatedly broken, and repeatedly and faithfully restored by God. Chapter 3 will record how this good order was shattered, and the path Scripture takes from there on is precisely this: through the one who alone truly and fully lived out what humanity was meant to be, leading a broken people into the rest that the seventh day foreshadowed but that they could never truly attain on their own. Today’s reading is the first — and the most secure — starting point of this long story of redemption.

Response

Your identity and worth today do not come from your achievements or your ability to manage your life — they come from what God declared to be true at the very beginning of creation: you were made in the image of God (Gen. 1:27). That image was later marred by human rebellion, but God did not let it be lost forever — he sent his Son to be the one who, perfectly and without flaw, lived out the image of God on our behalf, bearing the debt we owed, and himself accomplished the rest foreshadowed by the seventh day, the rest we could never reach on our own. So today you do not need to labor to earn rest; because Christ has already done all the work required to secure it, you need only enter, in confidence, into the rest he has already completed.

title: 从乐园到苦境
verse: 创世记三章十五节
content:
书卷背景

一、二章描绘了神所造「甚好」的世界与人：话语创造的次序、按神形象受造的尊贵，以及第七日的安息。三至五章要记载的，正是这美好次序如何因人的悖逆而破裂——这是全书「原史」（一至十一章）的核心转折，此后的家谱、洪水、巴别塔，都是这一次破裂的延伸后果。

在全书结构中的位置

三章记载堕落本身；四章记载堕落如何从个人的悖逆蔓延为该隐杀亚伯的暴力；五章以亚当的家谱作结，谱系中反复出现「……就死了」，正是神在三章所宣告的审判，如今一代一代应验。

主题与神学重点
  • 三章：蛇引诱女人怀疑神的话，二人吃了分别善恶树的果子，随即知罪羞耻、彼此推诿；神审判蛇、女人、男人和地，其中向蛇所说的话首次预告：「女人的后裔要伤你的头；你要伤他的脚跟」（创3:15）——这是圣经中第一句救赎应许；本章末了，「耶和华神为亚当和他妻子用皮子做衣服给他们穿」（创3:21），神亲自用牲畜的皮遮盖了人自己无法遮盖的赤身羞耻。
  • 四章：该隐杀亚伯，罪从个人的悖逆蔓延为流血的暴力；即便如此，「耶和华就给该隐立一个记号，免得人遇见他就杀他」（创4:15），神的怜悯仍临到那背叛祂的人。
  • 五章：亚当家谱一路数下来，反复出现「……就死了」，是三章审判宣告的现实应验；唯独以诺是例外——「以诺与神同行，神将他取去，他就不在世了」（创5:24），在满是死亡的家谱中留下一线盼望的缺口。
救赎历史脉络

创3:15神对蛇所说的话，是整本圣经应许—成就这条主线的第一个环节：女人的后裔终要伤蛇的头，但那击打要以自己被伤为代价——这预告了一条充满受苦却终必得胜的道路，最终在那位被钉十字架、却藉着死败坏那掌死权者的基督身上应验。神为亚当和夏娃所做的皮衣，也早早预表了后来的真理：人无法自己遮盖自己的罪，唯有神亲自付上代价、用流血为人预备遮蔽。

回应

你若因自己里面像亚当夏娃一样，本能地想用无花果叶——也就是自己的辩解、遮掩、表现——来遮盖羞耻，今天可以停下来：因为基督已经在十字架上流血，为你预备了那件你自己永远做不出来的遮盖；你不需要靠自己的手段处理罪疚，只需要像接受神所做的皮衣那样，接受祂已经为你成就的遮盖。
content_en:
Book Background

Chapters 1 and 2 depicted the world and humanity God made — “very good”: the ordered sequence of creation by his word, the dignity of being made in God’s image, and the rest of the seventh day. Chapters 3–5 record how this good order was shattered by human rebellion — the pivotal turning point of the whole “primeval history” (chapters 1–11); everything that follows — the genealogies, the flood, Babel — is the extended consequence of this one rupture.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapter 3 records the fall itself; chapter 4 records how the fall spread from one man’s rebellion into Cain’s violence against Abel; chapter 5 closes with Adam’s genealogy, where the refrain “…and he died” recurs again and again — the judgment God pronounced in chapter 3, now fulfilled generation after generation.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 3: The serpent tempts the woman to doubt God’s word; the two eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and immediately feel guilt and shame, blaming one another. God judges the serpent, the woman, the man, and the ground — and in his words to the serpent gives the first announcement of redemption: “he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel” (Gen. 3:15) — the first redemptive promise in Scripture. At the chapter’s close, “the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them” (Gen. 3:21) — God himself, using the skin of an animal, covers a nakedness and shame that man could not cover on his own.
  • Chapter 4: Cain kills Abel — sin spreads from one man’s rebellion into bloody violence. Even so, “the LORD put a mark on Cain, lest any who found him should attack him” (Gen. 4:15) — God’s mercy still reaches the one who has rebelled against him.
  • Chapter 5: Adam’s genealogy counts on and on, the refrain “…and he died” recurring as the fulfillment of the judgment pronounced in chapter 3 — except for Enoch, the one exception: “Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him” (Gen. 5:24), leaving a thread of hope in a genealogy otherwise full of death.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

What God says to the serpent in Genesis 3:15 is the first link in the whole Bible’s promise-and-fulfillment storyline: the offspring of the woman will finally crush the serpent’s head, but the blow will cost him his own heel — foreshadowing a road that runs through suffering to final victory, ultimately fulfilled in Christ, who was crucified yet through death destroyed the one who held the power of death. The garments of skin God made for Adam and Eve likewise foreshadow, early on, a truth still to come: man cannot cover his own sin; only God himself, at his own cost, through the shedding of blood, can provide covering for humanity.

Response

If, like Adam and Eve, you instinctively reach for fig leaves — your own excuses, cover-ups, performance — to hide your shame, you can stop today: Christ has already shed his blood on the cross to provide the covering you could never make for yourself. You don’t need your own strategies to deal with guilt; you need only receive the covering he has already accomplished for you, just as Adam and Eve received the garments God made.

title: 洪水的审判
verse: 创世记九章十二节至十三节
content:
书卷背景

三至五章记载罪如何从伊甸园里的悖逆，一路蔓延到该隐的杀机、以至遍满全地；六至九章要记载神对这普遍败坏所采取的审判——洪水，以及审判之后神向挪亚所立、要托住整个受造界直到末了的第一个正式的「约」。

在全书结构中的位置

六、七章记载败坏的顶点与神的宣判：「世界在神面前败坏，地上满了强暴」（创6:11），神吩咐挪亚造方舟，惟独挪亚一家和方舟里的活物藉着水得以存活；八章记载水退、挪亚出方舟献祭；九章记载神与挪亚、以及地上一切有血肉之物立约，应许不再用洪水毁灭全地，并以彩虹为证。

主题与神学重点
  • 六至七章：神观看世界败坏，定意用洪水施行审判，吩咐挪亚造方舟，将洁净与不洁净的活物各带若干进入方舟；「挪亚就这样行。凡神所吩咐的，他都照样行了」（创6:22）——在一个整体悖逆的世代中，惟独他的信心与顺服使他和家人蒙保全。
  • 八章：水势渐消，挪亚出方舟，第一件事是筑坛献祭；耶和华闻那馨香之气，心里说：「我不再因人的缘故咒诅地」（创8:21）——即便人心的败坏并未因洪水而改变，神却定意施怜悯、不再如此审判全地。
  • 九章：神与挪亚和地上各样活物立约，「我与你们并你们这里的各样活物所立的永约是有记号的。我把虹放在云彩中，这就可作我与地立约的记号了」（创9:12-13）；本章末了却也记载挪亚醉酒、含窥探父亲赤身的插曲，提醒读者：审判洗净了地，却没有洗净人心里的罪性。
救赎历史脉络

洪水是神对全地悖逆最彻底的一次审判，却也藉着方舟保全了一条通过审判、进入更新世界的道路——这预表了后来那位使凡投靠祂的人得以脱离神公义烈怒的基督：祂亲自担当了那本该临到我们的审判洪流，使信靠祂的人如同挪亚一家，安然从水的审判中被带到新造的另一边。而神向挪亚所立的约，是圣经中第一个以「记号」为凭据、单方面出于神的信实、不倚靠人的表现而持守的约，预告了后来那更美之约同样的性质——凡神应许的，必因祂自己的信实成就，不在乎人是否配得。

回应

因为基督已经亲自承受了你我本该承受的那场审判的烈怒，你今天不必惧怕将来还有一场洪水等着你——挪亚一家藉着方舟安然渡过审判进入新世界，你也照样藉着基督，已经被带到审判的那一边；你所能做的，不是像挪亚那样凭自己的义行赢得逃生，而是单单藏身在神已经为你预备好的那条出路里。
content_en:
Book Background

Chapters 3–5 recorded how sin spread from rebellion in Eden all the way to Cain’s murderous intent, and finally filled the whole earth. Chapters 6–9 record the judgment God brought on this universal corruption — the flood — and, after the judgment, the first formal covenant God made, with Noah, to sustain the whole created order until the end.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 6–7 record corruption at its peak and God’s sentence: “the earth was corrupt in God’s sight, and the earth was filled with violence” (Gen. 6:11); God commands Noah to build an ark, and only Noah’s household and the creatures in the ark survive the waters. Chapter 8 records the waters receding and Noah leaving the ark to offer sacrifice. Chapter 9 records God’s covenant with Noah and every living creature, promising never again to destroy the whole earth by flood, with the rainbow as the sign.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapters 6–7: God sees the world’s corruption and determines to judge it by flood; he commands Noah to build an ark and bring in clean and unclean creatures alike. “Noah did this; he did all that God commanded him” (Gen. 6:22) — in a generation of total rebellion, his faith and obedience alone preserve him and his family.
  • Chapter 8: As the waters recede, Noah leaves the ark, and his first act is to build an altar and offer sacrifice. The LORD smells the pleasing aroma and says in his heart, “I will never again curse the ground because of man” (Gen. 8:21) — even though the human heart’s corruption was not changed by the flood, God determines to show mercy and never again judge the whole earth this way.
  • Chapter 9: God makes a covenant with Noah and every living creature: “This is the sign of the covenant that I make between me and you and every living creature… I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant” (Gen. 9:12–13). Yet the chapter closes with the episode of Noah’s drunkenness and Ham’s disrespect toward his father — a reminder that judgment washed the earth, but it did not wash away sin from the human heart.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

The flood was God’s most thorough judgment on the rebellion of the whole earth — yet through the ark he also preserved a way through judgment into a renewed world. This foreshadows Christ, who later delivers everyone who takes refuge in him from God’s righteous wrath: he himself bore the flood of judgment that should have fallen on us, so that those who trust in him, like Noah’s family, are carried safely through the waters of judgment to the other side, into the new creation. And the covenant God made with Noah — the first in Scripture sealed by a “sign,” resting solely on God’s own faithfulness rather than on human performance — foretells the same character of the greater covenant to come: whatever God has promised will be fulfilled because of his own faithfulness, not because anyone deserves it.

Response

Because Christ has already borne, in your place, the full fury of the judgment you and I deserved, you don’t need to fear that another flood still awaits you. Noah’s family passed safely through judgment into a new world by means of the ark; you too have already been carried through judgment by Christ. What you’re called to do is not, like Noah, earn your escape by your own righteousness, but simply to take shelter in the way of escape God has already prepared for you.

title: 巴别塔与分散
title_en: The Tower of Babel and the Scattering
verse: 创世记十一章九节
content:
书卷背景

十、十一章是「原史」（一至十一章）的最后一段：创造、堕落、该隐的暴力、洪水的审判之后，人类再一次试图联合起来、为自己立名，神再一次介入审判、使人分散。这两章过去后，十二章亚伯兰蒙召，全书焦点从普世历史收窄到一个人、一个家庭。

在全书结构中的位置

十章先以「列国表」的形式，正面记载挪亚三个儿子的后裔如何分散、建立邦国：「这些都是挪亚三个儿子的宗族，各随他们的支派立国」（创10:32）；十一章则倒叙这分散背后的原因——巴别塔事件；本章末了以闪的家谱一路数到他拉、亚伯兰、拿鹤、哈兰，为下一章埋下伏笔。一至十一章的普世历史，到此正式收束；从十二章起，神拯救万国的计划，要藉着一个人来推进。

主题与神学重点
  • 十章：挪亚的三个儿子闪、含、雅弗的后裔各随宗族、方言分散建国，遍布全地，正应验了神起初的命定：「生养众多，遍满地面」（创1:28）。
  • 十一章：人类却不甘心分散，联合起来说：「来吧！我们要建造一座城和一座塔，塔顶通天，为要传扬我们的名」（创11:4）——这是要靠自己的成就立名，抵挡神分散全地的旨意；神却介入变乱他们的口音，「耶和华在那里变乱天下人的言语，使众人分散在全地上，所以那城名叫巴别」（创11:9）；本章末了却又记下他拉家谱、直到亚伯兰，悄悄埋下下一步救赎工作的种子。
救赎历史脉络

巴别是人类联合起来、想靠自己成就为自己立名的顶点，神使他们的言语纷乱、彼此分散，说明单凭人的团结与技术，永远无法解决罪所造成的破碎与悖逆。然而就在这一章的结尾，神并没有放弃万国：他悄悄引出了亚伯兰的家谱——从下一章起，神要藉着一个蒙召的人，成就一个远比巴别塔更伟大的应许：「地上的万族都要因你得福」（创12:3）。巴别使万族分散，神却应许要藉一个后裔使万族因祂重新联合、蒙福——这应许最终要在基督里得着成就。

回应

你若也曾试着靠自己的成就、名声，或与人联合来获得安全感和身份——就像巴别的人「要传扬我们的名」——今天可以放下这种努力：因为基督已经使凡属祂的人，无论出身何方、说什么语言，都藉着祂真实合一、被神称为儿女；你不需要为自己造一座通天的塔来证明自己存在的价值，因为神已经在基督里，把祂儿子的名分白白赐给了你。
content_en:
Book Background

Chapters 10 and 11 are the final section of the “primeval history” (chapters 1–11): after creation, the fall, Cain’s violence, and the judgment of the flood, humanity once again tries to unite and make a name for itself, and God once again intervenes in judgment, scattering the people. After these two chapters, Abram is called in chapter 12, and the book’s focus narrows from world history to one man, one family.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapter 10, the “Table of Nations,” first records, in a positive light, how the descendants of Noah’s three sons scattered and established nations: “These are the clans of the sons of Noah… and from these the nations spread abroad on the earth” (Gen. 10:32). Chapter 11 then goes back to tell the reason behind that scattering — the incident at Babel. The chapter closes by tracing Shem’s line down through Terah, Abram, Nahor, and Haran, setting up the next chapter. With this, the world history of chapters 1–11 formally concludes; from chapter 12 on, God’s plan to save the nations moves forward through one man.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 10: The descendants of Noah’s three sons — Shem, Ham, and Japheth — scatter and establish nations, each according to clan and language, spreading across the whole earth, fulfilling God’s original mandate: “be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28).
  • Chapter 11: Humanity, unwilling to be scattered, unites and says, “Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves” (Gen. 11:4) — seeking to make a name through their own achievement, resisting God’s purpose to fill and scatter across the earth. God intervenes and confuses their language: “the LORD confused the language of all the earth, and from there the LORD dispersed them over the face of all the earth… therefore its name was called Babel” (Gen. 11:9). Yet the chapter closes by quietly recording Terah’s genealogy down to Abram — the seed of the next stage of redemption already being planted.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

Babel is the high point of humanity uniting to achieve a name for itself by its own strength; God confuses their language and scatters them, showing that human unity and technology alone can never heal the brokenness and rebellion sin has caused. Yet at the very end of this chapter, God does not abandon the nations: he quietly introduces Abram’s genealogy — from the next chapter on, God will, through one called man, bring about a promise far greater than the tower of Babel: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 12:3). Babel scattered the nations; God promises that through one offspring the nations will be reunited and blessed — a promise ultimately fulfilled in Christ.

Response

If you too have tried to find security and identity through your own achievements, reputation, or uniting with others — like the people of Babel, wanting “to make a name for ourselves” — you can lay that effort down today: Christ has already made everyone who belongs to him, whatever their origin or language, truly one, and called children of God. You don’t need to build a tower reaching to heaven to prove your worth, because God has already, in Christ, freely given you the standing of his own Son.

title: 亚伯兰蒙召与神的应许
title_en: The Call of Abram and God's Promise
verse: 创世记十三章十四节至十五节
content:
书卷背景

一至十一章记载了神与全人类、全地的关系——创造、堕落、洪水、巴别塔；从十二章起，全书笔锋一转，收窄到一个人、一个家庭：神呼召亚伯兰，要藉着他的后裔使地上万族得福。十二至五十章的「族长故事」由此展开，这也是圣经此后应许—成就这条主线真正的起点。

在全书结构中的位置

十二章记载神呼召亚伯兰离开本地本族父家，赐下应许，随即插入一段亚伯兰下埃及、因惧怕说谎的失败插曲；十三章记载亚伯兰与侄儿罗得因财物增多而分地，亚伯兰谦让罗得先选，神在罗得离开后再次向他重申并扩大应许；十四章记载亚伯兰出兵救回被掳的罗得，凯旋归来时遇见撒冷王麦基洗德，是全书第一次出现「君王兼祭司」这个特殊身分的人物。

主题与神学重点
  • 十二章：耶和华对亚伯兰说：「你要离开本地、本族、父家，往我所要指示你的地去」（创12:1），又应许「我必叫你成为大国。我必赐福给你，叫你的名为大；你也要叫别人得福」（创12:2），并且「地上的万族都要因你得福」（创12:3）；然而亚伯兰随即下埃及，因怕死而谎称撒莱是自己的妹子，显明这蒙召之人当下的信心仍然软弱、有瑕疵。
  • 十三章：亚伯兰与罗得因财物增多、地容不下而分离，亚伯兰主动谦让、让罗得先选；罗得离开后，耶和华对亚伯兰说：「你举目向东西南北观看；凡你所看见的一切地，我都要赐给你和你的后裔，直到永远」（创13:14-15），应许在亚伯兰谦让、看似吃亏之后被重申、被扩大。
  • 十四章：四王攻打五王，罗得被掳，亚伯兰率家中精练壮丁追赶、救回罗得；凯旋归来，撒冷王麦基洗德带着饼和酒出来迎接，「他是至高神的祭司」（创14:18），为亚伯兰祝福，「亚伯兰就把所得的拿出十分之一来，给麦基洗德」（创14:20）。
救赎历史脉络

神对亚伯兰的应许——地、后裔，以及「地上的万族都要因你得福」——是整本圣经应许—成就这条主线真正的枢纽：此后律法、先知，以至新约，都是在追问这应许如何、藉着谁得以成就。麦基洗德这位既是君王又是祭司、又忽然出现又没有交代来历的人物，也在此预先埋下一个伏笔，指向那位真正、永远的君王兼大祭司。亚伯兰所领受的这一切应许，最终要藉着他的一个后裔——而不是靠着他自己或他众多的子孙——才得以完全成就。

回应

亚伯兰当年还看不到应许如何成就，只能凭着神的话起身、离开熟悉的一切；你今天所站的位置比他更清楚：因为基督已经是那使地上万族得福的「亚伯兰的后裔」，神向亚伯兰所应许的福，已经藉着祂临到你身上——你不需要像亚伯兰下埃及时那样，靠自己的手段确保安全，因为那使万族得福的应许，早已经在基督里稳稳地属于你了。
content_en:
Book Background

Chapters 1–11 recorded God’s dealings with all humanity and the whole earth — creation, the fall, the flood, Babel. From chapter 12 on, the book’s focus narrows to one man, one family: God calls Abram, promising that through his offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed. This launches the “patriarchal narratives” of chapters 12–50 — and this is the true starting point of Scripture’s promise-and-fulfillment storyline.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapter 12 records God calling Abram out of his land, his kindred, and his father’s house, giving him a promise — immediately followed by the episode of Abram going down to Egypt and lying out of fear. Chapter 13 records Abram and his nephew Lot separating because their possessions had grown too great for the land to support; Abram graciously lets Lot choose first, and after Lot leaves, God reaffirms and expands the promise to Abram. Chapter 14 records Abram going to war to rescue the captured Lot, and on his triumphant return meeting Melchizedek, king of Salem — the first appearance in the book of that singular figure, a king who is also a priest.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 12: The LORD says to Abram, “Go from your country and your kindred and your father’s house to the land that I will show you” (Gen. 12:1), and promises, “I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing” (Gen. 12:2), and “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 12:3). Yet Abram immediately goes down to Egypt and, for fear of death, lies that Sarai is his sister — showing that this called man’s faith, even now, is still weak and flawed.
  • Chapter 13: Abram and Lot separate because their possessions have grown too great for the land to support, and Abram graciously lets Lot choose first. After Lot leaves, the LORD says to Abram, “Lift up your eyes and look… for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever” (Gen. 13:14–15) — the promise reaffirmed and expanded right after Abram’s act of humility, which had seemed like a loss.
  • Chapter 14: Four kings attack five, Lot is captured, and Abram leads his trained men to pursue and rescue him. On his triumphant return, Melchizedek, king of Salem, comes out with bread and wine — “he was priest of God Most High” (Gen. 14:18) — and blesses Abram, and “Abram gave him a tenth of everything” (Gen. 14:20).
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

God’s promise to Abram — land, offspring, and “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” — is the true hinge of Scripture’s whole promise-and-fulfillment storyline: the Law, the Prophets, and finally the New Testament are all asking how, and through whom, this promise will be fulfilled. Melchizedek, this figure who is both king and priest, appearing suddenly with no account given of his origin, also plants a seed here pointing ahead to the one true, eternal king and great high priest. Everything Abram received in this promise would ultimately be fulfilled through one of his offspring — not through Abram himself, nor through the sheer number of his descendants.

Response

Abram, in his day, could not yet see how the promise would be fulfilled; all he could do was rise and go at God’s word, leaving behind everything familiar. Today you stand in a clearer place than he did: Christ is already that “offspring of Abram” who blesses all the families of the earth, and the blessing promised to Abram has already come to you through him. You don’t need, as Abram did going down to Egypt, to secure your own safety by your own devices — the promise that blesses all nations already belongs to you securely in Christ.

title: 神与亚伯兰立约
title_en: God Makes a Covenant with Abram
verse: 创世记十五章六节
content:
书卷背景

十二至十四章记载亚伯兰蒙召、南北迁徙，以及从麦基洗德手中领受祝福；十五至十七章要记载的，是神如何用正式的立约仪式和记号，把此前口头的应许，坐实为一个不可推翻的约。

在全书结构中的位置

十五章神以异象向亚伯兰重申应许，并且藉着古代近东立约的仪式（把祭牲劈开、从中经过）向他确认这约的确实；十六章却记载亚伯兰听从撒莱的主意、藉夏甲生以实玛利——这是人想靠自己的方法、抢先促成神应许的失败尝试；十七章神再次向亚伯兰显现，将他改名为「亚伯拉罕」，以割礼作立约的记号，并且明确指明承受应许的，将是撒拉所生的儿子。

主题与神学重点
  • 十五章：神领亚伯兰到外边，说「你的后裔将要如此」（创15:5），指着满天星宿应许他后裔的数目；「亚伯兰信耶和华，耶和华就以此为他的义」（创15:6）——他当时既没有儿子、也没有任何律法可守，单单因为相信神的应许，就被神算为义人；随后神以立约的仪式，向他保证这应许的确实不移。
  • 十六章：撒莱因不孕，将使女夏甲给亚伯兰为妾，「亚伯兰听从了撒莱的话」（创16:2）——蒙应许的人，仍然会想靠人的血气、抢在神的时间之前促成应许，其后果是家庭的破裂与长期的纷争。
  • 十七章：神再次向九十九岁的亚伯兰显现，「你的名不再叫亚伯兰，要叫亚伯拉罕，因为我已立你作多国的父」（创17:5），又吩咐「你们都要受割礼，这是我与你们立约的证据」（创17:11）作为约的记号；并且清楚宣告：「你妻子撒拉要给你生一个儿子，你要给他起名叫以撒」（创17:19）——承受应许的，不是亚伯兰用自己的方法所得的以实玛利，而是神照祂自己应许所赐的以撒。
救赎历史脉络

创十五章六节，是旧约中因信称义教义最清楚的根基经文：亚伯兰称义，不是因着他的行为——他当时还没有任何律法可守，甚至还没有受割礼——而单单因着他相信神所应许的话。使徒保罗后来在罗马书和加拉太书都直接引用这节经文，作为「因信称义」这条福音真理最原始、最权威的旧约根据：「亚伯拉罕信神，这就算为他的义」（罗4:3）；「正如亚伯拉罕信神，这就算为他的义」（加3:6）。十六章亚伯兰靠着夏甲抢先促成应许的失败，恰恰反衬出十五章那节经文的重量：神算人为义，从来不是因为人靠自己的方法把应许做成了，而单单是因着信靠那位赐应许、也必亲自成就应许的神。这也正是后来在基督里因信称义的福音——神以耶稣基督在十字架上所成就的义，白白算给凡相信的人，正如祂当年算给亚伯兰一样。

回应

因为基督已经在十字架上成就了亚伯兰当年所信、却还未曾亲眼看见应验的那义，所以你今天不需要像亚伯兰在十六章那样，想靠自己的方法、自己的时间表去催逼或证明神的应许；你所需要的，不过是像亚伯兰在十五章那样，单单相信那已经藉着基督完全成就的应许——神就照样算你为义。
content_en:
Book Background

Chapters 12–14 recorded Abram’s call, his journeys, and the blessing he received from Melchizedek. Chapters 15–17 record how God takes the promise given so far only by word, and makes it an unbreakable covenant through a formal covenant ceremony and sign.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

In chapter 15, God reaffirms the promise to Abram in a vision, and confirms its certainty through an ancient Near Eastern covenant ceremony (cutting animals in half and passing between the pieces). Chapter 16 records Abram following Sarai’s plan and fathering Ishmael through Hagar — a failed attempt to fulfill God’s promise by human means, ahead of God’s own timing. Chapter 17 records God appearing to Abram again, renaming him “Abraham,” giving circumcision as the sign of the covenant, and clearly specifying that the one who will inherit the promise is the son to be born of Sarah.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 15: God brings Abram outside and says, “So shall your offspring be” (Gen. 15:5), pointing to the stars to promise the number of his descendants. “Abram believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15:6) — at a time when he had no son and no law to keep, simply by believing God’s promise, he was counted righteous. God then confirms the certainty of this promise through the covenant ceremony.
  • Chapter 16: Because Sarai is childless, she gives her servant Hagar to Abram as a wife. “Abram listened to the voice of Sarai” (Gen. 16:2) — even a man who has received the promise can still try to force it into being ahead of God’s timing by human effort, and the result is family breakdown and lasting strife.
  • Chapter 17: God appears again to the ninety-nine-year-old Abram: “No longer shall your name be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham, for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations” (Gen. 17:5), and commands, “you shall be circumcised… it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you” (Gen. 17:11) as the sign of the covenant. He clearly declares, “Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac” (Gen. 17:19) — the one who will inherit the promise is not Ishmael, whom Abram obtained by his own methods, but Isaac, whom God gives according to his own promise.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

Genesis 15:6 is the clearest foundational text in the Old Testament for the doctrine of justification by faith: Abram is counted righteous not by works — at that point he had no law to keep, and had not even been circumcised — but solely because he believed what God had promised. The apostle Paul later quotes this verse directly in both Romans and Galatians as the earliest and most authoritative Old Testament basis for the gospel truth of justification by faith: “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (Rom. 4:3); “just as Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (Gal. 3:6). Abram’s failed attempt in chapter 16 to force the promise into being through Hagar only throws into relief the weight of that verse in chapter 15: God counts a person righteous never because they have brought the promise about by their own methods, but solely because they trust the God who gives the promise and will himself bring it to pass. This is exactly the gospel of justification by faith later fulfilled in Christ — God freely counts the righteousness Jesus Christ accomplished on the cross to everyone who believes, just as he counted it to Abram.

Response

Because Christ has already accomplished on the cross the righteousness Abram believed for but had not yet seen fulfilled, you don’t need, as Abram did in chapter 16, to force or prove God’s promise by your own methods and timetable. All you need is what Abram did in chapter 15 — simply believe the promise already fully accomplished through Christ — and God will count you righteous just the same.

title: 安息日：从创造到应许的一周
title_en: Sabbath: A Week from Creation to Promise
content:
今天是安息日——不需要新的经文进度，只是停下来，回顾过去一周，也在神里面稍作安歇。

这一周我们从创世记一章读到十七章：神六日创造天地（一至二章），人堕落又蒙应许（三至五章），洪水审判又立约（六至九章），巴别塔的悖逆与分散（十至十一章），亚伯兰的蒙召与信心之旅（十二至十七章）。短短几日，我们已经看见神怎样在悖逆的世界里，一次又一次地施行审判，又一次又一次地主动立约、施恩、寻找可以与祂同行的人。

有意思的是，「安息」本身就出现在这一周的经文里：神造物的工已经完毕，「就在第七日歇了他一切的工，安息了」（创2:2-3）。今天的安息日，正是效法这最初的样式——不是因为我们把事情都做完了才配歇息，而是照着神起初为我们所定的节奏，停下来，记念祂。

建议你今天：①回顾这一周读过的经文，挑一段你印象最深的重读一遍；②为下一周的读经计划向神祷告，求祂帮助你持续这个习惯；③什么都不做，只是安静，记念神是谁。

应用：今天刻意留一段时间，不查手机、不做待办事项，单单安静在神面前——像创世记二章所记的那样，操练「从工作中安息」。
content_en:
Today is a Sabbath day — no new reading to cover, just a pause to look back over the past week, and to rest a while in God.

This week we read from Genesis 1 through 17: God creating heaven and earth in six days (chapters 1–2), humanity falling and yet promised hope (chapters 3–5), the flood’s judgment and covenant (chapters 6–9), Babel’s rebellion and scattering (chapters 10–11), and Abram’s call and journey of faith (chapters 12–17). In just a few days, we’ve already seen God, again and again, bring judgment on a rebellious world — and again and again take the initiative to make covenant, show grace, and seek out those who would walk with him.

Interestingly, “rest” itself appears within this week’s reading: God’s work of creation was finished, and “on the seventh day God finished his work… and he rested” (Gen. 2:2–3). Today’s Sabbath follows that original pattern — not resting because we’ve finished everything we needed to do, but stopping, according to the rhythm God set for us from the beginning, to remember him.

Today, consider: (1) Look back over this week’s reading and reread the passage that struck you most. (2) Pray for God’s help to keep this habit of reading through the coming week. (3) Do nothing at all — just be still, and remember who God is.

Application: Deliberately set aside time today — no phone, no to-do list — simply to be still before God, practicing, as in Genesis 2, “resting from work.”

title: 神审判所多玛、蛾摩拉
verse: 创世记十八章廿五节
content:
书卷背景

神已应许亚伯拉罕后裔与土地（创十二至十七章），十八至廿章记载这应许如何在两个极端的处境中显明：一边是所多玛的败坏遭审判，一边是外邦君王亚比米勒被神保守，不至因无知而犯大罪。

在全书结构中的位置

十八至廿章夹在以撒出生的应许（十七、十八章）与以撒真正诞生（廿一章）之间，功能是延展悬念——应许的儿子还未出生，神却已在向世界显明祂审判的公义与拣选的恩典，为「应许之子」以撒的诞生预备背景。

主题与神学重点
  • 十八章：耶和华亲自向亚伯拉罕显现，重申撒拉必生子的应许，撒拉却心里暗笑不信；随后耶和华向亚伯拉罕透露要审判所多玛、蛾摩拉的罪恶，亚伯拉罕为义人代求，六次逼近神的怜悯，发出全章的神学核心提问：「审判全地的主岂不行公义吗」（创18:25）。
  • 十九章：两位天使进入所多玛，城中人企图凌辱客旅，暴露这城彻底的败坏；神施行审判，将硫磺与火从天上降下，唯独因亚伯拉罕的缘故打发罗得脱离倾覆——「他记念亚伯拉罕」（创19:29）；罗得的妻子因回头眷恋而变为盐柱，罗得两个女儿其后与父亲乱伦，生出摩押、亚扪二族的始祖，审判之后，罪的败坏仍在余生的家庭中延续。
  • 廿章：亚伯拉罕在基拉耳又一次谎称撒拉是他妹子，几乎使亚比米勒犯下大罪；神在梦中警诫亚比米勒：「你是个死人哪」（创20:3），亚比米勒却诚恳分诉：「我做这事是心正手洁的」（创20:5）；神后来医好了亚比米勒家中的妇人——这段插曲提醒读者，蒙拣选的族长并不比外邦君王更良善，应许的存续从头到尾都靠神自己的信实，而非亚伯拉罕的德行。
救赎历史脉络

亚伯拉罕的提问——审判全地的主岂不行公义吗——在这段经文里没有得着完全的答案：所多玛被毁，罗得却单单因亚伯拉罕代求而蒙拯救，公义与怜悯看似只能二选一。这问题要到十字架才得着最终解答：神在基督里施行审判的公义，又亲自担当了这审判，使凡因信基督的人都能蒙拯救——公义与怜悯，在各各他同时成就，没有牺牲任何一边。

回应

你或许也曾像罗得一样，明知危险却迟延离开罪中之地；又或许像亚比米勒一样，在无知中几乎陷入大罪。这段经文不是要你先证明自己配得搭救——罗得的存活单单出于神「记念亚伯拉罕」（创19:29），而你的存活，也单单出于神记念那位在十字架上真正担当了审判的中保基督。因祂已亲身承受了那烈火本该临到你的份，你此刻可以坦然无惧地来到审判全地的主面前。
content_en:
Book Background

God has already promised Abraham offspring and land (Genesis 12–17); chapters 18–20 show how that promise plays out in two extreme situations: on one side, Sodom’s corruption meets judgment; on the other, a Gentile king, Abimelech, is kept by God from unknowingly committing a great sin.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 18–20 sit between the promise of Isaac’s birth (chapters 17–18) and Isaac’s actual birth (chapter 21), and their function is to extend the suspense — the promised son is not yet born, yet God is already showing the world both the justice of his judgment and the grace of his election, preparing the backdrop for the birth of Isaac, the “child of promise.”

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 18: The LORD himself appears to Abraham and reaffirms the promise that Sarah will bear a son; Sarah laughs to herself in disbelief. The LORD then reveals to Abraham that he is about to judge the sin of Sodom and Gomorrah; Abraham intercedes for the righteous, pressing in on God’s mercy six times, and voices the theological question at the heart of the chapter: “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Gen. 18:25).
  • Chapter 19: Two angels enter Sodom, and the men of the city try to assault them — exposing the city’s utter corruption. God executes judgment, raining sulfur and fire from heaven, and sends Lot to safety solely for Abraham’s sake — “God remembered Abraham” (Gen. 19:29). Lot’s wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt; his two daughters later commit incest with him, giving rise to the ancestors of Moab and Ammon — even after judgment, sin’s corruption continues in the family that survived.
  • Chapter 20: Abraham again lies that Sarah is his sister, this time in Gerar, nearly causing Abimelech to commit a grave sin. God warns Abimelech in a dream: “you are a dead man” (Gen. 20:3); Abimelech earnestly protests, “In the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands I have done this” (Gen. 20:5). God then heals the women of Abimelech’s household — a reminder that the chosen patriarch is no more virtuous than a Gentile king, and that the survival of the promise rests entirely on God’s own faithfulness, not on Abraham’s character.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

Abraham’s question — shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just — is not fully answered in this passage: Sodom is destroyed, and Lot is saved solely because Abraham interceded; justice and mercy seem to be an either/or choice. That question finds its final answer only at the cross: God, in Christ, executes the justice of judgment, and himself bears that very judgment, so that everyone who believes in Christ can be saved — justice and mercy both fully accomplished at Calvary, neither sacrificed for the other.

Response

You may, like Lot, have known the danger and yet lingered in a place of sin; or, like Abimelech, come close to committing a grave sin without realizing it. This passage does not ask you to first prove yourself worthy of rescue — Lot survived solely because God “remembered Abraham” (Gen. 19:29), and your survival, too, rests solely on God remembering Christ, the true mediator who actually bore judgment on the cross. Because he has already personally endured the fire that should have fallen on you, you can now come before the Judge of all the earth without fear.

title: 顺服之子──以撒
verse: 创世记廿二章十四节
content:
书卷背景

神审判所多玛之余仍信实持守应许（十八至廿章）；廿一至廿四章要记载的，正是这应许如何具体成就在「以撒」这个孩子身上——从他出生、几乎被献为祭、到迎娶利百加，每一步都印证神所应许的话必然成就。

在全书结构中的位置

这四章构成一个完整的「以撒故事」单元：廿一章以撒出生、应验应许；廿二章神却吩咐亚伯拉罕将这应许之子献为燔祭，把「凭信心持守应许」的主题推向极致的试验；廿三、廿四章则处理产业（坟地）与后裔（婚娶）两件事，为亚伯拉罕一生的应许画上句点，也为以撒一系的延续铺路。

主题与神学重点
  • 廿一章：撒拉照神所说的日期为亚伯拉罕生了以撒；因以实玛利戏笑，夏甲母子被打发离开，神却应许也必使以实玛利的后裔成立一国；亚伯拉罕又与亚比米勒在别是巴立约，为神所赐的应许之地立下见证。
  • 廿二章：神吩咐亚伯拉罕将「你所爱的独生子」献为燔祭；亚伯拉罕对以撒说：「神必自己预备作燔祭的羊羔」（创22:8），随后果然见有一只公羊「两角扣在稠密的小树中」（创22:13），代替以撒被献上；亚伯拉罕就给那地方起名叫「耶和华以勒」，「直到今日人还说：在耶和华的山上必有预备」（创22:14）。
  • 廿三章：撒拉去世，亚伯拉罕在迦南地向赫人买下麦比拉洞作坟地——这是亚伯拉罕一生寄居应许之地、却唯一真正拥有的产业，是他存留盼望的具体记号。
  • 廿四章：亚伯拉罕差遣老仆人回本族为以撒求娶利百加，仆人凭祷告蒙神引导，恰好遇见利百加；以撒迎娶利百加，「以撒自从他母亲不在了，这才得了安慰」（创24:67）。
救赎历史脉络

廿二章是旧约里最清晰预表基督的段落之一：父亲带着「所爱的独生子」走上献祭之路，儿子背负着燔祭的柴，三日的路程、山上的献祭，都指向各各他。但要留意这预表并非逐点吻合的寓言——以撒最终活了下来，真正被杀的是那只两角扣在小树中的公羊，代替以撒承受了刀。这正是「代替性预备」的模式：神不是要人的儿子偿命，而是神自己预备了替代的祭牲。这预表要等到神真正将祂的独生爱子耶稣基督，献上作我们的代替，才得着完全的应验。

回应

亚伯拉罕对以撒说「神必自己预备」（创22:8）的时候，他还不知道那只公羊在哪里；但神确实预备了。今天，你也不必自己去寻找那足以赎罪的祭物——神已经在各各他自己预备了，用祂儿子的死代替你本该承受的审判。你无需靠恳求或善行去换取这预备，只需像以撒一样，安静地信靠那位已经预备好一切的父。
content_en:
Book Background

Even after judging Sodom, God remains faithful to his promise (chapters 18–20); chapters 21–24 record exactly how that promise is fulfilled in concrete form in the child Isaac — from his birth, to his near-sacrifice, to his marriage to Rebekah — each step confirming that what God has promised will surely come to pass.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

These four chapters form one complete “Isaac narrative”: chapter 21, Isaac is born, fulfilling the promise; chapter 22, God commands Abraham to offer up this very child of promise as a burnt offering, pushing the theme of “holding fast to the promise by faith” to its most extreme test; chapters 23–24 then deal with inheritance (a burial site) and offspring (a marriage), bringing Abraham’s lifelong story of promise to its close and paving the way for Isaac’s line to continue.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 21: Sarah bears Isaac to Abraham at the very time God had said; because Ishmael mocks him, Hagar and her son are sent away, though God promises to make a nation of Ishmael’s descendants too. Abraham also makes a covenant with Abimelech at Beersheba, marking his claim to the land God had promised.
  • Chapter 22: God commands Abraham to offer up “your son, your only son, whom you love” as a burnt offering. Abraham tells Isaac, “God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering” (Gen. 22:8), and indeed a ram appears, “caught in a thicket by his horns” (Gen. 22:13), offered up in Isaac’s place. Abraham names that place “The LORD Will Provide” — “as it is said to this day, ‘On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided’” (Gen. 22:14).
  • Chapter 23: Sarah dies, and Abraham buys the cave of Machpelah from the Hittites as a burial site — the only piece of the promised land Abraham ever actually owned in his lifetime as a sojourner, a concrete token of the hope he held onto.
  • Chapter 24: Abraham sends his elder servant back to his own people to find a wife for Isaac. Guided by God in answer to prayer, the servant meets Rebekah at just the right moment; Isaac marries her, and “Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death” (Gen. 24:67).
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

Chapter 22 is one of the clearest foreshadowings of Christ in the Old Testament: a father takes his “only son, whom he loves” on the road to sacrifice; the son carries the wood for his own burnt offering; a three-day journey, an offering on a mountain — all pointing toward Calvary. But note that this foreshadowing is not a point-by-point allegory — Isaac, in the end, lives; the one actually put to death is the ram caught by its horns in the thicket, dying in Isaac’s place. This is the pattern of “substitutionary provision”: God does not demand the death of a human son, but himself provides a substitute sacrifice. This foreshadowing finds its full and final fulfillment only when God truly offers up his own only, beloved Son, Jesus Christ, as our substitute.

Response

When Abraham told Isaac, “God will provide for himself” (Gen. 22:8), he did not yet know where the ram was. But God did provide. Today, you don’t need to go searching for a sacrifice sufficient to atone for sin either — God has already provided it at Calvary, giving his own Son’s death in place of the judgment you deserved. You don’t need to earn this provision through pleading or good works; you need only, like Isaac, quietly trust the Father who has already prepared everything.

title: 以撒的家庭及信行
verse: 创世记廿六章廿四节
content:
书卷背景

亚伯拉罕死后，创世记的焦点从他转向以撒——但以撒的故事分量甚轻，多半是重演父亲的脚踪：同样的应许、同样的软弱、同样蒙神信实的保守。

在全书结构中的位置

廿五章交接了两代人（亚伯拉罕之死、以扫雅各之生），也埋下了日后雅各故事的种子——长子名分被轻看的事，要到廿七章才引爆；廿六章则是以撒一生唯一独立成篇的记载，功能是向读者证明：神向亚伯拉罕所立的约，如今原样传给了以撒。

主题与神学重点
  • 廿五章：亚伯拉罕安然离世，归到他列祖那里；以实玛利、以撒二人的后裔分别展开；利百加所怀的双子在腹中相争，神预告「将来大的要服事小的」（创25:23）；以扫因一时饥饿把长子名分卖给雅各，「轻看了他长子的名分」（创25:34）。
  • 廿六章：遇饥荒时，耶和华向以撒显现，重申赐福应许：「我必与你同在，赐福给你……我必坚定我向你父亚伯拉罕所起的誓」（创26:3）；以撒却像父亲一样，谎称利百加是他妹子；他又重新挖开父亲所挖、被非利士人塞住的水井，最终在别是巴筑坛求告耶和华的名，与亚比米勒立约和好。
救赎历史脉络

以撒的一生几乎没有一件「新」事——他所行的每一步，都是走在父亲已经走过的路上：同样的饥荒、同样的谎言、同样蒙神眷顾、同样与亚比米勒立约。这提醒我们，神的应许不是靠某一代人特别杰出的信心来维系，而是靠神自己反复的信实：「我必坚定我向你父亚伯拉罕所起的誓」（创26:3）。神的约本质上是单方面的恩典之约——祂拣选的应许一代一代地传下去，直到那真正配得应许、又完全顺服的后裔基督来到，成就一切。

回应

以撒的软弱与父亲如出一辙，神却仍然坚定祂的约，不因人的失信而废弃自己的应许。你今天的软弱、你重复犯下与从前一样的过犯，也不会使神向你的应许落空——因为那应许的根基，从来不是你的信实，而是基督已经用祂完全的顺服和舍命，为你稳稳地成就在十字架上。你只管来，支取祂已经为你成就的赐福，而不是先证明你比以撒更配得。
content_en:
Book Background

After Abraham’s death, Genesis shifts its focus from him to Isaac — but Isaac’s own story carries relatively little weight; much of it simply retraces his father’s footsteps: the same promise, the same weaknesses, the same faithful preservation by God.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapter 25 hands off the story between two generations (Abraham’s death, Esau’s and Jacob’s birth), and quietly plants the seed of the coming Jacob narrative — the matter of the birthright being despised will not detonate until chapter 27. Chapter 26 is the only independent narrative in Isaac’s whole life, and its function is to show the reader: the covenant God made with Abraham has now been handed down to Isaac unchanged.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 25: Abraham dies in peace and is gathered to his fathers; the descendants of Ishmael and Isaac each go their separate ways. The twins in Rebekah’s womb struggle together, and God foretells, “the older shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25:23). Esau, driven by momentary hunger, sells his birthright to Jacob — “thus Esau despised his birthright” (Gen. 25:34).
  • Chapter 26: During a famine, the LORD appears to Isaac and reaffirms the blessing: “I will be with you and will bless you… I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father” (Gen. 26:3). Yet Isaac, like his father, lies that Rebekah is his sister. He also reopens the wells his father had dug, which the Philistines had stopped up, and finally builds an altar at Beersheba, calling on the name of the LORD, and makes a peace covenant with Abimelech.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

There is hardly a single “new” event in Isaac’s life — every step he takes retraces a path his father has already walked: the same famine, the same lie, the same divine care, the same covenant with Abimelech. This reminds us that God’s promise is sustained not by any one generation’s exceptional faith, but by God’s own repeated faithfulness: “I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father” (Gen. 26:3). God’s covenant is, at its heart, a one-sided covenant of grace — the promise he has chosen is passed down generation after generation, until Christ, the offspring who truly deserves the promise and is perfectly obedient, comes to fulfill it all.

Response

Isaac’s weaknesses were the very image of his father’s, yet God still held firm to his covenant, never annulling his promise because of human unfaithfulness. Your weaknesses today, and your repeating the same failures as before, will not make God’s promise to you fall through either — because the foundation of that promise was never your faithfulness, but Christ, who has already, through his perfect obedience and his death, firmly accomplished it for you on the cross. You need only come and draw on the blessing he has already secured for you — not first prove yourself more deserving than Isaac.

title: 雅各离家出走
verse: 创世记廿八章十五节
content:
书卷背景

以扫已轻看了长子的名分（创25:34），这两章要记载的，是这名分与祝福如何藉着一场彻头彻尾的欺骗，正式转移到雅各身上——而神竟在这团家庭破碎之中，仍然向逃亡的雅各显现，坚定祂的应许。

在全书结构中的位置

廿七章把家庭的败坏推向顶点：以撒偏爱、利百加设计、雅各行诡诈、以扫怀恨，没有一个人是无辜的；廿八章却是全书一个重要的转折——雅各独自逃亡，离开了应许之地，神却在旷野中主动向他显现，第一次亲自向雅各重申对亚伯拉罕、以撒所立的约，标志着雅各的故事真正开始。

主题与神学重点
  • 廿七章：利百加与雅各合谋，用诡计骗取以撒本要给以扫的祝福；以扫发现后放声痛哭：「我父啊，求你也为我祝福」（创27:34），以撒却已无法收回；以扫怀恨在心，图谋杀雅各，雅各被迫逃往舅父拉班那里。
  • 廿八章：以撒差遣雅各前往巴旦亚兰，并将应许亚伯拉罕的福正式传给他；雅各在旷野露宿，梦见天梯，「有神的使者在梯子上，上去下来」（创28:12）；耶和华亲自站在梯子以上，重申赐地、赐后裔、普世蒙福的应许，又加上一句雅各此刻最需要听见的话：「我也与你同在……总不离弃你，直到我成全了向你所应许的」（创28:15）。
救赎历史脉络

雅各是靠诡诈夺得祝福的，他理当被神弃绝、任他独自面对以扫的杀机和旷野的孤单；但神却在他最不配得的时刻主动向他显现，把应许白白地加在他身上。天梯所连结的，是破碎的地与圣洁的天；新约里耶稣把自己比作那连接天地的梯子，因为唯有藉着基督，圣洁的神与悖逆的人才真正相通。

回应

雅各带着一身的诡诈与愧疚逃离家门，神却主动向他说「我总不离弃你」——这句话不是因为雅各配得，而是出于神纯粹的恩典。你若也曾因自己的过犯觉得配不上神的同在，请记得：那真正的天梯基督已经降下，把你这样的人与圣洁的神连接起来，你所需要的不是先洗净自己再来，而是像雅各一样，在旷野里、在你最狼狈的时刻，单单支取这份已经向你敞开的应许。
content_en:
Book Background

Esau has already despised his birthright (Gen. 25:34); these two chapters record how that birthright and blessing are formally transferred to Jacob through an act of thoroughgoing deception — and how, in the very midst of this family’s brokenness, God still appears to the fleeing Jacob and confirms his promise.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapter 27 pushes the family’s dysfunction to its peak — Isaac’s favoritism, Rebekah’s scheming, Jacob’s deceit, Esau’s bitter resentment: no one comes out innocent. Chapter 28 is a crucial turning point in the whole book — Jacob flees alone, leaving the promised land, yet God takes the initiative to appear to him in the wilderness, reaffirming for the first time, directly to Jacob himself, the covenant made with Abraham and Isaac — marking the true beginning of Jacob’s own story.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 27: Rebekah conspires with Jacob to trick Isaac into giving Jacob the blessing meant for Esau. When Esau discovers this, he weeps aloud: “Bless me, even me also, O my father!” (Gen. 27:34), but Isaac cannot take it back. Esau, harboring hatred, plots to kill Jacob, forcing Jacob to flee to his uncle Laban.
  • Chapter 28: Isaac sends Jacob to Paddan-aram and formally passes on to him the blessing promised to Abraham. Camping in the wilderness, Jacob dreams of a ladder: “the angels of God were ascending and descending on it” (Gen. 28:12). The LORD himself stands above the ladder, reaffirming the promise of land, offspring, and blessing to all nations, adding the very words Jacob most needs to hear at this moment: “Behold, I am with you… I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you” (Gen. 28:15).
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

Jacob obtained the blessing through deceit; by rights he should have been cast off by God, left to face Esau’s murderous intent and the wilderness alone. Yet God takes the initiative to appear to him at the very moment he least deserves it, freely adding the promise to him. The ladder connects a broken earth to a holy heaven; in the New Testament, Jesus applies this image to himself as the one who connects heaven and earth, because only through Christ can a holy God and a rebellious people truly be joined.

Response

Jacob fled his home carrying deceit and guilt, and yet God took the initiative to say to him, “I will not leave you” — not because Jacob deserved it, but out of God’s pure grace. If you too have felt unworthy of God’s presence because of your own wrongdoing, remember: Christ, the true ladder from heaven, has already come down, joining someone like you to a holy God. What you need is not to clean yourself up first — but, like Jacob, in the wilderness, at your most desperate, simply to lay hold of the promise already held open to you.

title: 雅各成家与逃走
title_en: Jacob Builds a Family, Then Flees
verse: 创世记卅一章四十九节
content:
书卷背景

雅各在伯特利蒙神应许同在之后，来到舅父拉班家中——这三章记载他在那里成家立业二十年，也在这段被岳父反复欺哄的岁月里，亲身经历神在暗中信实地成就祂所应许的同在。

在全书结构中的位置

廿九至卅一章是雅各流亡岁月的核心：他在异地建立起十二个儿子（除便雅悯外）的家庭，为日后以色列十二支派奠定根基；卅一章神吩咐他回迦南，标志着流亡阶段的结束，也预备了卅二章雅博渡口与以扫和解的高潮。

主题与神学重点
  • 廿九章：雅各爱拉结，为她服事拉班七年，「因为深爱拉结，就看这七年如同几天」（创29:20）；成婚之夜却被拉班掉包，先娶了利亚，又为拉结再服事七年；利亚因失宠而蒙耶和华眷顾生育，接连生下吕便、西缅、利未、犹大。
  • 卅章：拉结因不育与姊姊相争，两人先后把使女给雅各为妾，家庭在嫉妒与竞争中不断添丁；神后来顾念拉结，使她生了约瑟；雅各又用牧养的智谋使自己的羊群极其发大。
  • 卅一章：耶和华吩咐雅各回迦南地；雅各背着拉班离开，拉班带人追上，指控他偷了家中的神像（其实是拉结所偷）；二人立约，拉班说：「我们彼此离别以后，愿耶和华在你我中间鉴察」（创31:49）——这不是一句祝福的话，而是两个彼此提防、无法真正互信的人，只能求神亲自居中监察的无奈之言。
救赎历史脉络

雅各一家的组成，充满了嫉妒、竞争、欺哄与不公——利亚因不被爱而痛苦，拉结因不能生育而痛苦，两个使女被当作生育的工具；但神却在这一团破碎的关系里，一个一个地建立起以色列十二支派的根基，其中犹大——利亚所生、后来大卫与弥赛亚所出的支派——正诞生在这最不被爱的母亲的眼泪中。神从不需要等家庭「健全」了才施行祂的计划；祂惯常在破碎和不义中，仍然信实地成就祂拣选的应许。

回应

利亚一生活在失宠的阴影里，却是神特意眷顾、赐给她四个儿子、并使弥赛亚的血脉从她而出的那一位——这提醒你，神眼中的价值，从不按世人衡量宠爱的方式来分配。你若也觉得自己是那个不被偏爱、被忽略的一个，请记得：神看的是暗中的忧伤，祂差遣祂的儿子，正是要寻找和拯救这样被人看轻、却被祂看重的人，不是因为你先讨祂喜悦，而是因为祂本是满有怜悯的父。
content_en:
Book Background

After Jacob receives God’s promise of his presence at Bethel, he arrives at his uncle Laban’s house — these three chapters record the twenty years he spends there building a family and a livelihood, years in which he is repeatedly deceived by his father-in-law, yet in which he personally experiences God quietly and faithfully fulfilling the presence he had promised.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 29–31 are the core of Jacob’s years of exile: in a foreign land he builds a household of twelve sons (all but Benjamin), laying the foundation for the twelve tribes of Israel to come. Chapter 31, God’s command for him to return to Canaan, marks the end of the exile stage and prepares for the climactic reconciliation with Esau at the Jabbok in chapter 32.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 29: Jacob loves Rachel and serves Laban seven years for her — “they seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her” (Gen. 29:20). On the wedding night, however, Laban switches brides, and Jacob marries Leah first, then serves another seven years for Rachel. Leah, unloved, is favored by the LORD with children, bearing Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah in succession.
  • Chapter 30: Rachel, unable to bear children, competes with her sister, and both give their servants to Jacob as wives; the family grows amid jealousy and rivalry. God later remembers Rachel, and she bears Joseph. Jacob also uses shrewd breeding tactics to greatly increase his own flocks.
  • Chapter 31: The LORD commands Jacob to return to Canaan. Jacob leaves secretly, without telling Laban, who pursues and catches up with him, accusing him of stealing the household idols (which Rachel had actually taken). The two make a covenant, and Laban says, “The LORD watch between you and me, when we are out of one another’s sight” (Gen. 31:49) — not a blessing, but the resigned words of two men who distrust each other and can only ask God himself to keep watch between them.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

Jacob’s family is built amid jealousy, rivalry, deceit, and injustice — Leah suffers from being unloved, Rachel suffers from being unable to bear children, and both servants are used as instruments for bearing children. Yet in the midst of this tangled brokenness, God builds, one by one, the foundations of the twelve tribes of Israel — and Judah, born to Leah, the tribe from which David and the Messiah would come, is born out of the tears of this least-loved mother. God has never needed a family to be “healthy” before he carries out his plan; he habitually and faithfully fulfills his chosen promise in the midst of brokenness and injustice.

Response

Leah lived her whole life in the shadow of being unloved — yet she is the very one God specially favored, giving her four sons and bringing the Messiah’s bloodline through her. This reminds you that the value God sees never follows the world’s way of distributing favor. If you too feel like the unfavored one, the one overlooked, remember: God sees hidden sorrow, and he sent his Son precisely to seek and save those the world looks down on but whom he values — not because you first pleased him, but because he is by nature a Father full of mercy.

title: 雅博渡口：与神摔跤，得着新名
title_en: The Jabbok: Wrestling with God, Receiving a New Name
verse: 创世记卅二章廿八节
content:
书卷背景

雅各二十年前因惧怕以扫的杀机而逃离迦南，如今神吩咐他回去——这两章记载的，正是他在重新面对以扫之前，先要在雅博渡口面对那位真正掌管他一生的神。

在全书结构中的位置

卅二至卅三章是雅各故事的高潮与转折：卅二章雅博渡口的摔跤是雅各生命的转折点——他从此不再单靠自己的诡计谋求生存，而是带着一个新名字、一个瘸腿的记号，去面对他一生逃避的哥哥；卅三章的和解，则证明了神应许的同在真实可靠，也为雅各一家最终定居迦南铺路。

主题与神学重点
  • 卅二章：雅各听闻以扫带着四百人前来，极其惧怕，一面打发礼物讨好以扫，一面向神祷告：「求你救我脱离我哥哥以扫的手」（创32:11）；当夜，有一人与他摔跤直到黎明，那人为他改名说：「你的名不要再叫雅各，要叫以色列；因为你与神与人较力，都得了胜」（创32:28）；雅各的大腿窝从此扭伤，成了他一生带着的记号。
  • 卅三章：雅各与以扫重逢，「以扫跑来迎接他，将他抱住……与他亲嘴，两个人就哭了」（创33:4）；二十年的仇恨在这一刻化解，雅各对以扫说：「我见了你的面，如同见了神的面」（创33:10），随后平平安安地进入迦南地，在示剑筑坛。
救赎历史脉络

雅各这一生都在抓取——抓住以扫的脚跟出生、抓住长子名分、抓住父亲的祝福；雅博渡口是这一切的顶点：他这一次紧紧抓住的，不再是人的祝福，而是神自己，且宁可瘸腿也不放手。神容许人与祂较力并得胜，不是因为人真能胜过神，而是因为神愿意俯就，把得胜白白赐给一个残缺无力、只能抓住祂不放的人——这正是恩典的样式：以色列这个新名字，日后要成为神子民的名字，纪念的不是雅各的强壮，而是他的软弱如何被神的恩典托住。

回应

雅各带着瘸腿走向以扫，不再是那个靠诡计求生存的人，而是一个承认自己无力、只能抓住神的人。你若也在人生某个雅博渡口般的时刻，被神的手摸着、被迫承认自己一无所能，不要以为那是失败——这正是恩典进入的入口。基督自己在客西马尼园彻夜祷告、担当十字架上的击打，为要使凡像雅各一样紧紧抓住祂不放的人，都能带着新名字、带着虽软弱却蒙保守的印记，坦然进到神面前。
content_en:
Book Background

Twenty years ago Jacob fled Canaan in fear of Esau’s murderous intent; now God commands him to return — these two chapters record how, before facing Esau again, he must first face the God who truly governs his entire life, at the ford of the Jabbok.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 32–33 are the climax and turning point of Jacob’s story: the wrestling match at the Jabbok in chapter 32 is the turning point of his life — from then on he no longer relies solely on his own schemes to survive, but goes, carrying a new name and the mark of a limp, to face the brother he had spent his whole life fleeing. The reconciliation in chapter 33 then proves that God’s promised presence is real and reliable, and paves the way for Jacob’s family to finally settle in Canaan.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 32: Hearing that Esau is coming with four hundred men, Jacob is greatly afraid. He sends gifts ahead to appease Esau, while praying to God, “Please deliver me from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau” (Gen. 32:11). That night a man wrestles with him until daybreak, and renames him, saying, “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed” (Gen. 32:28). Jacob’s hip is wrenched from then on, a mark he carries the rest of his life.
  • Chapter 33: Jacob and Esau are reunited: “Esau ran to meet him and embraced him and fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept” (Gen. 33:4). Twenty years of hostility dissolve in this moment; Jacob tells Esau, “to see your face is like seeing the face of God” (Gen. 33:10), and afterward enters Canaan in peace, building an altar at Shechem.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

Jacob’s whole life has been a story of grasping — grasping Esau’s heel at birth, grasping the birthright, grasping his father’s blessing. The Jabbok is the climax of all this: what he grasps this time, and refuses to let go of even at the cost of a limp, is no longer a human blessing, but God himself. God allows a man to strive with him and even to “prevail” — not because a person can truly overcome God, but because God chooses to stoop down and freely grant victory to someone broken and powerless who can only cling to him and refuse to let go — this is exactly the shape of grace: the new name Israel, which would later become the name of God’s own people, commemorates not Jacob’s strength, but how his weakness was upheld by God’s grace.

Response

Jacob walks toward Esau with a limp — no longer the man who survived by scheming, but a man who admits his own powerlessness and can only cling to God. If you too find yourself at a Jabbok-like moment in your life, touched by God’s hand and forced to admit you can do nothing — don’t think of that as failure. That is exactly where grace enters. Christ himself prayed all night in Gethsemane and bore the blows of the cross, so that everyone who, like Jacob, clings tightly to him and will not let go, can come before God carrying a new name and the mark of a weakness that was nonetheless kept safe.

title: 安息日：记念神的创造 (Remembering Creation)
content:
今天是安息日——照着神起初所定的节奏，停下脚步，回顾这一周所读的经文，也安歇在神里面。

这一周我们从创世记十八章读到卅三章：亚伯拉罕为所多玛代求、以撒的诞生与几乎被献（十八至廿四章），以撒一代信心的延续（廿五至廿六章），雅各夺取祝福、逃亡路上遇见神（廿七至廿八章），在拉班家二十年的经历（廿九至卅一章），最后在雅博渡口与神摔跤、改名以色列，又与以扫和好（卅二至卅三章）。这一周的主角，从满有信心的亚伯拉罕，到用诡计上位的雅各，神都没有因着他们的软弱而收回应许——祂的信实，从不建立在人的完全上。

回顾这一周，你会发现一个反复出现的模式：神总是主动向不配、甚至正在逃避的人显现——向说谎的亚伯拉罕、向逃亡的雅各。这提醒我们：神的同在，从不是我们靠自己挣来的奖赏，而是祂主动赐下的恩典。

建议你今天：①回顾这一周读过的经文，挑一段你印象最深的重读一遍；②为你生命中一段需要「与人和好」的关系向神祷告；③安静片刻，单单记念神起初创造与其后不断施恩的信实。

应用：今天效法雅各在雅博渡口的操练——找一段安静的时间，诚实地在神面前「角力」，把你正逃避或挣扎的事带到祂面前，求祂的祝福与新的身份。
content_en:
Today is a Sabbath day — following the rhythm God set from the beginning, stop, look back over this week’s reading, and rest in God.

This week we read from Genesis 18 through 33: Abraham’s intercession for Sodom, Isaac’s birth and near-sacrifice (chapters 18–24); the continuation of faith in Isaac’s generation (chapters 25–26); Jacob taking the blessing and meeting God as he fled (chapters 27–28); his twenty years with Laban (chapters 29–31); and finally, wrestling with God and receiving the name Israel at the Jabbok, and being reconciled with Esau (chapters 32–33). This week’s cast ranges from the faith-filled Abraham to the scheming, self-advancing Jacob — and God withdrew his promise from neither because of their weakness. His faithfulness was never built on human perfection.

Looking back over this week, you’ll notice a recurring pattern: God consistently takes the initiative to appear to the undeserving, even to those actively fleeing — to a lying Abraham, to a fleeing Jacob. This reminds us that God’s presence is never a reward we earn for ourselves, but a grace he freely gives.

Today, consider: (1) Look back over this week’s reading and reread the passage that struck you most. (2) Pray to God about a relationship in your life that needs reconciliation. (3) Be still for a moment, simply remembering God’s faithfulness — in creation at the beginning, and in his continual grace ever since.

Application: Follow Jacob’s example at the Jabbok today — set aside a quiet time and honestly “wrestle” before God, bringing whatever you’re fleeing or struggling with to him, asking for his blessing and a new identity.

title: 人的软弱与神的怜悯
verse: 创世记卅五章十节
content:
书卷背景

创世记记载神拣选一个满有软弱的家族，要藉着这家族赐福万国；卅四至卅六章紧接在雅各与以扫和好（卅三章）之后，是雅各一家初回应许地便深陷失败与死丧的一段插曲。

在全书结构中的位置

这三章是全书的一个过渡：雅各个人的故事在这里收尾——以撒去世、雅各正式领受「以色列」之名；同时以扫一系（以东）的家谱被交代清楚，正式与承受应许的雅各一系分道扬镳，为后面以色列与以东的关系埋下伏笔；约瑟的故事（卅七章起）即将登场，创世记下半部的重心也随之从雅各转向他的众子。

主题与神学重点
  • 卅四章：底拿被示剑玷污，她的哥哥西缅、利未以割礼为诡计，「把一切男丁都杀了」（创34:25），血洗全城为妹妹报复；圣经如实记载这场暴行，却并未称许——这也是雅各临终严厉责备这二子的原因（创49:5-7）。
  • 卅五章：神吩咐雅各「起来，上伯特利去」（创35:1），回到当年逃亡时与神相遇之地；神在那里再次坚立祂起初赐下的应许与新名：「你的名原是雅各，从今以后不要再叫雅各，要叫以色列」（创35:10）。此后拉结难产而死，以撒也离世——应许的更新与丧亲的哀伤交织在同一章里。
  • 卅六章：以扫（以东）后裔的家谱，正式记录这一支与承受应许的雅各一系分道扬镳，各自成为一族。
救赎历史脉络

这三章把「人的软弱」与「神的怜悯」并置在一起：雅各一家刚经历屠城的暴行，久后又要面对丧妻丧父之痛，神却主动来寻雅各，不是因为这个家族配得，而是因为祂信实持守自己起初的应许。神更新雅各的名字，不是因为他已经洁净自己，而是要藉此提醒他：他的身份从始至终建立在神的呼召与应许上，而非自己的德行——这正是神一路藉软弱、失败的器皿成就救赎计划的模式，直到那位真正配得「以色列」之名、却甘愿为悖逆的百姓受死的君王耶稣基督。

回应

神并没有等雅各一家洗净自己的暴行、平息丧亲的哀伤，才回到伯特利重申应许；祂主动呼召软弱的雅各回到与祂相遇之地。今天无论你正因自己或家人的失败而蒙羞，还是正被丧失与哀伤压垮，「你的名原是雅各……要叫以色列」（创35:10）这句应许提醒你：神愿意在你最软弱的时刻，仍然坚立祂在基督里向你所定的新身份——不是因为你配得，而是因为祂信实。
content_en:
Book Background

Genesis records God choosing a family full of weakness, in order to bless the nations through it. Chapters 34–36 follow right after Jacob’s reconciliation with Esau (chapter 33), and form an episode in which Jacob’s family, just back in the promised land, immediately falls into failure and mourning.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

These three chapters form a transition in the book: Jacob’s personal story concludes here — Isaac dies, and Jacob formally receives the name “Israel”; at the same time, Esau’s line (Edom) is fully accounted for, formally parting ways with Jacob’s line, which carries the promise, setting up the later relationship between Israel and Edom. Joseph’s story (from chapter 37) is about to begin, and the second half of Genesis shifts its center of gravity from Jacob to his sons.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 34: Dinah is violated by Shechem; her brothers Simeon and Levi use circumcision as a ruse and “killed all the males” (Gen. 34:25), massacring the whole city in revenge for their sister. Scripture records this atrocity honestly, but does not commend it — this is also why Jacob, on his deathbed, severely rebukes these two sons (Gen. 49:5–7).
  • Chapter 35: God commands Jacob, “Arise, go up to Bethel” (Gen. 35:1), back to the place where he had met God when he first fled. There God again establishes the promise and new name first given to him: “Your name is Jacob; no more shall your name be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name” (Gen. 35:10). Afterward, Rachel dies in childbirth, and Isaac also dies — the renewal of the promise and the grief of bereavement woven together in the very same chapter.
  • Chapter 36: The genealogy of Esau (Edom)’s descendants formally records this line parting ways with Jacob’s line, which carries the promise, each becoming its own nation.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

These three chapters set “human weakness” and “God’s mercy” side by side: Jacob’s family has just experienced the atrocity of a massacred city, and not long after must face the grief of losing a wife and a father — yet God takes the initiative to seek Jacob out, not because this family deserves it, but because he faithfully keeps the promise he first gave. God renews Jacob’s name not because Jacob has cleansed himself, but to remind him that his identity, from beginning to end, rests on God’s calling and promise, not on his own character — exactly the pattern by which God, all along, accomplishes his plan of redemption through weak and failing vessels, until the King who truly deserves the name “Israel,” yet willingly dies for a rebellious people, Jesus Christ, comes.

Response

God did not wait for Jacob’s family to wash away the guilt of their atrocity, or for their grief over loss to subside, before returning to Bethel to reaffirm the promise. He took the initiative to call the weak Jacob back to the place where they had met. Today, whether you are ashamed because of your own or your family’s failures, or crushed under loss and grief, the promise “Your name is Jacob… Israel shall be your name” (Gen. 35:10) reminds you: God is willing, at your weakest moment, to still establish the new identity he has determined for you in Christ — not because you deserve it, but because he is faithful.

title: 一个王的诞生
verse: 创世记卅七章四节
content:
书卷背景

卅七章起，创世记的焦点从雅各本人转向他的众子，尤其是约瑟——这段故事将占据创世记剩下的篇幅，直到全书末了。

在全书结构中的位置

卅七章记约瑟被卖到埃及，卅八章却插入犹大与他玛的故事，看似打断了约瑟叙事的节奏；但这正是希伯来叙事常见的手法——藉着插入的家族故事，交代日后要承接应许血脉的支派（犹大）的起源，为回头看雅各临终祝福中犹大得着君王应许（创49:8-10）埋下伏笔。

主题与神学重点
  • 卅七章：约瑟因父亲雅各偏爱、又因两个预表自己要管辖弟兄的异梦，招来哥哥们「不与他说和睦的话」（创37:4）；他们本要杀他，后来卖给以实玛利商人，带到埃及为奴——人的嫉妒与恶意，成了神日后拯救全家性命的起点。
  • 卅八章：犹大离开弟兄，娶迦南女子为妻，长子珥、次子俄南相继因恶行被耶和华击杀；犹大迟迟不肯把三子示拉给儿媳他玛，他玛便设计与犹大同房，生下双生子法勒斯、谢拉——法勒斯正是后来犹大支派、大卫王朝、直到基督降生所出的世系（太1:3）。
救赎历史脉络

卅八章表面上是一段令人不安的插曲——欺骗、失职、羞耻的圈套——却在创世记的家谱主线上留下极关键的一笔：法勒斯，这个在羞耻与失职中诞生的孩子，正是大卫的先祖，也是弥赛亚谱系上的一环。神并没有拣选一个洁净无瑕的世系来预备君王的诞生，反倒藉着一段满是人的失败与羞耻的故事，亲手编织出通向大卫、通向基督的血脉。这提醒我们，神的救赎历史从不依赖人的洁净配得，而是祂主权的怜悯，能从最黑暗的插曲里，生出祂荣耀计划的下一步。

回应

你或许也曾因自己或家族历史中不堪启齿的一段过去而自惭，觉得自己配不上被神使用；但法勒斯的诞生提醒你，神的救赎计划从不因人的污点而搁浅——祂能藉着人的失败成就祂公义又满有恩典的旨意，正如祂最终藉着一位从这满有污点的世系而出、自己却全然无罪的君王耶稣基督，来洗净凡投靠祂之人的一切羞耻。
content_en:
Book Background

From chapter 37 on, Genesis shifts its focus from Jacob himself to his sons, especially Joseph — this story will occupy the rest of Genesis, all the way to the book’s end.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapter 37 records Joseph being sold into Egypt, while chapter 38 inserts the story of Judah and Tamar, seemingly interrupting the pace of the Joseph narrative. But this is a common technique in Hebrew narrative — using an inserted family story to account for the origin of the tribe (Judah) that will later carry the promised line, foreshadowing Judah’s royal promise in Jacob’s deathbed blessing (Gen. 49:8–10).

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 37: Joseph, favored by his father Jacob and given two dreams foreshadowing that he would rule over his brothers, provokes his brothers so that they “could not speak peacefully to him” (Gen. 37:4). They intend to kill him, but instead sell him to Ishmaelite traders, who bring him to Egypt as a slave — human jealousy and malice become the starting point for God’s later preservation of the whole family’s life.
  • Chapter 38: Judah leaves his brothers and marries a Canaanite woman; his firstborn Er and second son Onan are struck down by the LORD one after another for their wickedness. Judah delays giving his third son Shelah to his daughter-in-law Tamar, so Tamar schemes to sleep with Judah himself, bearing the twins Perez and Zerah — Perez being the very line from which the tribe of Judah, the Davidic dynasty, and ultimately Christ’s birth descend (Matt. 1:3).
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

On the surface, chapter 38 is an unsettling episode — deception, dereliction of duty, a trap laid in shame — yet it leaves an absolutely crucial mark on Genesis’s genealogical thread: Perez, this child born out of shame and failure, is the very ancestor of David, and a link in the Messianic line. God did not choose a spotless line to prepare for the birth of the king; instead, through a story full of human failure and shame, he himself wove together the bloodline leading to David, and to Christ. This reminds us that God’s redemptive history has never depended on human purity or worthiness — his sovereign mercy can bring forth the next step of his glorious plan even out of the darkest episode.

Response

You too may feel ashamed of some unspeakable chapter in your own or your family’s past, feeling unworthy of being used by God. But Perez’s birth reminds you that God’s plan of redemption is never derailed by human stains — he can accomplish his righteous and gracious purposes through human failure, just as he ultimately brought forth, from this stained line, a King, Jesus Christ, himself entirely without sin, to wash away all the shame of everyone who takes refuge in him.

title: 从最低升至最高
title_en: From the Lowest Place to the Highest
verse: 创世记四十章八节
content:
书卷背景

创世记进入约瑟故事的核心段落，追踪他从为奴、下监，直到升为埃及宰相的历程。

在全书结构中的位置

卅九至四十一章记载约瑟一路下沉又一路被神高举的经历，是全书「神藉苦难成就拯救」这条主线最完整的示范：约瑟越是被人陷害、被人遗忘，神的同在与智慧反倒越发彰显，直到他登上仅次于法老的高位——这一切都是为了预备他成为日后全家、乃至周围列国存活的关键。

主题与神学重点
  • 卅九章：约瑟在波提乏家尽心服事，主人见「耶和华与他同在」（创39:3），凡事尽都顺利；后因主母诬告无辜下监，从奴仆沦为囚犯，但即使身陷囹圄，经文仍再次记道「耶和华与约瑟同在」（创39:21）。
  • 四十章：约瑟在监中为法老的酒政、膳长解梦，坚持「解梦不是出于神吗」（创40:8）——他清楚把一切智慧的来源都归给神；然而酒政官复原职后却「不记念约瑟」（创40:23），约瑟继续被遗忘在监里。
  • 四十一章：法老两次做梦无人能解，酒政终于想起约瑟；约瑟解梦，又献上丰年积粮之策，法老就立他治理埃及全地——正如约瑟自己所说，「神已将所要做的事指示法老了」（创41:25），他从囚犯一跃升为宰相，全然出于神的安排，而非自己的筹算。
救赎历史脉络

约瑟从被卖、被诬告、被遗忘，到被高举治理埃及，这条「先降卑、后升高」的路径，是神拯救计划反复出现的模式——祂常常先让祂所拣选的器皿经过无人能解释的苦难与羞辱，再照祂自己的时间表将他们高举，为要成就远超个人得释放的拯救。这条路径最终、最完整地应验在耶稣基督身上：祂被自己的百姓拒绝、被出卖、受尽羞辱，钉死在十字架上，又照神的定意从死里复活，被高举在万有之上（腓2:9）——约瑟先苦后荣的经历，是这更大拯救故事的预表。

回应

当你正身处约瑟式的「监牢」——被误解、被遗忘、看不到出路——今天的经文提醒你，神的同在与作为，并不因你眼前的处境而缺席；正如神没有撇下狱中的约瑟，祂也没有撇下那位真正先降卑、后升为至高的基督（腓2:8），你可以将自己此刻的等候，交托给这位掌管时间、也掌管高举卑微之人的神。
content_en:
Book Background

Genesis now enters the core section of the Joseph narrative, tracing his path from slavery, to prison, to becoming Egypt’s prime minister.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 39–41 record Joseph’s journey of being brought ever lower while God lifts him ever higher — the fullest demonstration in the book of its central thread, that God accomplishes salvation through suffering. The more Joseph is wronged and forgotten, the more God’s presence and wisdom are displayed, until he rises to the position second only to Pharaoh — all to prepare him to become the key to his family’s survival, and that of the surrounding nations.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 39: Joseph serves faithfully in Potiphar’s house; his master sees that “the LORD was with him” (Gen. 39:3), and everything succeeds in his hand. He is later falsely accused by his master’s wife and thrown into prison, an innocent man reduced from servant to prisoner — yet even in prison, Scripture again records, “the LORD was with Joseph” (Gen. 39:21).
  • Chapter 40: In prison, Joseph interprets dreams for Pharaoh’s cupbearer and baker, insisting, “Do not interpretations belong to God?” (Gen. 40:8) — he clearly attributes the source of all wisdom to God. Yet once restored to his post, the cupbearer “did not remember Joseph, but forgot him” (Gen. 40:23), and Joseph remains forgotten in prison.
  • Chapter 41: Pharaoh has two dreams that no one can interpret, and the cupbearer finally remembers Joseph. Joseph interprets the dreams and offers a plan to store grain for the coming years of plenty, and Pharaoh sets him over all the land of Egypt — just as Joseph himself says, “God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do” (Gen. 41:25). His leap from prisoner to prime minister is entirely God’s doing, not his own scheming.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

Joseph’s path from being sold, falsely accused, and forgotten, to being exalted to rule over Egypt — this pattern of “first brought low, then lifted high” recurs throughout God’s plan of salvation. He often first lets his chosen vessels pass through inexplicable suffering and humiliation, then, according to his own timetable, lifts them up, to accomplish a salvation far beyond any one person’s deliverance. This path finds its final, fullest fulfillment in Jesus Christ: rejected by his own people, betrayed, utterly humiliated, put to death on a cross — yet, according to God’s purpose, raised from the dead and exalted above all things (Phil. 2:9). Joseph’s experience of suffering before glory foreshadows this greater story of salvation.

Response

When you find yourself in a Joseph-like “prison” — misunderstood, forgotten, unable to see a way out — today’s reading reminds you that God’s presence and work are not absent just because of your present circumstances. Just as God did not abandon Joseph in prison, he did not abandon Christ, who was first brought low and then exalted to the highest place (Phil. 2:8) — you can entrust your present waiting to this God who governs time itself, and who lifts up the lowly.

title: 兄弟重逢未相认
verse: 创世记四十二章廿一节
content:
书卷背景

埃及大丰年之后随即而来的大饥荒，把雅各一家再次带回约瑟面前——只是这一次，众兄弟认不出眼前这位埃及宰相，正是他们多年前卖掉的弟弟。

在全书结构中的位置

四十二至四十四章记载约瑟兄弟三次下埃及籴粮的过程，是整个约瑟故事的高潮铺垫：约瑟一路试验哥哥们，为要看清他们的心是否真已悔改、是否愿意为最小的弟弟便雅悯挺身而出——这也直接预备了四十五章那场泪流满面的相认。

主题与神学重点
  • 四十二章：十个哥哥下埃及籴粮，向约瑟下拜；约瑟认出他们，他们却认不出他；被约瑟严厉的话语逼问之下，众兄弟彼此承认当年的罪：「我们在兄弟身上实在有罪……所以这场苦难临到我们身上」（创42:21）。
  • 四十三章：饥荒持续，犹大向父亲担保带便雅悯同去埃及；约瑟设宴款待，见到同母弟弟便雅悯，「爱弟之情发动」（创43:30），便急忙躲起来哭了一场。
  • 四十四章：约瑟设计把自己的银杯藏在便雅悯的口袋里，试验哥哥们会不会像当年撇下自己一样撇下便雅悯；犹大挺身而出，「求你容仆人住下，替这童子作我主的奴仆」（创44:33），情愿代替便雅悯为奴，只求不要让父亲再承受丧子之痛。
救赎历史脉络

众兄弟的这句认罪——「我们在兄弟身上实在有罪」（创42:21）——是创世记里少见的、清楚而具体的悔罪告白，标志着这个满有嫉妒与欺骗的家族开始转向。犹大在四十四章甘愿代替便雅悯为奴，与他多年前提议把约瑟卖为奴隶（创37:26-27）形成鲜明对照——那个曾经出卖弟弟的人，如今愿意舍己代赎弟弟。这份「愿意代替所爱之人受苦」的心志，正预表着后来那位真正、完全代替罪人受刑罚的救赎者——不是被迫，而是甘心为祂所爱的人舍命的耶稣基督。

回应

你是否也曾像约瑟的哥哥们一样，把某个不愿面对的罪深埋心底多年，直到某个患难的处境把它重新翻搅出来？今天的经文提醒你，真实的悔改从来不是靠自己压抑或遗忘，而是坦然承认自己「实在有罪」；而你可以坦然如此认罪，正是因为已经有一位甘心代替你受苦、担当你一切罪债的耶稣，使你不必惧怕认罪后无路可退。
content_en:
Book Background

The great famine that follows Egypt’s years of plenty brings Jacob’s family back before Joseph once more — except this time, the brothers cannot recognize that the Egyptian prime minister before them is the very brother they sold years ago.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 42–44 record three trips by Joseph’s brothers down to Egypt for grain, forming the buildup to the climax of the whole Joseph narrative: Joseph tests his brothers at every turn, wanting to see whether their hearts have truly repented, and whether they will stand up for their youngest brother Benjamin — this also directly prepares for the tearful recognition scene in chapter 45.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 42: The ten brothers go down to Egypt for grain and bow before Joseph; Joseph recognizes them, but they do not recognize him. Pressed by Joseph’s harsh words, the brothers admit their guilt to one another over what they did years ago: “In truth we are guilty concerning our brother… that is why this distress has come upon us” (Gen. 42:21).
  • Chapter 43: As the famine continues, Judah guarantees to his father that he will bring Benjamin to Egypt. Joseph hosts a banquet, and on seeing his full brother Benjamin, “his compassion grew warm for his brother” (Gen. 43:30), so he hurries away to weep.
  • Chapter 44: Joseph arranges for his own silver cup to be hidden in Benjamin’s sack, testing whether his brothers will abandon Benjamin the way they once abandoned him. Judah steps forward: “please let your servant remain instead of the boy as a servant to my lord” (Gen. 44:33), willing to become a slave in Benjamin’s place, only so that their father would not have to bear the loss of another son.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

The brothers’ confession — “In truth we are guilty concerning our brother” (Gen. 42:21) — is a rare, clear, and concrete confession of guilt in Genesis, marking the turning point for this family so full of jealousy and deceit. Judah’s willingness in chapter 44 to become a slave in Benjamin’s place stands in stark contrast to his proposal years earlier to sell Joseph into slavery (Gen. 37:26–27) — the very man who once sold his brother is now willing to give himself up to redeem his brother. This willingness to “suffer in place of the one he loves” foreshadows the later, true and complete Redeemer who bore the penalty for sinners in their place — not by compulsion, but willingly laying down his life for those he loves: Jesus Christ.

Response

Have you ever, like Joseph’s brothers, buried some sin you didn’t want to face deep inside for years, until some hardship stirred it back up? Today’s reading reminds you that real repentance never comes from suppressing or forgetting, but from honestly admitting, “In truth we are guilty.” And you can confess this freely precisely because there is already a Jesus who was willing to suffer in your place and bear the full weight of your sin-debt, so that you need not fear having nowhere to turn after confessing.

title: 饶恕与接纳
verse: 创世记四十五章五节
content:
书卷背景

经过前面几章的试验与内心挣扎，约瑟终于向哥哥们表明身份——这是创世记中最动人的相认场景之一。

在全书结构中的位置

四十五至四十七章记载相认、接雅各全家下埃及、以及约瑟治理饥荒的后续安排；这也是创世记从「应许之地」过渡到「寄居埃及」的关键枢纽，为以色列人日后在埃及为奴的处境预先铺陈背景。

主题与神学重点
  • 四十五章：约瑟向哥哥们表明身份，说出全书最重要的神学总结之一：「不要因为把我卖到这里自忧自恨，这是神差我在你们以先来，为要保全生命」（创45:5）；他清楚指出，「差我到这里来的不是你们，乃是神」（创45:8）。
  • 四十六章：神在异象中向雅各保证「我要和你同下埃及去，也必定带你上来」（创46:4），雅各一家七十人下到埃及，在歌珊地安顿。
  • 四十七章：约瑟安排全家住在歌珊，又在饥荒中以粮食为法老换取埃及全地；雅各临终前请约瑟起誓，必不将他葬在埃及，而要带他归回应许之地（创47:29-30）。
救赎历史脉络

「不要因为把我卖到这里自忧自恨，这是神差我在你们以先来，为要保全生命」（创45:5），是圣经论神的护理最清楚的宣告之一——人以恶意行的事，神却在其中运行，使之成就祂拯救的美意。这句话与后面五十章末了「你们的意思是要害我，但神的意思原是好的」（创50:20）前后呼应，构成一条贯穿全书、也贯穿全部救赎历史的主线：神惯常藉着人极大的恶行，成就祂更大的美意——这条主线最终、最完整地应验在十字架上：人以最大的恶意钉死无辜的基督，神却藉着这最大的恶事，成就了世上最大的美善，就是罪人得赎。

回应

若你此刻正因某个人对你犯下的伤害而心怀苦毒，或正因自己曾经的过犯而无法原谅自己，约瑟这句话给你一个新的角度：神能在人的恶意之上工作，成就祂自己的美意——这不是要你轻看伤害本身，而是邀请你相信，那位在约瑟的苦难背后掌权的神，也同样在你的境遇背后掌权；正如祂曾使用人对约瑟、更是对基督的恶意，成就了拯救，祂也能使用你生命中的破碎，成就祂的美意。
content_en:
Book Background

After the testing and inner struggle of the preceding chapters, Joseph finally reveals his identity to his brothers — one of the most moving recognition scenes in all of Genesis.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 45–47 record the recognition, Jacob’s whole family being brought down to Egypt, and the arrangements Joseph makes as he administers the famine relief. This is also the key hinge where Genesis transitions from “the promised land” to “sojourning in Egypt,” laying the groundwork for the Israelites’ later enslavement in Egypt.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 45: Joseph reveals his identity to his brothers, speaking one of the most important theological summaries in the whole book: “do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life” (Gen. 45:5). He states clearly, “it was not you who sent me here, but God” (Gen. 45:8).
  • Chapter 46: God assures Jacob in a vision, “I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again” (Gen. 46:4); Jacob’s family of seventy goes down to Egypt and settles in the land of Goshen.
  • Chapter 47: Joseph arranges for his whole family to live in Goshen, and during the famine trades food for all the land of Egypt on Pharaoh’s behalf. Before his death, Jacob makes Joseph swear not to bury him in Egypt, but to carry him back to the promised land (Gen. 47:29–30).
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

“Do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life” (Gen. 45:5) is one of the clearest declarations in Scripture of God’s providence — what people do in malice, God is at work within, to accomplish his good purpose of salvation. This statement echoes forward to the end of chapter 50: “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Gen. 50:20), forming a thread that runs through the whole book, and indeed the whole of redemptive history: God habitually accomplishes his greater good through humanity’s greatest evil — a thread that finds its final, fullest fulfillment at the cross: humanity, with its greatest malice, crucified the innocent Christ, yet God, through this greatest evil, accomplished the greatest good the world has ever known — the redemption of sinners.

Response

If you are carrying bitterness right now over some injury someone has done to you, or unable to forgive yourself for some past wrong, Joseph’s words offer you a new perspective: God can work above human malice to accomplish his own good purpose — not to minimize the injury itself, but to invite you to believe that the same God who reigned behind Joseph’s suffering also reigns behind your circumstances. Just as he once used human malice against Joseph — and even more, against Christ — to accomplish salvation, he can also use the brokenness in your life to accomplish his good purpose.
