title: 寄望于应许地
title_en: Hope Set on the Promised Land
verse: 创世记五十章十九节至廿节
content:
书卷背景

创世记以神创造万有开始，经过人的堕落、洪水审判、巴别塔的分散，神拣选亚伯拉罕一人，应许要藉他的后裔赐福万国；这应许一路藉着以撒、雅各，来到雅各众子——尤其犹大与约瑟身上，四十八至五十章正是全书画上句点的最后一幕。

在全书结构中的位置

这三章记载雅各临终前给约瑟两个儿子祝福（并预示以法莲要超越玛拿西）、向十二个儿子逐一说预言性的祝福（尤其犹大支派得着君王的应许）、雅各去世归葬应许之地，以及约瑟临终前的遗言——这些都是全书的收束：雅各一家看似寄居异乡埃及，但他们的盼望始终指向那应许之地，以及那应许之地上要兴起的一位君王。

主题与神学重点
  • 四十八章：雅各将约瑟的两个儿子收纳为自己的儿子，又按着自己的心意，把长子的福分给了次子以法莲，说「他的兄弟将来比他还大」（创48:19）——神拣选的次序常常出人意表，不按人看重的长幼常规。
  • 四十九章：雅各临终前逐一祝福十二个儿子，其中最关键的一句临到犹大：「圭必不离犹大，杖必不离他两脚之间，直等细罗来到，万民都必归顺」（创49:10）——这是旧约中最早、也最清楚指向一位要从犹大支派而出、掌权直到万民归顺的君王的预言之一。
  • 五十章：雅各去世，按他遗命葬在迦南地的麦比拉洞；约瑟的哥哥们惧怕他秋后算账，约瑟却说：「从前你们的意思是要害我，但神的意思原是好的，要保全许多人的性命，成就今日的光景」（创50:20）；约瑟临终前吩咐：「神必定看顾你们，你们要把我的骸骨从这里搬上去」（创50:25），全书末了以「约瑟死了……把他收殓在棺材里，停在埃及」（创50:26）作结——一具停在埃及、却盼望有一天被搬回应许之地的棺材，成了创世记最后的画面。
救赎历史脉络

创世记从神说「要有光」开始，到约瑟的棺材停在埃及结束——这看似是从荣耀跌落到寄居异乡的下坡路，其实不然。回顾全书：神造了美好的世界，人却在伊甸园中悖逆，招来咒诅与死亡；罪迅速蔓延，直到神用洪水审判全地，却留下挪亚一家，重新赐下「生养众多，遍满地面」的托付；人在巴别塔再次想要传扬自己的名，神便使人分散、言语变乱。正是在这一片破碎之中，神拣选亚伯拉罕一人，应许要藉他的后裔使地上万族都得福——这应许一路藉着以撒、雅各的软弱与失败被持守下来，如今来到雅各众子身上：犹大——那个曾经提议卖掉约瑟、又与他玛有过一段羞耻往事的儿子——竟领受了「圭必不离犹大……直等细罗来到」（创49:10）这句指向未来君王的祝福；约瑟——那个被卖为奴、无辜下监、又满有智慧保全全家性命的儿子——他一生「你们的意思是要害我，但神的意思原是好的」（创50:20）这句总结，几乎就是整卷创世记神护理之工的缩影：人一路失败、悖逆、彼此加害，神却始终在人的恶意与软弱之上，编织祂拯救的计划。全书末了，约瑟的骸骨停留在埃及，等候着一位日后要眷顾以色列人、领他们出埃及、进入应许之地的拯救者（出3:16-17）——这具悬而未葬的棺材，是创世记留给读者最后的悬念，也是指向那位真正「细罗」、真正从犹大支派而出、要执掌王权直到万民归顺的耶稣基督（启5:5）最实在的伏笔。

回应

创世记从伊甸园的破碎写起，却以一口盼望归回应许之地的棺材作结——这提醒你，神的百姓从起初就是「活在应许中、还没有得着应许」的群体；你今天或许也像约瑟一样，活在一个还未完全成就应许的世界里，被环境、被他人的恶意、被自己的软弱重重围困。但那位从犹大支派而出的真君王——真正的「细罗」、真正执掌王权直到万民归顺的耶稣基督——已经来过，藉着十字架与复活，成就了比出埃及更大的拯救；祂的复活，是神向你保证：凡投靠祂的人，最终必要归回那更美的应许之地，正如约瑟当年所信的一样。
content_en:
Book Background

Genesis begins with God creating all things, moves through humanity’s fall, the flood’s judgment, and the scattering at Babel; God then chooses one man, Abraham, promising to bless all nations through his offspring. This promise is carried forward through Isaac and Jacob, down to Jacob’s sons — especially Judah and Joseph. Chapters 48–50 are the final scene that brings the whole book to its close.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

These three chapters record Jacob’s deathbed blessing of Joseph’s two sons (foretelling that Ephraim would surpass Manasseh), his prophetic blessings spoken one by one over his twelve sons (with the tribe of Judah especially receiving the promise of kingship), Jacob’s death and burial in the promised land, and Joseph’s dying words — all bringing the book to its conclusion: Jacob’s family, though sojourning in a foreign land, Egypt, still has its hope fixed on the promised land, and on the king who would arise from it.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 48: Jacob adopts Joseph’s two sons as his own, and, following his own judgment rather than birth order, gives the firstborn’s blessing to the younger son Ephraim, saying, “his younger brother shall be greater than he” (Gen. 48:19) — God’s order of election is often surprising, not bound by the customary priority humans give to birth order.
  • Chapter 49: Before his death, Jacob blesses his twelve sons one by one; the most crucial line falls to Judah: “The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples” (Gen. 49:10) — one of the earliest and clearest prophecies in the Old Testament pointing to a king who would come from the tribe of Judah and reign until all peoples submit to him.
  • Chapter 50: Jacob dies and, as he had commanded, is buried in the cave of Machpelah in Canaan. Joseph’s brothers fear he will now take revenge, but Joseph says, “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today” (Gen. 50:20). Before his own death, Joseph commands, “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here” (Gen. 50:25). The book closes with “Joseph died… and he was put in a coffin in Egypt” (Gen. 50:26) — a coffin left in Egypt, yet waiting in hope to one day be carried back to the promised land, becomes Genesis’s final image.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

Genesis begins with God saying, “Let there be light,” and ends with Joseph’s coffin left in Egypt — this looks like a fall from glory into foreign exile, but it is not. Looking back over the whole book: God made a good world, yet man rebelled in Eden, bringing curse and death; sin spread rapidly, until God judged the whole earth by flood, yet preserved Noah’s family, renewing the mandate to “be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.” Humanity, at Babel, again tried to make a name for itself, and God scattered them and confused their language. It is precisely amid this brokenness that God chose one man, Abraham, promising to bless all the families of the earth through his offspring — a promise carried forward through the weakness and failure of Isaac and Jacob, now arriving at Jacob’s sons: Judah — the very son who once proposed selling Joseph, and who had his own shameful episode with Tamar — receives the blessing pointing to a future king: “the scepter shall not depart from Judah… until tribute comes to him” (Gen. 49:10). Joseph — the son sold into slavery, unjustly imprisoned, yet full of wisdom to preserve his family’s life — sums up his whole life in the words, “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Gen. 50:20), almost a miniature of the whole book’s message of God’s providence: humanity fails, rebels, and harms one another again and again, yet God is forever weaving his plan of salvation above human malice and weakness. At the book’s end, Joseph’s bones remain in Egypt, awaiting a deliverer who would one day visit the Israelites and lead them out of Egypt into the promised land (Ex. 3:16–17) — this unburied coffin is the final suspended thread Genesis leaves its readers, and the most concrete foreshadowing pointing to the true “Shiloh,” the one truly descended from the tribe of Judah who would hold royal power until all peoples submit to him: Jesus Christ (Rev. 5:5).

Response

Genesis begins with the brokenness of Eden and ends with a coffin hoping to return to the promised land — this reminds you that God’s people have, from the very beginning, been a people “living within the promise, yet not having received the promise.” You too may, like Joseph, be living in a world where the promise is not yet fully fulfilled, hemmed in by circumstances, by others’ malice, by your own weakness. But the true King who comes from the tribe of Judah — the true “Shiloh,” who truly holds royal power until all peoples submit to him, Jesus Christ — has already come, and through the cross and resurrection, accomplished a salvation greater than the exodus. His resurrection is God’s assurance to you: everyone who takes refuge in him will finally return to that better promised land, just as Joseph believed.

title: 安息日：在主里得自由 (Freedom in Him)
content:
今天是安息日，也是一个值得纪念的日子——我们读完了创世记全书！照着神起初所定的节奏，今天不读新的经文，只是停下来，回顾、感恩、安歇。

这一周（卅四至五十章）我们读到这个家族最难堪的一面（底拿事件），也读到约瑟从被卖为奴、含冤下监，到位极人臣、饶恕全家的整个历程，最后以雅各、约瑟相继离世、全家仍寄居埃及、心系应许之地作结。回顾整卷创世记，从起初的创造，到人的堕落，到挪亚方舟，到巴别塔，再到亚伯拉罕、以撒、雅各、约瑟四代人的信心旅程——你会发现一条清楚的线索：人一次又一次地失败、跌倒，神却一次又一次地施恩、拣选、成就祂起初的应许，从未间断。

约瑟的一生尤其浓缩了整卷书的信息：他被至亲出卖，却在神手中，成了保全全家性命的人；他本可以用权力报复，却选择饶恕。这提醒我们：神能使用人生命中最黑暗的遭遇，成就祂最美好的心意。

建议你今天：①回顾创世记这三周的旅程，为自己坚持读完这一卷书献上感恩；②挑一位创世记里的人物（挪亚、亚伯拉罕、雅各或约瑟），想想他的哪一点最触动你；③安静祷告，求神帮助你带着这份盼望，继续接下来的读经旅程（下一卷是出埃及记）。

应用：今天用一句话，为自己写下「完成创世记」的纪念——可以是一句祷告，也可以是一句提醒未来自己的话。
content_en:
Today is a Sabbath day, and also a day worth marking — we’ve finished reading the whole book of Genesis! Following the rhythm God set from the beginning, today we read nothing new, just stop, look back, give thanks, and rest.

This week (chapters 34–50) we read the most shameful side of this family (the incident with Dinah), as well as Joseph’s whole journey from being sold into slavery and unjustly imprisoned, to becoming second only to Pharaoh, and forgiving his whole family — ending with Jacob and then Joseph dying, the family still sojourning in Egypt, their hearts set on the promised land. Looking back over the whole book of Genesis, from creation at the beginning, through humanity’s fall, Noah’s ark, Babel, and then the four-generation journey of faith of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph — you’ll find one clear thread: humanity fails and stumbles again and again, yet God, again and again, shows grace, chooses, and fulfills his original promise, without ever breaking off.

Joseph’s life especially condenses the message of the whole book: betrayed by his own closest kin, yet in God’s hand he became the one who preserved his whole family’s life; he could have used his power for revenge, but chose to forgive instead. This reminds us that God can use the darkest experiences of a life to accomplish his very best purposes.

Today, consider: (1) Look back over these three weeks’ journey through Genesis, and give thanks for having persevered through this whole book. (2) Pick one figure from Genesis (Noah, Abraham, Jacob, or Joseph) and reflect on what about him moves you most. (3) Pray quietly, asking God to help you carry this hope forward into the next stage of your reading journey (the next book is Exodus).

Application: Write yourself a one-sentence memorial today for “finishing Genesis” — it can be a prayer, or a reminder to your future self.

title: 以色列人埃及为奴
verse: 出埃及记二章廿三节至廿五节
content:
书卷背景

出埃及记的希伯来书卷名，取自开头一语「他们的名字记在下面」（出1:1）的原文（Shemot，即「名字」）——焦点一开始就落在雅各全家一个个具体的名字上，提醒读者这卷书要记的不是抽象的民族史，而是神纪念、认识、呼唤这一个个真实的人。中文与英文书名「出埃及记／Exodus」（原意「离开」）则取自全书的核心事件：神如何把这群为奴之民从埃及领出来。传统上，本书与摩西五经其余四卷同出摩西之手；他既是这段历史的核心当事人，也是神启示律法、吩咐建造会幕的直接领受者。全书大致分三段：以色列在埃及为奴、神藉摩西施行拯救（1-18章）；西奈山下立约、颁布律法（19-24章）；会幕的样式与建造（25-40章）。出埃及记记载的，是旧约中最核心、最具范式意义的救赎事件——后来的先知一再借用这次拯救的语言来描绘神未来的作为，新约更直接沿用这个框架——路加福音记耶稣在山上向摩西、以利亚「谈论耶稣去世的事」（路9:31），原文「去世」一词正是「出埃及」（exodos）；出埃及记因此不只是一段历史，更是神百姓认识救赎是什么样式的原型。

在全书结构中的位置

一至二章是全书的起点，承接创世记末了雅各全家寄居埃及、约瑟已死的处境，展开为奴与拯救主题的铺垫：一章交代以色列人如何从寄居沦为奴仆，二章记载拯救者摩西的出生与预备——但这预备本身还未见神亲自出场说话；神的沉默与百姓的哀声，正把读者引向三章荆棘火焰的伏笔。

主题与神学重点
  • 一章：约瑟已死，「有不认识约瑟的新王起来」（出1:8），以色列人「生养众多，并且繁茂，极其强盛」（出1:7），正应验神向亚伯拉罕的应许，却也招来埃及王的忌惮与压迫，从苦役升级到命收生婆杀婴，末了竟下令把男婴丢在河里；收生婆因「敬畏神」（出1:17）拒绝从命，神也厚待她们。
  • 二章：摩西出生，被藏三个月后放在蒲草箱中，被法老的女儿收养，长大后因打死一个欺压同胞的埃及人而逃往米甸——这拯救者自己，也是从死地被水救出来的人；本章末了笔锋一转，离开摩西的个人际遇，交代埃及王已死，而以色列人「因做苦工，就叹息哀求，他们的哀声达于神」（出2:23），神也未曾忘记他们。
救赎历史脉络

这两章看似只是背景铺垫，实则已经把全书的救赎逻辑立好了：以色列人生养众多、极其强盛（出1:7），正应验神向亚伯拉罕列祖的应许；他们所受的苦待与为奴，也不是神计划之外的意外。真正关键的是二章末了神的动作——不是因百姓做了什么配得拯救的事，而单单因为神「记念他与亚伯拉罕、以撒、雅各所立的约」（出2:24）。这与后来神差遣祂儿子的次序完全一致：不是因为世人配得，乃是因祂立约的信实。摩西从水中被救、从死地被留存性命，也预表了神一贯的拯救方式——透过一位蒙拣选、经历死里逃生的中保，来成就百姓的拯救。

回应

你若觉得自己的处境像以色列人在埃及那样，只能「叹息哀求」（出2:23），却看不到神在哪里——这两章要告诉你：神的沉默从不等于神的缺席。「神听见他们的哀声，就记念他与亚伯拉罕、以撒、雅各所立的约」（出2:24），「神看顾以色列人，也知道他们的苦情」（出2:25）；而在基督里，这份纪念已经成就到底——十字架正是神为祂百姓所行的、比出埃及更大的拯救。你不需要先证明自己配得纪念，只需要像当日的以色列人一样，在苦情中转向那位垂听祈求的神。
content_en:
Book Background

Exodus’s Hebrew title is taken from its opening words, “these are the names” (Ex. 1:1) — in Hebrew, Shemot, meaning “names.” The focus falls, from the very start, on the individual, specific names of Jacob’s whole family, reminding readers that this book is not recording abstract national history, but the story of God remembering, knowing, and calling real, individual people. The Chinese and English titles, “Exodus” (meaning “departure”), are drawn from the book’s central event: how God led this enslaved people out of Egypt. Tradition attributes this book, along with the rest of the Pentateuch, to Moses, who was both the central figure in this history and the direct recipient of God’s revelation of the law and instructions for building the tabernacle. The book falls broadly into three sections: Israel enslaved in Egypt and God’s deliverance through Moses (chapters 1–18); the covenant made and the law given at Sinai (chapters 19–24); and the pattern and construction of the tabernacle (chapters 25–40). Exodus records the most central, paradigmatic act of redemption in the Old Testament — later prophets repeatedly borrow the language of this deliverance to describe God’s future acts, and the New Testament directly adopts this same framework. Luke’s Gospel records Jesus on the mountain speaking with Moses and Elijah “of his departure” (Luke 9:31) — the Greek word for “departure” there is exodos itself. Exodus, then, is not merely a piece of history, but the prototype by which God’s people come to understand the very shape of redemption.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 1–2 are the book’s starting point, picking up from the end of Genesis, where Jacob’s whole family sojourns in Egypt and Joseph has died, and laying the groundwork for the themes of slavery and deliverance: chapter 1 tells how the Israelites went from sojourners to slaves; chapter 2 records the birth and preparation of the deliverer Moses — but this preparation itself does not yet include God stepping forward to speak. God’s silence and the people’s groaning are precisely what draws the reader toward the burning bush of chapter 3.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 1: Joseph has died, and “a new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph” (Ex. 1:8). The Israelites “were fruitful and increased greatly; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong” (Ex. 1:7), exactly fulfilling God’s promise to Abraham — yet this also stirs the Egyptian king’s fear and oppression, escalating from forced labor to ordering the midwives to kill the infant boys, and finally commanding that baby boys be thrown into the river. The midwives, “because they feared God” (Ex. 1:17), refuse to obey, and God deals well with them.
  • Chapter 2: Moses is born, hidden for three months, then placed in a basket of reeds and adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter. Grown, he flees to Midian after killing an Egyptian who was oppressing a fellow Hebrew — this deliverer himself is a man saved from death by water. The chapter then turns from Moses’s personal story to note that the king of Egypt has died, and the Israelites, “because of their slavery, cried out for help. Their cry for rescue from slavery came up to God” (Ex. 2:23), and God had not forgotten them.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

These two chapters seem to be mere background, but they have already set in place the redemptive logic of the whole book: the Israelites being fruitful and exceedingly strong (Ex. 1:7) exactly fulfills God’s promise to the patriarch Abraham; the suffering and slavery they endure are not an accident outside God’s plan either. What truly matters is God’s action at the end of chapter 2 — not because the people did anything to deserve rescue, but solely because God “remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob” (Ex. 2:24). This is entirely consistent with the later order in which God sends his Son: not because the world deserves it, but because of his covenant faithfulness. Moses being saved from the water, his life preserved from death, also foreshadows God’s consistent pattern of salvation — accomplishing his people’s deliverance through a chosen mediator who himself passes through a brush with death.

Response

If you feel your situation is like Israel’s in Egypt — able only to “cry out for help” (Ex. 2:23), unable to see where God is — these two chapters tell you: God’s silence never means God’s absence. “God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob… God saw the people of Israel — and God knew” (Ex. 2:24–25). And in Christ, this remembering has been fulfilled to the very end — the cross is precisely the greater deliverance God accomplished for his people, greater even than the exodus. You don’t need to first prove yourself worthy of being remembered; you need only, like Israel then, turn in your distress to the God who hears the cry for help.

title: 救主的出现
verse: 出埃及记三章十四节
content:
书卷背景

出埃及记记载神救赎百姓脱离埃及为奴之地、在西奈立约、并吩咐建造会幕；三至五章正处在拯救行动正式展开的起点。

在全书结构中的位置

承接一至二章的铺垫——神应许纪念祂的约，如今在何烈山的荆棘火焰中亲自向摩西显现，正式差遣他去；四至五章记摩西的推辞与装备，以及他与亚伦初次求见法老，却换来百姓更重的苦役——拯救的开始，看起来反倒像雪上加霜。

主题与神学重点
  • 三章：荆棘被火烧却不烧毁，神在何烈山向摩西显现，自称「我是自有永有的」（出3:14），并应许「我必与你同在」（出3:12），差遣摩西去领以色列人出埃及。
  • 四章：神赐摩西行神迹的能力（杖变蛇、手长大麻风又复原），摩西仍以「我本是拙口笨舌的」（出4:10）推辞，神便派亚伦作他的口；摩西回埃及途中几乎被神击杀，因西坡拉为儿子行割礼才得脱免（出4:24-26）。
  • 五章：摩西、亚伦初次求见法老，法老不但拒绝，反倒加重以色列人的苦工，不再供应做砖的草料；摩西也向耶和华诉苦：「你为什么苦待这百姓呢」（出5:22）
救赎历史脉络

神的名字「我是自有永有的」（出3:14）是全旧约对神自身最核心的自我启示——祂的存在不依附任何受造之物，祂的信实也不受任何处境左右；这个名字随即成了神与以色列立约关系的根基：「耶和华是我的名，直到永远」（出3:15）。这同一个「我是」，正是耶稣在世上刻意重提的宣告——祂对犹太人说「还没有亚伯拉罕就有了我」（约8:58），用的正是荆棘火焰中那位神自称的方式，宣告自己与那位向摩西显现的耶和华同一位格。

回应

摩西在荆棘前问「我是什么人，竟能去见法老」（出3:11），神却没有回答摩西够不够格，而只应许「我必与你同在」（出3:12）——这也是你今天可以支取的应许：你的资格从不是神差遣、神同在的基础，神自己的信实才是。那位向摩西自称「我是自有永有的」的神，也是那位在耶稣基督里说「还没有亚伯拉罕就有了我」的神——你不必先证明自己配得被用，只需要回应祂差遣的呼召。
content_en:
Book Background

Exodus records God redeeming his people out of slavery in Egypt, making covenant at Sinai, and commanding the building of the tabernacle; chapters 3–5 stand at the very start of the deliverance being formally set in motion.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Picking up from the groundwork of chapters 1–2 — God’s promise to remember his covenant — he now personally appears to Moses in the burning bush at Horeb, formally commissioning him. Chapters 4–5 record Moses’s reluctance and equipping, and his and Aaron’s first appeal to Pharaoh, which instead brings even heavier labor on the people — the beginning of deliverance looks, at first, more like things getting worse.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 3: A bush burns yet is not consumed; God appears to Moses at Horeb, declaring himself, “I AM WHO I AM” (Ex. 3:14), and promises, “I will be with you” (Ex. 3:12), sending Moses to lead the Israelites out of Egypt.
  • Chapter 4: God gives Moses the power to perform signs (a staff turned to a snake, a hand made leprous and then restored), yet Moses still protests, “I am slow of speech and of tongue” (Ex. 4:10), so God appoints Aaron as his mouth. On the way back to Egypt, Moses nearly dies at God’s hand, and is spared only when Zipporah circumcises their son (Ex. 4:24–26).
  • Chapter 5: Moses and Aaron make their first appeal to Pharaoh, who not only refuses but increases the Israelites’ labor, no longer supplying straw for making bricks. Moses even complains to the LORD: “Why have you done evil to this people?” (Ex. 5:22).
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

God’s name, “I AM WHO I AM” (Ex. 3:14), is the Old Testament’s most central self-revelation of who God is — his existence depends on nothing created, and his faithfulness is unaffected by any circumstance. This name immediately becomes the foundation of God’s covenant relationship with Israel: “the LORD… this is my name forever” (Ex. 3:15). This very same “I AM” is the declaration Jesus deliberately reasserts on earth — he tells the Jews, “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58), using the very self-designation of the God of the burning bush, declaring that he is one and the same person as the LORD who appeared to Moses.

Response

Moses, before the bush, asks, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh?” (Ex. 3:11), yet God does not answer whether Moses is qualified — he only promises, “I will be with you” (Ex. 3:12). This is also a promise you can draw on today: your qualification was never the basis for God’s sending or God’s presence; God’s own faithfulness is. The God who declared himself to Moses as “I AM WHO I AM” is also the God who, in Jesus Christ, said, “before Abraham was, I am” — you don’t need to first prove yourself worthy to be used; you need only respond to his call.

title: 九灾降埃及：起头四灾
title_en: Nine Plagues on Egypt: The First Four
verse: 出埃及记六章六节至七节
content:
书卷背景

神救赎百姓脱离埃及为奴之地的作为，藉摩西向法老一次次显明祂的大能；六至八章正式拉开十灾的序幕。

在全书结构中的位置

五章百姓因摩西、亚伦的介入反倒加重苦役，六章神便再次向摩西重申祂的救赎心意与祂的圣名；七至八章展开头四灾——血灾、蛙灾、虱灾、蝇灾，是神与埃及诸神正面交锋的开始，也是法老心一次次刚硬、神一次次显明大能这循环模式的起点。

主题与神学重点
  • 六章：神向摩西重申祂的圣名「耶和华」，并宣告完整的救赎应许：「我要用伸出来的膀臂重重地刑罚埃及人，救赎你们脱离他们的重担」（出6:6），「我要以你们为我的百姓，我也要作你们的神」（出6:7）；然而百姓「因苦工愁烦，不肯听他的话」（出6:9）。
  • 七章：摩西八十岁、亚伦八十三岁再次面见法老，杖变蛇、埃及术士也能照样行，但亚伦的杖吞了他们的杖；随后第一灾降下——尼罗河水变血，鱼都死了，埃及人不能喝这河里的水（出7:20-21），法老的心仍然刚硬。
  • 八章：蛙灾、虱灾、蝇灾接连降下；术士能仿制蛙灾、虱灾，到了虱灾却已无能为力，只能承认「这是神的手段」（出8:19）；至蝇灾，神更「将我的百姓和你的百姓分别出来」（出8:23）——歌珊地毫发无损，灾殃只临到埃及人身上。
救赎历史脉络

六章那句「我要以你们为我的百姓，我也要作你们的神」（出6:7），是圣经「立约公式」最早、最完整的表达之一，日后先知反复用同一句话描绘神与祂子民的关系。而灾殃本身不只是惩罚，更是神与埃及众神的公开较量——每一灾都直指埃及人所倚靠的自然与神祇，为要显明耶和华才是独一掌管万有的神。这种神以大能审判假神、拯救属祂之民的模式，也预表了十字架上更深一层的得胜——基督在十字架上「既将一切执政的、掌权的掳来，明显给众人看，就仗着十字架夸胜」（西2:15），成就了比出埃及更彻底的拯救。

回应

你或许也曾像六章的以色列人一样，「因苦工愁烦，不肯听」（出6:9）神应许的话，觉得拯救太过遥远、太过抽象。但神应许要「救赎你们脱离他们的重担」（出6:6），从不取决于你当下有没有力气去相信；祂照样施行了头四灾，照样一步步把百姓领出埃及。在基督里，神已经用祂儿子的死向你显明祂救赎的决心何等确实——你可以带着尚未痊愈的愁烦，仍旧支取这份应许。
content_en:
Book Background

God’s work of redeeming his people out of slavery in Egypt is displayed again and again to Pharaoh through Moses; chapters 6–8 formally open the curtain on the ten plagues.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

In chapter 5, the people’s labor is made even heavier by Moses and Aaron’s intervention; in chapter 6, God reaffirms to Moses his redemptive intent and his holy name. Chapters 7–8 unfold the first four plagues — blood, frogs, gnats, and flies — the opening of a direct confrontation between God and the gods of Egypt, and the start of the recurring pattern of Pharaoh’s heart hardening again and again while God demonstrates his power again and again.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 6: God reaffirms his holy name “the LORD” to Moses, and declares the full promise of redemption: “I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment… I will deliver you from slavery to them” (Ex. 6:6), “I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God” (Ex. 6:7). Yet the people, “because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery,” would not listen to him (Ex. 6:9).
  • Chapter 7: Moses, eighty years old, and Aaron, eighty-three, appear before Pharaoh again; the staff turns to a snake, and the Egyptian magicians do the same, but Aaron’s staff swallows theirs. Then the first plague falls — the water of the Nile turns to blood, the fish die, and the Egyptians cannot drink from the river (Ex. 7:20–21) — yet Pharaoh’s heart remains hard.
  • Chapter 8: Frogs, gnats, and flies follow one after another. The magicians can imitate the frogs and at first the gnats, but by the plague of gnats they are already powerless, forced to admit, “This is the finger of God” (Ex. 8:19). By the plague of flies, God further “makes a distinction between my people and your people” (Ex. 8:23) — Goshen is left untouched, and the plague falls only on the Egyptians.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

The words in chapter 6, “I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God” (Ex. 6:7), are one of the earliest and most complete expressions of the biblical “covenant formula,” a phrase the prophets would repeat again and again to describe God’s relationship with his people. The plagues themselves are not merely punishment, but a public contest between God and the gods of Egypt — each plague strikes directly at what the Egyptians relied on in nature and in their deities, to show that the LORD alone truly governs all things. This pattern of God judging false gods by his power to save his own people also foreshadows a deeper victory at the cross — Christ on the cross “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Col. 2:15), accomplishing a deliverance more thorough even than the exodus.

Response

You too may, like the Israelites in chapter 6, have your “broken spirit” keep you from listening (Ex. 6:9) to God’s promise, feeling that deliverance is too distant, too abstract. But God’s promise to “deliver you from slavery to them” (Ex. 6:6) never depended on whether you currently have the strength to believe it — he carried out the first four plagues just the same, and led the people out of Egypt step by step just the same. In Christ, God has already shown you, through his own Son’s death, how certain his resolve to redeem truly is — you can draw on this promise while still carrying an unhealed, troubled spirit.

title: 死别与生离
verse: 出埃及记十二章十三节
content:
书卷背景

神救赎百姓脱离埃及为奴之地的大能一路彰显；十一至十二章是十灾的最高潮，也是全书救赎主题最核心的一幕。

在全书结构中的位置

十一至十二章是十灾的高潮与转折——从九灾的逐步升级，到第十灾（长子之死）这一击致命；逾越节的设立（十二章）从此把以色列的整个历法、身份、敬拜都重新校准在这一夜的拯救之上。

主题与神学重点
  • 十一章：神宣告最后一灾——「约到半夜，我必出去巡行埃及遍地……凡在埃及地……所有的长子……都必死」（出11:4-5），但「以色列中，无论是人是牲畜，连狗也不敢向他们摇舌」（出11:7），神要把埃及人和以色列人分别出来。
  • 十二章：神吩咐以色列人在正月十四日，各家宰一只无残疾的一岁羊羔，「取点血，涂在吃羊羔的房屋左右的门框上和门楣上」（出12:7），当夜快速吃羊羔的肉；神应许：「这血要在你们所住的房屋上作记号；我一见这血，就越过你们去」（出12:13）；那夜，埃及遍地长子被击杀，「无一家不死一个人的」（出12:30），法老终于容以色列人离开——这一夜从此定为逾越节，「作为你们世世代代永远的定例」（出12:14）。
救赎历史脉络

逾越节的羊羔，是全旧约中最直接、最完整的基督预表——保罗在林前五章直接说：「我们逾越节的羔羊基督已经被杀献祭了」（林前5:7），把这一章的意象不加转弯地安在耶稣身上；这不是后人牵强附会的类比，而是圣经自己给出的解读：羊羔必须「无残疾」（出12:5），预表基督的无罪；羊羔的血涂在门框上，长子才得存活，预表基督的血成了神审判越过我们的记号；律法又吩咐羊羔「骨头一根也不可折断」（出12:46）——约翰福音记载耶稣被钉十字架、兵丁见祂已经死了就没有打断祂的腿，应验了经上「他的骨头一根也不可折断」（约19:36）的话。逾越节从不是一个孤立的礼仪，而是神提前把十字架的道理，写进以色列人每年要吃的这一顿饭里。

回应

「我一见这血，就越过你们去」（出12:13）——这句话的重点，从来不是以色列人有多虔诚、多害怕、多用力祈祷，而单单是血本身在不在门框上。今天，你不需要用自己的良善去说服神放过你；基督已经作了那无残疾的逾越节羔羊，祂的血已经涂在你生命的门框上，神审判的使者已经越过你去了——你所要做的，只是安心留在那血所遮盖的房屋里，如同当夜的以色列人一样，凭信心接受这一已经成就的记号。
content_en:
Book Background

God’s power to redeem his people out of slavery in Egypt has been displayed step by step; chapters 11–12 are the climax of the ten plagues, and the single most central scene in the whole book’s theme of redemption.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 11–12 are the climax and turning point of the ten plagues — from the gradual escalation of nine plagues to the tenth (the death of the firstborn), a single fatal blow. The institution of the Passover (chapter 12) recalibrates Israel’s entire calendar, identity, and worship around this one night of deliverance from then on.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 11: God announces the final plague — “about midnight I will go out in the midst of Egypt, and every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die” (Ex. 11:4–5) — yet “not a dog shall growl” against any of the Israelites, “that you may know that the LORD makes a distinction” (Ex. 11:7) between Egypt and Israel.
  • Chapter 12: God commands each Israelite household to slaughter a year-old lamb without blemish on the fourteenth day of the first month, “take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses” (Ex. 12:7), and eat the lamb’s flesh hurriedly that same night. God promises: “The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are… and when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Ex. 12:13). That night, the firstborn throughout Egypt are struck down — “there was not a house where someone was not dead” (Ex. 12:30) — and Pharaoh finally lets Israel go. This night is established from then on as the Passover, “a statute forever” throughout their generations (Ex. 12:14).
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

The Passover lamb is the most direct and complete foreshadowing of Christ in the whole Old Testament — Paul says directly in 1 Corinthians 5, “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7), applying this chapter’s imagery to Jesus without any hesitation — this is not a strained later analogy, but Scripture’s own interpretation. The lamb had to be “without blemish” (Ex. 12:5), foreshadowing Christ’s sinlessness; the lamb’s blood on the doorposts is what preserved the firstborn, foreshadowing Christ’s blood as the sign that causes God’s judgment to pass over us. The law also commanded that “you shall not break any of its bones” (Ex. 12:46) — John’s Gospel records that when Jesus was crucified, the soldiers, seeing he was already dead, did not break his legs, fulfilling the Scripture, “Not one of his bones will be broken” (John 19:36). The Passover was never an isolated ritual, but God writing the meaning of the cross, ahead of time, into a meal the Israelites would eat every single year.

Response

“When I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Ex. 12:13) — the point of this sentence was never how devout, how afraid, or how earnestly the Israelites prayed, but solely whether the blood itself was on the doorframe. Today, you don’t need to persuade God to spare you with your own goodness; Christ has already become that lamb without blemish, and his blood has already been placed on the doorframe of your life — the angel of God’s judgment has already passed over you. All you need to do is remain safely in the house covered by that blood, just as the Israelites did that night, receiving by faith this sign already accomplished.

title: 过红海与凯歌
title_en: Crossing the Red Sea, and the Song of Victory
verse: 出埃及记十五章二节
content:
书卷背景

神领百姓脱离埃及为奴之地、又要经西奈带他们到应许之地；十三至十五章记载出埃及行动的实际完成，与百姓第一次的敬拜回应。

在全书结构中的位置

十二章末了以色列人已经离开埃及，十三章交代无酵节、头生的分别为圣，以及神以云柱火柱引路；十四章是全书戏剧性的高潮——红海在以色列人面前分开，法老全军却被海水吞没；十五章摩西之歌是以色列人经历拯救后第一首向神发出的敬拜诗歌，为全书从「拯救」转向「西奈立约」做了预备。

主题与神学重点
  • 十三章：神吩咐分别一切头生的「分别为圣归我」（出13:2），又吩咐世世代代守无酵节记念出埃及的日子；神不领百姓走近路，反倒「领百姓绕道而行，走红海旷野的路」（出13:18），日间用云柱、夜间用火柱引导他们（出13:21）。
  • 十四章：法老后悔放走以色列人，率全军追赶，百姓在红海前惧怕，向摩西抱怨「你把我们带来死在旷野吗」（出14:11）；摩西宣告「耶和华必为你们争战；你们只管静默，不要作声」（出14:14），神使海水分开，「以色列人下海中走干地」（出14:22），随后海水回流，法老的全军「连一个也没有剩下」（出14:28）。
  • 十五章：摩西和以色列人唱歌赞美耶和华：「耶和华是我的力量，我的诗歌，也成了我的拯救」（出15:2）；随后百姓在旷野三日找不着水，到玛拉水苦不能喝，耶和华指示一棵树使水变甜（出15:22-25）。
救赎历史脉络

红海之工，是出埃及记里神拯救大能最戏剧化的展示——百姓什么也没有做，只是站住、静默（出14:13-14），神却亲自「为你们争战」（出14:14），一举了结埃及全军。这正是恩典最纯粹的样式：拯救的功劳全然在神，人只是在受造者的地位上经历、领受，然后歌唱回应。摩西的歌不是靠自己的能力换来的凯歌，而是「你凭慈爱领了你所赎的百姓」（出15:13）之后自然涌出的敬拜——这也预表了十字架之后教会敬拜的原型：不是靠行为换来拯救然后歌唱，而是先经历神单方面成就的拯救，才有话可唱。启示录论到末后得胜的圣徒，用的正是这幅图画：「唱神仆人摩西的歌和羔羊的歌」（启15:3）——红海的拯救与羔羊十字架的拯救，被圣经自己连成一首歌。

回应

以色列人在红海边所做的，只是「站住」，看耶和华为他们争战（出14:13-14）；他们过红海、唱凯歌，靠的不是自己的勇气或行为，而单单是神主动的拯救。你今天若还在为自己配不配得救恩挣扎，摩西的歌提醒你：「耶和华是我的力量，我的诗歌，也成了我的拯救」（出15:2）——这句话的主词，从头到尾都是神的作为，而不是你的表现；你所要做的，只是像那日的以色列人一样，因所领受的拯救而歌唱、而敬拜。
content_en:
Book Background

God leads his people out of slavery in Egypt, and will bring them, by way of Sinai, to the promised land; chapters 13–15 record the actual completion of the exodus, and the people’s first response of worship.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

By the end of chapter 12 the Israelites have already left Egypt; chapter 13 tells of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the consecration of the firstborn, and God leading the way by pillar of cloud and fire. Chapter 14 is the book’s dramatic climax — the Red Sea parts before Israel, while Pharaoh’s whole army is swallowed by the returning waters. Chapter 15, the Song of Moses, is Israel’s first hymn of worship offered to God after experiencing deliverance, and prepares the transition from “deliverance” to “covenant at Sinai.”

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 13: God commands that every firstborn be set apart, “consecrated to me” (Ex. 13:2), and that all generations keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread to commemorate the day of the exodus. God does not lead the people by the shortest route, but instead “led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea” (Ex. 13:18), guiding them by a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night (Ex. 13:21).
  • Chapter 14: Pharaoh regrets letting Israel go and pursues them with his whole army; the people, terrified before the Red Sea, complain to Moses, “have you brought us out to die in the wilderness?” (Ex. 14:11). Moses declares, “The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent” (Ex. 14:14); God parts the sea, “the people of Israel walked on dry ground through the sea” (Ex. 14:22), and when the waters return, not one of Pharaoh’s whole army is left (Ex. 14:28).
  • Chapter 15: Moses and the Israelites sing to the LORD: “The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation” (Ex. 15:2). Afterward, the people find no water for three days in the wilderness, and at Marah the water is too bitter to drink, until the LORD shows Moses a piece of wood that sweetens the water (Ex. 15:22–25).
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

The parting of the Red Sea is the most dramatic display of God’s saving power in Exodus — the people do nothing at all but stand still and be silent (Ex. 14:13–14), while God himself “fights for you” (Ex. 14:14), single-handedly finishing off Pharaoh’s entire army. This is grace in its purest form: the credit for salvation belongs entirely to God; humanity, in its creaturely place, simply experiences and receives it, and then responds in song. Moses’s song is not a victory song purchased by his own ability, but worship that naturally overflows after “you have led in your steadfast love the people whom you have redeemed” (Ex. 15:13) — this also foreshadows the pattern of the church’s worship after the cross: not earning salvation through works and then singing, but first experiencing the salvation God alone accomplished, and only then having something to sing about. Revelation, describing the saints who overcome at the end, uses this very image: they “sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (Rev. 15:3) — Scripture itself joins the deliverance at the Red Sea and the deliverance of the Lamb’s cross into a single song.

Response

All the Israelites did at the Red Sea was “stand still” and watch the LORD fight for them (Ex. 14:13–14); their crossing the sea and singing the song of victory rested not on their own courage or works, but solely on God’s own initiative to save. If you are still struggling today over whether you deserve salvation, Moses’s song reminds you: “The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation” (Ex. 15:2) — the subject of this sentence, from start to finish, is God’s action, not your performance. All you need to do is, like Israel that day, sing and worship because of the salvation you have received.

title: 安息日：属灵的加油站 (Spiritual Refuelling)
content:
今天是安息日——不读新经文，只是停下脚步，回顾这一周神何等奇妙的拯救，也安歇在祂里面。

这一周我们进入出埃及记：以色列人在埃及为奴受苦（一至二章），摩西蒙召、初次交涉却招来更重的苦役（三至五章），神重申救赎的应许、降下头三样灾（六至八章），逾越节的设立与埃及长子被击杀（十一至十二章），最后以红海分开、以色列人高唱凯歌作结（十三至十五章）。短短一周，我们看着一群为奴四百年的百姓，经历神一步步、按着祂自己的时间表，把他们从埃及带出来——这正是全本圣经里最重要的「拯救」预表之一，后来新约多次以「出埃及」来描绘基督救赎我们脱离罪的奴役。

留意这段旅程里，以色列人从未靠自己的力量成就拯救——是神听见他们的哀声，是神使法老让步，是神分开红海，也是神使他们唱出凯歌。拯救从头到尾都是神的作为，人的角色只是回应与信靠。

建议你今天：①回顾出埃及记一至十五章，挑一幕印象最深的场景重读一遍；②想一想自己生命中是否也有一段「红海」式的绝境，神是怎样为你开路的；③安静片刻，单单为神的拯救献上感恩与赞美。

应用：今天用一句话，把你自己的「出埃及」故事写下来——神曾经怎样把你从某种捆绑中领出来？
content_en:
Today is a Sabbath day — no new reading, just stop, look back over how wonderfully God has saved this week, and rest in him.

This week we entered Exodus: Israel suffering as slaves in Egypt (chapters 1–2), Moses’s call and his first negotiation, which instead brought heavier labor (chapters 3–5), God reaffirming his promise of redemption and sending the first three plagues (chapters 6–8), the institution of the Passover and the death of Egypt’s firstborn (chapters 11–12), and finally the Red Sea parting and Israel singing its song of victory (chapters 13–15). In just one week, we’ve watched a people enslaved for four hundred years experience God, step by step, on his own timetable, bringing them out of Egypt — one of the most important foreshadowings of “deliverance” in the whole Bible, one the New Testament repeatedly uses the language of “exodus” to describe as Christ redeeming us from slavery to sin.

Notice that throughout this journey, the Israelites never accomplished their own deliverance by their own strength — it was God who heard their cry, God who made Pharaoh yield, God who parted the Red Sea, and God who put the song of victory in their mouths. From beginning to end, salvation was God’s work; humanity’s role was only to respond and to trust.

Today, consider: (1) Look back over Exodus 1–15 and reread the scene that struck you most. (2) Think about whether there has been a “Red Sea” moment of your own — a dead end in your life — and how God made a way for you there. (3) Be still for a moment, simply offering thanks and praise for God’s salvation.

Application: Write down, in one sentence, your own “exodus” story today — how has God once led you out of some kind of bondage?

title: 旷野里最大的敌人
title_en: The Greatest Enemy in the Wilderness
verse: 出埃及记十六章四节
content:
书卷背景

以色列人才刚经过红海、脱离追兵（十五章），出埃及记接下来要记的，却不是凯旋进迦南，而是一连串旷野中的抱怨与失败——从汛的旷野到西奈山下，这段路正是神藉着环境考验这群刚蒙救赎之民的信心。

在全书结构中的位置

十六至十八章夹在「神救以色列出埃及」（一至十五章）与「神在西奈山与以色列立约」（十九章起）之间，是一段过渡：百姓要在旷野学会仰赖那位已经救赎他们的神，才能预备好在西奈山下领受律法。

主题与神学重点
  • 十六章：百姓因缺粮向摩西、亚伦发怨言，说「巴不得我们早死在埃及地」（出16:3）——竟宁愿为奴而死，也不肯信靠那位刚用大能救他们出埃及的神；耶和华却不以怒气回应，反而应许「我要将粮食从天降给你们」（出16:4），并说明这吗哪其实是每日一次的信心考验：「我好试验他们遵不遵我的法度」（出16:4）。
  • 十七章：利非订缺水，百姓再次「与摩西争闹」（出17:2），摩西称那地为玛撒、米利巴，因百姓「试探耶和华」（出17:7）；随后亚玛力人来袭，摩西举手以色列得胜、垂手亚玛力人得胜——得胜不是靠拳头，而是靠那双被亚伦、户珥扶住的代祷之手。
  • 十八章：摩西的岳父叶忒罗提醒他不可事事独自审判，「你和这些百姓必都疲惫」（出18:18），建议设立千夫长、百夫长等分层治理，预备百姓即将在西奈山下承受更完整的律法与体制。
救赎历史脉络

十六章的吗哪，是全本圣经最重要的预表之一。耶稣在约翰福音六章亲自把这段历史接过来说：「你们的祖宗在旷野吃过吗哪，还是死了。这是从天上降下来的粮，叫人吃了就不死」（约6:49-50），又宣告「我就是生命的粮。到我这里来的，必定不饿；信我的，永远不渴」（约6:35）。吗哪只能维系以色列人肉身一天的性命，且吃过的人终究都死了；耶稣却说：「我是从天上降下来生命的粮；人若吃这粮，就必永远活着」（约6:51）——祂就是吗哪一直指向、却无法真正成就的那实体。

回应

以色列人在缺粮时的第一反应是抱怨，甚至宁愿死在为奴之地，也不信靠那位已经用大能救赎他们的神——这也常是你我面对缺乏时的光景。但耶稣基督已经把自己当作从天上降下来的粮，白白赐给世人：「我所要赐的粮就是我的肉，为世人之生命所赐的」（约6:51）；你不需要先证明自己配得，只需要来到祂面前领受——「凡父所赐给我的人必到我这里来；到我这里来的，我总不丢弃他」（约6:37）。
content_en:
Book Background

The Israelites have only just crossed the Red Sea and escaped their pursuers (chapter 15); what Exodus records next, though, is not a triumphant march into Canaan, but a string of complaints and failures in the wilderness — from the Wilderness of Sin to the foot of Mount Sinai, this stretch of road is where God tests, through circumstance, the faith of this newly redeemed people.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 16–18 sit between “God saving Israel out of Egypt” (chapters 1–15) and “God making covenant with Israel at Sinai” (from chapter 19), a transitional section: the people must learn in the wilderness to depend on the God who has already redeemed them, before they are ready to receive the law at the foot of Sinai.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 16: Lacking food, the people grumble against Moses and Aaron, saying, “Would that we had died… in the land of Egypt” (Ex. 16:3) — actually preferring death in slavery to trusting the God who had just powerfully brought them out of Egypt. Yet the LORD does not respond in anger, but instead promises, “I will rain bread from heaven for you” (Ex. 16:4), explaining that this manna is in fact a daily test of faith: “that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not” (Ex. 16:4).
  • Chapter 17: At Rephidim, water runs out, and the people again “quarrel with Moses” (Ex. 17:2). Moses names that place Massah and Meribah, because the people “tested the LORD” (Ex. 17:7). Then the Amalekites attack; when Moses raises his hands Israel prevails, when he lowers them Amalek prevails — victory comes not from raw strength, but from those hands held up by Aaron and Hur in intercession.
  • Chapter 18: Moses’s father-in-law Jethro warns him not to judge everything alone — “you and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out” (Ex. 18:18) — and suggests appointing chiefs of thousands, hundreds, and so on to share the governing, preparing the people to receive a fuller law and structure at Sinai.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

The manna in chapter 16 is one of the most important foreshadowings in the whole Bible. Jesus himself takes up this history in John 6: “Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die” (John 6:49–50), and declares, “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6:35). Manna could only sustain the Israelites’ physical life for a single day, and everyone who ate it eventually died. But Jesus says, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (John 6:51) — he is the very reality the manna always pointed to but could never truly provide.

Response

The Israelites’ first reaction, when food ran short, was to complain, even preferring death in slavery to trusting the God who had already redeemed them with such power — this is also often the state you and I are in when we face lack. But Jesus Christ has already given himself as the bread come down from heaven, freely given to the world: “the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh” (John 6:51). You don’t need to first prove yourself worthy; you need only come to him and receive — “All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

title: 摩西的约──十诫
title_en: The Covenant at Sinai: The Ten Commandments
verse: 出埃及记十九章五节至六节
content:
书卷背景

以色列人出埃及后满了三个月，来到西奈山下——从红海到西奈，一路经历了吗哪、磐石出水、亚玛力之战、叶忒罗设立审判体制的操练。

在全书结构中的位置

十九至二十章是全书神学重心的开端：从「神如何救赎百姓」（一至十八章）转向「蒙救赎的百姓当如何生活」（十九章起）。这个次序至关重要——出埃及记先记拯救，后记律法；西奈之约不是以色列换取拯救的条件，而是已经蒙拯救之民与神立约、领受生活样式的场景。

主题与神学重点
  • 十九章：神呼召以色列之前，先陈明祂已经做成的事——「我如鹰将你们背在翅膀上，带来归我」（出19:4）；然后才说「如今你们若实在听从我的话，遵守我的约，就要在万民中作属我的子民」（出19:5），并宣告「你们要归我作祭司的国度，为圣洁的国民」（出19:6）；百姓自洁三日，在雷轰、闪电、密云、角声中战兢迎见神降临西奈山。
  • 二十章：十诫的序言已经点明整段律法的根基——「我是耶和华－你的神，曾将你从埃及地为奴之家领出来」（出20:2）；先讲拯救之恩，再讲十条诫命，涵盖敬拜独一真神（不可拜偶像、不可妄称主名、当守安息日）与爱人如己的伦理（孝敬父母、不可杀人奸淫偷盗作假见证贪恋）；百姓因惧怕神的荣光，请摩西代为传话。
救赎历史脉络

西奈之约的次序，是整本圣经神学上极重要的一点：律法不是以色列「必须先做到」才能被神拯救的条件，而是神已经在一至十五章单方面、凭恩典救他们出埃及之后，才在十九至二十章赐下的生活准则。以色列的身份先由神的拯救行动确立，诫命只是回应这拯救、活出这身份的方式。新约把这同一次序说得更清楚：「你们得救是本乎恩，也因着信……也不是出于行为，免得有人自夸」（弗2:8-9），行为（善行）总是恩典之后的果子，而非换取恩典的筹码。

回应

以色列被召作「祭司的国度，为圣洁的国民」（出19:6），后来却一再失败，未能活出这身份。但彼得前书把这称呼原封不动地用在教会身上：「惟有你们是被拣选的族类，是有君尊的祭司，是圣洁的国度，是属神的子民」（彼前2:9），而这身份的根据同样不是行为的成就，乃是怜恤：「你们从前算不得子民，现在却作了神的子民；从前未曾蒙怜恤，现在却蒙了怜恤」（彼前2:10）。你若在基督里，也是先蒙了怜恤，才被呼召去过圣洁国民的生活——顺服是感恩的回应，不是换取悦纳的代价。
content_en:
Book Background

Three months after leaving Egypt, the Israelites arrive at the foot of Mount Sinai — from the Red Sea to Sinai, the journey has included manna, water from the rock, war with Amalek, and Jethro’s establishment of a judicial structure.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 19–20 mark the beginning of the book’s theological center of gravity: shifting from “how God redeems his people” (chapters 1–18) to “how a redeemed people ought to live” (from chapter 19 on). This order matters immensely — Exodus records deliverance first, and law second; the covenant at Sinai is not the condition by which Israel earns deliverance, but the setting in which an already-redeemed people enter covenant with God and receive a pattern for life.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 19: Before calling Israel to anything, God first lays out what he has already done: “I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself” (Ex. 19:4); only then does he say, “Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples” (Ex. 19:5), declaring, “you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Ex. 19:6). The people consecrate themselves for three days, and meet God’s descent on Sinai trembling amid thunder, lightning, thick cloud, and trumpet blast.
  • Chapter 20: The preface to the Ten Commandments already states the foundation of the whole law: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Ex. 20:2) — the grace of deliverance is spoken first, the ten commandments second, covering both the worship of the one true God (no idols, no misusing his name, keeping the Sabbath) and the ethic of loving one’s neighbor (honoring parents, and prohibitions against murder, adultery, theft, false testimony, and covetousness). The people, afraid of God’s glory, ask Moses to speak on their behalf.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

The order of the Sinai covenant is a point of immense theological importance for the whole Bible: the law is not a condition Israel “must first meet” in order to be saved by God; it is the pattern for living that God gives only after he has already, unilaterally and by grace, saved them out of Egypt in chapters 1–15. Israel’s identity is established first by God’s act of deliverance; the commandments are simply the way of responding to that deliverance and living out that identity. The New Testament states this same order even more clearly: “For by grace you have been saved through faith… and this is not your own doing… not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. 2:8–9) — works (good deeds) are always the fruit that follows grace, never the currency that purchases it.

Response

Israel was called to be “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Ex. 19:6), yet failed again and again afterward, unable to live out that identity. Yet 1 Peter applies this very title, unchanged, to the church: “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession” (1 Pet. 2:9), and the basis for this identity is likewise not achievement, but mercy: “Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy” (1 Pet. 2:10). If you are in Christ, you too have first received mercy, and only then been called to live as a holy nation — obedience is the grateful response, not the price of acceptance.

title: 典章之颁布
verse: 出埃及记廿一章廿四节
content:
书卷背景

十九至二十章颁布了十诫这总纲，廿一至廿三章（传统称为「约书」）接着把总纲具体应用在日常处境中——奴仆、伤害、财产、审判、节期，各样典章一一展开。

在全书结构中的位置

这几章仍属于西奈之约的范围（廿四章才记百姓正式立约、洒血为凭），是把「不可杀人」「不可奸淫」「不可偷盗」等诫命，转化为具体判例、可以操作的日常律法——从总纲原则走向具体应用。

主题与神学重点
  • 廿一章：希伯来奴仆条例限定了服事的年限（出21:2），保障了奴仆最基本的人身权益；伤害人身的条例订立「若有别害，就要以命偿命，以眼还眼，以牙还牙」（出21:23-24）的原则——这不是鼓励私人报复，而是限制报复，使刑罚必须与所受的伤害相称，不可无限扩大或私自了结。
  • 廿二章：财产纠纷的赔偿细则之外，特别保护社会中最弱势的群体：「不可苦待寡妇和孤儿；若是苦待他们一点，他们向我一哀求，我总要听他们的哀声」（出22:22-23）——神亲自作寡妇孤儿的听讼者。
  • 廿三章：要求审判公正、不可屈枉正直、不可受贿赂，安息年与安息日使土地与人都得歇息，以及一年三次的节期（除酵节、收割节、收藏节）；神应许差遣使者在百姓前面，渐渐把迦南居民从他们面前赶出去。
救赎历史脉络

「以眼还眼，以牙还牙」原是为了限制报复、使刑罚不超过所受伤害的良法，到了耶稣的时代却常被人拿来当作个人报复的借口。耶稣在登山宝训中直接引用这条典章「以眼还眼，以牙还牙」（太5:38），随即说：「只是我告诉你们，不要与恶人作对」（太5:39），进一步呼召门徒「要爱你们的仇敌，为那逼迫你们的祷告」（太5:44）。耶稣并没有废掉这条典章所维护的公义原则——祂自己在十字架上正是承受了那本该按公义追讨在罪人身上的全部代价；祂却呼召蒙恩的人，不再靠自己的手讨回公道，而是效法那位为仇敌舍命代求的主。

回应

你若曾因被亏待而渴望讨回公道，这渴望本身并不邪恶——公义确实该被伸张。但耶稣基督已经在十字架上，担当了公义所要追讨的全部代价，使你不必再靠自己的手报复；祂反倒呼召你效法祂饶恕仇敌的样式去爱、去为逼迫你的人祷告——这不是律法之外多加的重担，而是蒙了怜恤的人，活出怜恤最自然的流露。
content_en:
Book Background

Chapters 19–20 gave the Ten Commandments as the overarching summary; chapters 21–23 (traditionally called the “Book of the Covenant”) then apply that summary concretely to everyday situations — servants, injuries, property, judgment, festivals — with each case law unfolding one by one.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

These chapters still fall within the scope of the Sinai covenant (it is not until chapter 24 that the people formally enter the covenant, sealed with sprinkled blood) — they translate commandments like “you shall not murder,” “you shall not commit adultery,” and “you shall not steal” into concrete, workable case law for daily life, moving from general principle to specific application.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 21: The regulations for Hebrew servants set a limit on the years of service (Ex. 21:2), safeguarding a servant’s most basic personal rights. The regulations for bodily injury establish the principle “life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Ex. 21:23–24) — not to encourage private revenge, but to limit it, ensuring the penalty matches the injury rather than escalating without bound or being settled by private vengeance.
  • Chapter 22: Beyond the details of restitution for property disputes, special protection is given to the most vulnerable in society: “You shall not mistreat any widow or fatherless child. If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry” (Ex. 22:22–23) — God himself acts as the one who hears the case of the widow and the orphan.
  • Chapter 23: Justice must be impartial, never perverted or bribed; the sabbatical year and the Sabbath day give both land and people rest; and three annual feasts are set (Unleavened Bread, Harvest, Ingathering). God promises to send his angel ahead of the people, gradually driving out the inhabitants of Canaan before them.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

“Eye for eye, tooth for tooth” was originally a good law meant to limit retaliation, so that punishment would never exceed the injury suffered — yet by Jesus’s day it was often used as an excuse for personal revenge. Jesus directly quotes this very statute in the Sermon on the Mount, “an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth” (Matt. 5:38), and immediately says, “Do not resist the one who is evil” (Matt. 5:39), further calling his disciples to “love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matt. 5:44). Jesus does not abolish the principle of justice this statute upholds — he himself, on the cross, bore the full penalty justice demanded against sinners; but he calls those who have received his grace no longer to seek redress by their own hand, but to follow the Lord who laid down his life interceding for his enemies.

Response

If you have ever longed for justice after being wronged, that longing itself is not evil — justice truly ought to be done. But Jesus Christ has already borne, on the cross, the full cost that justice demanded, so that you no longer need to take revenge by your own hand. Instead, he calls you to follow his pattern of forgiving enemies — to love, and to pray for those who persecute you. This is not an extra burden added on top of the law, but the most natural overflow of a heart that has itself received mercy.

title: 有关会幕敬拜之指示
verse: 出埃及记廿五章八节
content:
书卷背景

廿四章记百姓正式与神立约、洒血为凭，摩西随后上山四十昼夜；从廿五章起，神开始颁布建造会幕及其器具的详细指示，直到卅一章。

在全书结构中的位置

廿四至廿七章承接十九至廿三章的西奈之约——立约之后，神随即启示祂要如何具体地「与祂的百姓同住」；会幕的指示不只是建筑说明，而是神学蓝图：神要透过一个可携带的圣所，住在祂刚拯救、刚立约的百姓中间。

主题与神学重点
  • 廿四章：摩西将约书念给百姓听，百姓应允遵行，摩西将血洒在百姓身上，说：「这是立约的血，是耶和华按这一切话与你们立约的凭据」（出24:8）；随后摩西、亚伦、拿答、亚比户和七十位长老上山，「他们观看神；他们又吃又喝」（出24:11）——这是极不寻常的近距离亲近；摩西其后独自上山，在云中四十昼夜领受律法与建造会幕的指示。
  • 廿五章：神吩咐建造约柜、施恩座、陈设饼的桌子、金灯台，并说明整个会幕工程的核心目的：「又当为我造圣所，使我可以住在他们中间」（出25:8）——一切材料、尺寸、样式，都是为了这一个目的服务。
  • 廿六至廿七章：帐幕的幔子、木板、银座，幔子隔开圣所与至圣所，以及院子中的燔祭坛与院墙的详细尺寸——从最内层的至圣所（神与人相会之处）到最外层的院子，构成一层层由圣入俗的空间，指示百姓如何靠着中保、靠着献祭才能逐步靠近神。
救赎历史脉络

「使我可以住在他们中间」（出25:8）是贯穿全本圣经的核心应许，从伊甸园神与人同行开始，到会幕、圣殿，最终指向新约。约翰福音开宗明义说「道成了肉身，住在我们中间」（约1:14）——耶稣基督亲自成了那终极的会幕，神藉着祂的身体与人同住。这条线索的终点，在启示录被明确宣告：「神的帐幕在人间。他要与人同住，他们要作他的子民。神要亲自与他们同在，作他们的神」（启21:3）——会幕所预表、所渴望却始终隔着幔子的那种同在，到了新天新地终于毫无阻隔地成全。

回应

出埃及记里的会幕，靠着重重幔子、层层献祭，才勉强让百姓与神保持有限度的同在；但耶稣基督道成肉身、亲自成了神与人相会之处，又在十字架上舍命的那一刻，圣殿的幔子从上到下裂开——隔开的墙已经拆毁。你不必再靠着遥远的献祭才能靠近神；藉着基督，你此刻就可以坦然来到神面前，因为祂已经亲自住在凡属祂之人的中间。
content_en:
Book Background

Chapter 24 records the people formally entering covenant with God, sealed with sprinkled blood; Moses then goes up the mountain for forty days and nights. From chapter 25 on, God begins giving detailed instructions for building the tabernacle and its furnishings, continuing through chapter 31.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 24–27 pick up from the Sinai covenant of chapters 19–23 — once the covenant is made, God immediately reveals exactly how he will “dwell among his people.” The tabernacle instructions are not merely architectural specifications, but a theological blueprint: God will dwell, by means of a portable sanctuary, in the midst of the people he has just redeemed and just entered covenant with.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 24: Moses reads the Book of the Covenant to the people, who agree to obey; Moses sprinkles the blood on the people, saying, “Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words” (Ex. 24:8). Then Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders go up the mountain, “and they beheld God, and ate and drank” (Ex. 24:11) — an extraordinarily close encounter. Moses then goes up alone, in the cloud for forty days and nights, receiving the law and the instructions for building the tabernacle.
  • Chapter 25: God commands the building of the ark, the mercy seat, the table for the bread of the Presence, and the golden lampstand, and states the core purpose of the entire tabernacle project: “let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst” (Ex. 25:8) — every material, dimension, and design serves this one purpose.
  • Chapters 26–27: The curtains, frames, and bases of the tabernacle; the curtain separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place; and the detailed dimensions of the bronze altar and the courtyard walls — from the innermost Most Holy Place (where God meets man) to the outermost courtyard, forming layer upon layer of space from holy to common, instructing the people how they may draw near to God only step by step, through a mediator and through sacrifice.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

“That I may dwell in their midst” (Ex. 25:8) is a core promise running through the whole Bible, beginning with God walking with man in Eden, through the tabernacle and the temple, and ultimately pointing to the New Testament. John’s Gospel opens by declaring, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14) — Jesus Christ himself became the ultimate tabernacle, God dwelling with man through his own body. This thread finds its endpoint clearly declared in Revelation: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Rev. 21:3) — the presence the tabernacle foreshadowed and longed for, yet always kept at a distance behind a curtain, is finally, completely, and without any barrier fulfilled in the new heaven and new earth.

Response

The tabernacle in Exodus, with its layers of curtains and repeated sacrifices, could only barely maintain a limited presence between the people and God. But Jesus Christ became flesh, himself became the place where God and man meet, and at the very moment he laid down his life on the cross, the temple curtain was torn from top to bottom — the dividing wall was torn down. You no longer need distant sacrifices to draw near to God; through Christ, you can come before God with confidence right now, because he already dwells in the midst of everyone who belongs to him.

title: 给祭司的指示
verse: 出埃及记廿九章四十五节
content:
书卷背景

承接廿五至廿七章会幕的建造指示，廿八至卅一章接着指示谁可以在这会幕中事奉——大祭司亚伦和他儿子们的圣衣、承接圣职的礼仪，以及安息日、比撒列受召建造会幕等收尾的吩咐。

在全书结构中的位置

有了会幕（神的居所）之后，接下来的问题是：谁能进去、如何进去？廿八至卅一章正是回答这个问题——一整套祭司圣衣与承接圣职的礼仪，让罪人能够合宜地、蒙悦纳地在圣洁的神面前事奉。

主题与神学重点
  • 廿八章：亚伦要穿的圣衣极为讲究——以弗得、胸牌、外袍、冠冕，每一样都刻上以色列十二支派的名字，「亚伦要在两肩上担他们的名字，在耶和华面前作为纪念」（出28:12）；大祭司是代表全体百姓进到神面前的中保。
  • 廿九章：承接圣职的礼仪极其具体——献公牛为赎罪祭、公绵羊为燔祭，又把另一只公绵羊的血抹在亚伦和儿子们的耳垂、大拇指、脚趾上，象征全人（所听、所做、所行）都归神为圣；这一切的目的在结尾清楚陈明：「我要住在以色列人中间，作他们的神」（出29:45）。
  • 三十至卅一章：香坛、赎罪银、洗濯盆、圣膏油、圣香的条例，以及神亲自拣选比撒列、亚何利亚伯，「以我的灵充满了他，使他有智慧」（出31:3）去承造这一切；末了再次重申守安息日为「你我之间世世代代的证据」（出31:13）。
救赎历史脉络

亚伦一系的祭司需要繁复的圣衣、每日的献祭、反复的洗濯才能勉强站立在神面前事奉，且这职分会因死亡而中断，需要世代更替。希伯来书指出，耶稣基督才是那位真正、永不更换的大祭司：「他祭司的职任就长久不更换。凡靠着他进到神面前的人，他都能拯救到底；因为他是长远活着，替他们祈求」（来7:24-25）；祂不必像亚伦一样反复献祭：「他不像那些大祭司，每日必须先为自己的罪，后为百姓的罪献祭……因为他只一次将自己献上，就把这事成全了」（来7:27）。

回应

亚伦一系的祭司需要靠着圣衣、洗濯、反复的赎罪祭才能站立在神面前；你却不需要靠自己的洁净或资格来到神面前——耶稣基督已经一次性地将自己献上，成了那长远活着、替你祈求的大祭司。「所以，我们只管坦然无惧地来到施恩的宝座前，为要得怜恤，蒙恩惠，作随时的帮助」（来4:16）——这份坦然，不是因为你配得，而是因为祂已经完全成就了那需要。
content_en:
Book Background

Following the instructions for building the tabernacle in chapters 25–27, chapters 28–31 give instructions for who may serve within it — the garments of the high priest Aaron and his sons, the ordination ceremony, and closing instructions on the Sabbath and Bezalel’s call to build the tabernacle.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

With the tabernacle (God’s dwelling) in place, the next question is: who may enter, and how? Chapters 28–31 answer exactly this — a whole system of priestly garments and ordination rites, so that sinners can serve appropriately and acceptably before a holy God.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 28: The garments Aaron is to wear are extraordinarily elaborate — the ephod, the breastpiece, the robe, the turban — each engraved with the names of Israel’s twelve tribes: “Aaron shall bear their names… on his two shoulders for remembrance before the LORD” (Ex. 28:12); the high priest is the mediator representing the whole people before God.
  • Chapter 29: The ordination ceremony is extremely specific — a bull offered as a sin offering, a ram as a burnt offering, and the blood of another ram put on the earlobes, thumbs, and big toes of Aaron and his sons, symbolizing that the whole person (what they hear, do, and walk in) is consecrated to God. The purpose of all this is clearly stated at the close: “I will dwell among the people of Israel and will be their God” (Ex. 29:45).
  • Chapters 30–31: The regulations for the altar of incense, the atonement money, the bronze basin, the anointing oil, and the incense, and God personally choosing Bezalel and Oholiab, “filling him with my Spirit, with skill” (Ex. 31:3), to carry out all this construction. At the close, the keeping of the Sabbath is reaffirmed as “a sign between me and you throughout your generations” (Ex. 31:13).
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

The priests of Aaron’s line needed elaborate garments, daily sacrifices, and repeated washings just to barely stand and serve before God, and this office was interrupted by death, requiring generation after generation of succession. Hebrews points out that Jesus Christ is the true, never-changing high priest: “he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever. Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them” (Heb. 7:24–25); he does not need, like Aaron, to offer sacrifices repeatedly: “He does not need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people… he did this once for all when he offered up himself” (Heb. 7:27).

Response

The priests of Aaron’s line needed garments, washings, and repeated sin offerings just to stand before God. But you don’t need your own purity or qualifications to come before God — Jesus Christ has already offered himself once for all, becoming the high priest who lives forever, interceding for you. “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Heb. 4:16) — this confidence is not because you deserve it, but because he has already fully accomplished what was needed.

title: 叛逆的百姓与荣耀的神
title_en: A Rebellious People and a Glorious God
verse: 出埃及记卅四章六节至七节
content:
书卷背景

摩西在山上四十昼夜领受律法的同时，山下的百姓已经等得不耐烦——卅二至卅四章记的是立约后最严重的一次背约（金牛犊事件），以及神在审判与怜悯之间如何向摩西启示祂自己的名。

在全书结构中的位置

这三章是整个西奈叙事（十九至卅四章）的转折与高潮：百姓才刚应许「耶和华所吩咐的，我们都必遵行」（出24:7），转眼就在山下拜金牛犊，几乎使神与以色列的约立即破裂；卅三至卅四章记的，是这约如何在神主动的怜悯中得以存续。

主题与神学重点
  • 卅二章：百姓见摩西迟延不下山，怂恿亚伦铸造金牛犊，说「以色列啊，这是领你出埃及地的神」（出32:4）；神向摩西说要「将他们灭绝」（出32:10），摩西却恳求耶和华「转意，不发你的烈怒」（出32:12），神就后悔，不把所说的祸降与百姓——随后利未人奉命审判营中拜偶像者，百姓中被杀约有三千。
  • 卅三章：神因百姓硬着颈项，一度说「我自己不同你们上去」（出33:3），摩西却恳求「你若不亲自和我同去，就不要把我们从这里领上去」（出33:15），又求「求你显出你的荣耀给我看」（出33:18）。
  • 卅四章：摩西重新凿石版上山，耶和华在他面前经过，亲自宣告自己的名：「耶和华，耶和华，是有怜悯有恩典的神，不轻易发怒，并有丰盛的慈爱和诚实，为千万人存留慈爱，赦免罪孽、过犯，和罪恶，万不以有罪的为无罪，必追讨他的罪」（出34:6-7）——这是全本圣经中神最完整的自我宣告，日后被诗篇、约拿书等一再引用。
救赎历史脉络

出埃及记卅四章六至七节这段自我宣告，同时包含两个看似张力的真理：神「有怜悯有恩典……丰盛的慈爱」，又「必追讨他的罪」——祂既不轻慢罪、也不废弃恩典。这两者如何同时成立，直到新约才彻底显明：保罗说神设立耶稣基督作挽回祭，「要显明神的义；因为他用忍耐的心宽容人先时所犯的罪，好在今时显明他的义，使人知道他自己为义，也称信耶稣的人为义」（罗3:25-26）——十字架正是这段自我启示的成全之处：神的公义（必追讨罪）与神的慈爱（赦免罪孽），在耶稣基督替罪人受死的那一刻，同时得到满足，而非彼此取消。约翰福音开头说耶稣「充充满满地有恩典有真理」（约1:14），正是刻意呼应出埃及记卅四章六节神向摩西显现时的自我宣告——道成肉身的耶稣，就是那位在西奈山上向摩西宣告己名之耶和华的显现。

回应

你我心里都不缺金牛犊——总有什么东西，比那位已经用大能救赎我们的神更快抓住我们的心。但神向背约的百姓所显明的第一个名字，不是审判者，而是「有怜悯有恩典的神」（出34:6）；这怜悯与公义之间的张力，不必靠你自己去平衡——耶稣基督在十字架上担当了公义所要追讨的那一切，好叫神能「使人知道他自己为义，也称信耶稣的人为义」（罗3:26）。你所需要的，不是先洗净自己再靠近神，而是像摩西一样，单单转向那位主动向罪人宣告自己名字的神。
content_en:
Book Background

While Moses is on the mountain for forty days and nights receiving the law, the people below have already grown impatient — chapters 32–34 record the most serious breach of covenant since it was made (the golden calf), and how God reveals his own name to Moses between judgment and mercy.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

These three chapters are the turning point and climax of the whole Sinai narrative (chapters 19–34): the people had only just promised, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do” (Ex. 24:7), and in a moment, at the foot of the mountain, they worship a golden calf, nearly shattering God’s covenant with Israel on the spot. Chapters 33–34 record how this covenant survives, through God’s own initiative of mercy.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 32: Seeing Moses delayed in coming down the mountain, the people urge Aaron to cast a golden calf, saying, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (Ex. 32:4). God tells Moses he will “consume them” (Ex. 32:10), but Moses pleads with the LORD to “turn from your burning anger” (Ex. 32:12), and the LORD relents from the disaster he had spoken of bringing on the people. The Levites are then commanded to judge the idolaters in the camp, and about three thousand of the people die.
  • Chapter 33: Because the people are stiff-necked, God at one point says, “I will not go up among you” (Ex. 33:3), but Moses pleads, “If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here” (Ex. 33:15), and further asks, “Please show me your glory” (Ex. 33:18).
  • Chapter 34: Moses cuts new stone tablets and goes up the mountain again; the LORD passes before him and personally proclaims his own name: “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty” (Ex. 34:6–7) — this is the most complete self-declaration of God in the whole Bible, later quoted again and again in the Psalms, Jonah, and elsewhere.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

This self-declaration in Exodus 34:6–7 holds together two truths that seem, at first, to be in tension: God is “merciful and gracious… abounding in steadfast love,” and yet he “will by no means clear the guilty” — he neither treats sin lightly nor sets aside grace. How both can be true at once is not fully revealed until the New Testament. Paul says God put forward Jesus Christ as a propitiation, “to show God’s righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins… to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Rom. 3:25–26) — the cross is precisely where this self-revelation finds its fulfillment: God’s justice (which must punish sin) and God’s love (which forgives iniquity) are both satisfied at once, at the very moment Jesus Christ dies in the place of sinners, rather than canceling each other out. John’s Gospel opens by saying Jesus was “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14) — deliberately echoing God’s self-declaration to Moses in Exodus 34:6 — the incarnate Jesus is the very appearing of the LORD who declared his own name to Moses on Sinai.

Response

Neither you nor I lack our own golden calf — there is always something that seizes our hearts faster than the God who has already redeemed us by his mighty power. But the first name God reveals to a covenant-breaking people is not “Judge,” but “a God merciful and gracious” (Ex. 34:6); this tension between mercy and justice is not yours to resolve — Jesus Christ, on the cross, bore everything justice demanded, so that God could “be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Rom. 3:26). What you need is not to clean yourself up before drawing near to God, but, like Moses, simply to turn toward the God who takes the initiative to proclaim his own name to sinners.

title: 安息日：数算恩典 (Count Your Blessings)
content:
今天是安息日——照着神吩咐以色列人「守安息日为永远的证据」的心意，今天也停下脚步，数算这一周所领受的恩典。

这一周（十六至卅四章）份量厚重：神赐吗哪操练百姓天天倚靠祂（十六至十八章），在西奈山颁布十诫与详细的律法（十九至廿三章），吩咐建造会幕、设立祭司职分，为要「住在他们中间」（廿四至卅一章），百姓却在摩西上山期间铸造金牛犊悖逆神，神却仍然施怜悯，向摩西显明祂「有怜悯有恩典」的性情（卅二至卅四章）。这一周的经文份量大、条例多，读起来不容易，但贯穿其中的，始终是同一条主线：神渴望与祂的百姓同住，即使他们一再软弱悖逆。

建议你今天：①回顾这一周，挑一段你觉得最难读、也最有收获的经文，重读一次；②为神在你软弱悖逆时仍然施恩怜悯，向祂献上感恩；③默想出埃及记卅四章6至7节神的自我启示，把它当作今天认识神的起点。

应用：今天数算三件神在过去这一周（或这段时间）向你显明的具体恩典，写下来，为此感谢祂。
content_en:
Today is a Sabbath day — following the spirit of God’s command to Israel to “keep the Sabbath as a sign forever,” today too we stop and count the grace we’ve received this week.

This week (chapters 16–34) has been dense: God gave manna to train the people to depend on him daily (chapters 16–18); gave the Ten Commandments and detailed laws at Sinai (chapters 19–23); commanded the building of the tabernacle and the establishment of the priesthood, so that he might “dwell among them” (chapters 24–31); yet the people cast a golden calf and rebelled against God while Moses was on the mountain — and God still showed mercy, revealing to Moses his character of being “merciful and gracious” (chapters 32–34). This week’s reading is dense and full of regulations, not easy to get through — but running through it all is the same single thread: God longs to dwell with his people, even though they fail and rebel again and again.

Today, consider: (1) Look back over this week and reread the passage you found hardest to read yet most rewarding. (2) Give thanks to God for still showing grace and mercy even in your weakness and rebellion. (3) Meditate on God’s self-revelation in Exodus 34:6–7, and let it be your starting point for knowing God today.

Application: Count three specific instances of grace God has shown you this past week (or season), write them down, and give him thanks for them.

title: 会幕各物之建造
scripture: 出卅五至四十章（参廿五至三十章）
verse: 出埃及记四十章卅四节至卅五节
content:
书卷背景

出埃及记记载耶和华如何藉着摩西，把在埃及为奴的以色列百姓领出来，在西奈山与他们立约，又指示摩西照着在山上所看见的样式建造会幕，好使圣洁的神可以住在这群悖逆的百姓中间。卅二至卅四章记下百姓拜金牛犊、神的怒气几乎焚尽全会众、以及摩西恳求代祷后约得以更新；卅五至四十章记的，就是百姓从这一次悖逆中回转过来，实际动手，把神所吩咐的会幕造成。

在全书结构中的位置

这六章是全书最后一段，几乎逐字重复廿五至三十一章「耶和华要怎样做」的指示，唯一不同的是动词从「要做」换成「做了」。这刻意的重复把焦点从建筑细节移到一件事上：这一次，百姓从心里甘愿、毫无保留地顺服；全书从「神吩咐」到「百姓做成」，画上一个完整的句点。

主题与神学重点
  • 卅五至卅六章：百姓「无论男女，凡甘心乐意献礼物给耶和华的，都将礼物拿来」（出35:29），甚至多到摩西要传令拦阻，不必再拿——这与卅二章百姓凑金子铸牛犊的甘心，形成尖锐对比：同一群人的「甘心」，这一次用对了地方。神又以祂的灵充满比撒列，「使他有智慧、聪明、知识，能做各样的工」（出35:31），可见连巧匠的手艺，也是神所赐、为祂所用的恩赐。
  • 卅七至卅九章：约柜、桌子、灯台、香坛、圣衣一一造成，每一段末了都重复同一句话——是照耶和华所吩咐摩西的；直到卅九章末了总结说：「凡耶和华所吩咐摩西的，以色列人都照样做了」（出39:32）。神未曾容百姓凭己意增删一件器具的样式或尺寸。
  • 四十章：帐幕在出埃及后第二年正月初一日立起（出40:17），摩西按神所吩咐把柜、桌子、灯台、坛逐一安放就位、膏抹成圣；末了「云彩遮盖会幕，耶和华的荣光就充满了帐幕」（出40:34），摩西甚至不能进去，因耶和华的荣光充满了帐幕（出40:35）。
救赎历史脉络

出埃及记开卷时，以色列人在埃及为奴，「因做苦工，就叹息哀求，他们的哀声达于神」（出2:23）——神看似不在，百姓看似被弃。到了全书末了，「云彩遮盖会幕，耶和华的荣光就充满了帐幕」（出40:34），摩西甚至不能进去，因耶和华的荣光充满了帐幕。全书从头到尾走的，就是这一条轨迹：神不但要救百姓脱离为奴之地，更要住在他们中间、作他们的神——这是开头那声哀求里所盼望、却说不出口的答案。会幕本身是一幅预表：圣洁的神支搭帐棚、住在污秽悖逆的百姓当中，预表了后来「道成了肉身，住在我们中间」（约1:14）的基督——祂才是真正、完全的会幕，使神与人相会的应许，终于不再受幔子和帐幕的限制。

回应

会幕能立起、荣光能充满，不是因为以色列人配得神的同在——他们才刚拜过金牛犊——而是因为神愿意按着自己所定的方式，与悖逆的百姓同住。今天你我能坦然来到神面前，也不是因为已经把自己的心整理干净，而是因为那真会幕基督已经亲自成就了洁净与同在：你不必等到配得，才能来到祂面前；正因祂已经是那充满荣光、又愿意与人同住的神，这邀请此刻就向你敞开。
content_en:
Book Background

Exodus records how the LORD, through Moses, led the enslaved Israelites out of Egypt, made covenant with them at Sinai, and instructed Moses to build the tabernacle according to the pattern he had seen on the mountain, so that the holy God might dwell among this rebellious people. Chapters 32–34 recorded the golden calf, God’s wrath nearly consuming the whole assembly, and the covenant being renewed after Moses’s intercession. Chapters 35–40 record how the people turned back from that rebellion and actually set to work, building the tabernacle just as God had commanded.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

These six chapters are the book’s final section, repeating almost word for word the instructions of chapters 25–31 for “what the LORD said to make,” the only difference being the verb shifts from “shall make” to “made.” This deliberate repetition shifts the focus away from architectural detail onto one single thing: this time, the people obey wholeheartedly and without reservation. The whole book comes to a full close, from “God commands” to “the people accomplish.”

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapters 35–36: The people, “every one whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him, brought the LORD’s contribution” (Ex. 35:29) — so much that Moses had to send word to stop them from bringing more. This stands in sharp contrast to the willingness with which the people, in chapter 32, contributed their gold to cast the calf — the same people’s “willing heart,” this time put to right use. God also fills Bezalel with his Spirit, “with ability, with intelligence, with knowledge, and with all craftsmanship” (Ex. 35:31) — even a craftsman’s skill is shown to be a gift from God, given for his own use.
  • Chapters 37–39: The ark, the table, the lampstand, the altar of incense, and the priestly garments are made one by one, each section closing with the same refrain — that it was made just as the LORD had commanded Moses — until chapter 39 concludes: “according to all that the LORD had commanded Moses, so the people of Israel had done all the work” (Ex. 39:32). God never allowed the people to alter, by their own judgment, the design or dimensions of a single furnishing.
  • Chapter 40: The tabernacle is set up on the first day of the first month of the second year after leaving Egypt (Ex. 40:17); Moses, following God’s instructions, sets the ark, table, lampstand, and altar each in its place and anoints them holy. At the close, “the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (Ex. 40:34), and Moses himself could not even enter, because the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle (Ex. 40:35).
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

Exodus opens with the Israelites enslaved in Egypt, “because of their slavery, crying out for help; their cry came up to God” (Ex. 2:23) — God seemed absent, the people seemed forsaken. By the book’s end, “the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (Ex. 40:34), and Moses could not even enter, because the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. The whole book, from beginning to end, traces this one trajectory: God not only wants to save his people out of slavery, but to dwell in their midst, to be their God — this is the answer, unspoken but hoped for, in that opening cry. The tabernacle itself is a foreshadowing: a holy God pitching his tent to dwell among a defiled and rebellious people, foreshadowing the later coming of Christ, who “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14) — he is the true, complete tabernacle, so that the promise of God and man meeting is finally no longer limited by curtains and tent walls.

Response

The tabernacle was raised and the glory filled it, not because Israel deserved God’s presence — they had only just worshiped the golden calf — but because God was willing, in the way he himself determined, to dwell with a rebellious people. Today, you and I can come before God with confidence, not because we’ve already cleaned up our hearts, but because Christ, the true tabernacle, has already accomplished both cleansing and presence: you don’t need to wait until you’re worthy to come before him — precisely because he is already the God full of glory who is willing to dwell with people, this invitation stands open to you right now.

title: 三种自动的献祭
verse: 利未记一章九节
content:
书卷背景

利未记承接出埃及记的结尾：帐幕刚刚造成、耶和华的荣光刚刚充满帐幕（出40:34），这卷书要处理的，正是随之而来的问题——一位圣洁到无法直视的神，如今住在营中央，悖逆易犯罪的百姓要怎样才能安全地亲近祂、事奉祂？这卷书反复申明的命题，后来在十一章说得最直接：「你们要成为圣洁，因为我是圣洁的」（利11:44），彼得后来在新约引用同一句话：「你们要圣洁，因为我是圣洁的」（彼前1:16）。为此，神设立了一整套献祭制度——燔祭、素祭、平安祭、赎罪祭、赎愆祭——用血与火处理罪与污秽的问题，使百姓可以藉着蒙神所悦纳的方式来到祂面前；而这套制度本身的重复性，恰恰指向它无法一次解决罪的问题，这也是希伯来书后来展开的论证（来10:1）。

在全书结构中的位置

利未记上承出埃及记末了帐幕的建成，下启民数记百姓从西奈起行的旅程，全卷几乎都发生在西奈山下的同一个地点、同一段时间之内。一至七章处理「如何献祭」，八至十章处理「谁来献祭」，十一至十五章处理「日常生活中的洁净」，十六章是全书的顶点——赎罪日，十七至廿七章则是圣洁生活的具体条例。今天所读的一至三章，是全书的第一步：三种可以自愿献上的祭——燔祭、素祭、平安祭。

主题与神学重点
  • 一章：燔祭——献的人要「按手在燔祭牲的头上」（利1:4），使祭牲代替他死；祭牲全烧在坛上，一点不留给人，是「献与耶和华为馨香的火祭」（利1:9），表达完全、毫无保留的献上。
  • 二章：素祭——用细面、油、乳香做成，是三祭中唯一不流血的一种，附在燔祭之后献上，表达对赐粮之神的感恩与忠诚；条例特别要求「不可缺了你神立约的盐」（利2:13），提醒这一切都在神与百姓所立之约的框架内进行。
  • 三章：平安祭——祭牲的脂油烧在坛上归神，胸和腿归祭司，其余的肉则归献祭之人与家人朋友分享；这是三祭中唯一有「同吃」的祭，图画式地表明献祭不只是处理罪的问题，更是要恢复与神、与人之间同席共聚的团契。
救赎历史脉络

这三种祭都是百姓可以自愿、随时献上的敬拜方式，却仍然要藉着祭牲的死才能蒙神悦纳——纵是最出于感恩、团契的敬拜，也无法绕过赎罪这一步。希伯来书后来指出，这一切「不过是属肉体的条例，命定到振兴的时候为止」（来9:10），公牛山羊的血「断不能除罪」（来10:4）；基督却「只一次进入圣所，成了永远赎罪的事」（来9:12）。利未记开篇这三种祭所描绘的完全献上、感恩、团契，最终都在基督一次献上自己里得着满足与实底。

回应

利未记的献祭制度让我们看见：亲近圣洁的神，从来不是靠自己一分虔诚或一次感恩的心意就能达到的，总要有代替的死。基督已经成就了那一次永远的献上——「基督献了一次永远的赎罪祭，就在神的右边坐下了」（来10:12）；因此你今天来到神面前的燔祭般的献上、素祭般的感恩、平安祭般的团契，不是要为自己挣得悦纳，而是本于基督已经为你成就的悦纳，才能真实地献上。
content_en:
Book Background

Leviticus picks up right where Exodus left off: the tabernacle has just been completed, and the glory of the LORD has just filled it (Ex. 40:34). This book addresses the question that immediately follows: now that a God too holy to look upon dwells in the very center of the camp, how can a rebellious, sin-prone people safely draw near to him and serve him? The proposition this book states again and again is put most directly in chapter 11: “you shall be holy, for I am holy” (Lev. 11:44) — a line Peter later quotes in the New Testament: “You shall be holy, for I am holy” (1 Pet. 1:16). For this purpose, God establishes an entire system of sacrifice — burnt offerings, grain offerings, peace offerings, sin offerings, guilt offerings — using blood and fire to deal with sin and impurity, so the people can come before him in a way he accepts; and the very repetitiveness of this system points to the fact that it cannot solve the problem of sin once and for all — an argument Hebrews later develops (Heb. 10:1).

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Leviticus picks up from the completed tabernacle at the end of Exodus, and leads into the people’s journey from Sinai in Numbers; nearly the whole book takes place at the same location, the foot of Mount Sinai, within the same span of time. Chapters 1–7 deal with “how to sacrifice,” chapters 8–10 with “who may sacrifice,” chapters 11–15 with “purity in daily life,” chapter 16 is the peak of the whole book — the Day of Atonement — and chapters 17–27 are the concrete regulations for a holy life. Today’s reading, chapters 1–3, is the book’s first step: three offerings that may be given voluntarily — the burnt offering, the grain offering, and the peace offering.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 1: The burnt offering — the offerer must “lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering” (Lev. 1:4), so that the animal dies in his place. The animal is burned entirely on the altar, nothing left for the offerer, “a food offering… a pleasing aroma to the LORD” (Lev. 1:9), expressing complete, unreserved surrender.
  • Chapter 2: The grain offering — made of fine flour, oil, and frankincense, the only one of the three offerings that involves no bloodshed, offered alongside the burnt offering to express gratitude and loyalty to the God who provides grain. The regulations specifically require, “You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing” (Lev. 2:13), reminding the offerer that all this takes place within the framework of the covenant between God and his people.
  • Chapter 3: The peace offering — the fat of the animal is burned on the altar for God, the breast and thigh go to the priest, and the rest of the meat is shared by the offerer with family and friends. This is the only one of the three offerings that involves “eating together,” pictorially showing that sacrifice is not only about dealing with sin, but about restoring shared fellowship at a table with God and with others.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

All three of these offerings are ways of worship the people could give voluntarily, at any time — yet even so, they still required the death of an animal to be accepted by God. Even worship that flows purely from gratitude and fellowship cannot bypass this step of atonement. Hebrews later points out that all this was “but regulations for the body, imposed until the time of reformation” (Heb. 9:10), and that the blood of bulls and goats “can never take away sins” (Heb. 10:4); but Christ “entered once for all into the holy places… thus securing an eternal redemption” (Heb. 9:12). The complete surrender, gratitude, and fellowship pictured in these opening three offerings of Leviticus all find their satisfaction and substance, in the end, in Christ’s single offering of himself.

Response

The sacrificial system of Leviticus shows us: drawing near to a holy God has never been achieved by our own devotion or a single grateful gesture — there must always be a death in our place. Christ has already accomplished that one, eternal offering — “when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God” (Heb. 10:12); so your burnt-offering-like surrender, grain-offering-like gratitude, and peace-offering-like fellowship, when you come before God today, are not efforts to earn acceptance for yourself, but can only be truly offered on the basis of the acceptance Christ has already secured for you.
