title: 义务的祭及祭司献祭须知
title_en: Mandatory Offerings and Instructions for Priests
verse: 利未记四章二节
content:
书卷背景

利未记一至三章处理的是百姓可以自愿献上的祭；四至七章接着处理的，是当罪已经发生、无法回避时当献的义务性祭——赎罪祭与赎愆祭，以及给祭司的补充细则。

在全书结构中的位置

四至七章仍属于全书第一大段「如何献祭」的范围，与一至三章的自愿之祭前后呼应，构成完整的祭祀条例；七章末了的总结——「这就是燔祭、素祭、赎罪祭、赎愆祭，和平安祭的条例」（利7:37）——为这一整段画上句点，也为下一段八至十章祭司的按立做好准备。

主题与神学重点
  • 四章：赎罪祭因人的身份而有不同规格——受膏的祭司、全会众、官长、平民各有各的祭牲——「若有人在耶和华所吩咐不可行的什么事上误犯了一件」（利4:2），就是误犯、无心之失，也仍然构成罪，需要赎罪；地位越高、责任越大，所献的祭牲规格也越重，可见罪不是按感觉衡量，而是按神的圣洁标准衡量。
  • 五至六章：赎愆祭处理的是在圣物或邻舍财物上有亏欠的罪，除了献祭赎罪，还必须「另外加上五分之一」（利6:5）归还本主——赎罪与赔偿并行，赎罪祭不能取代当尽的人事责任。
  • 六至七章：补充祭司在坛前的操作细则——「在坛上必有常常烧着的火，不可熄灭」（利6:13），各祭牲哪些部分归祭司享用、如何吃、在何处吃，都有明文规定，显明事奉圣物的人自己也活在圣洁的界限之内，没有随意支配圣物的自由。
救赎历史脉络

赎罪祭与赎愆祭清楚显明：罪不因是否蓄意、是否被人发现而改变性质，凡违背神吩咐的，都需要用血来遮盖；按身份等级递增的献祭规格，也预表责任越大，过犯的严重性越大——直到希伯来书指出，无论献多少次、多细致的祭牲规格，都「断不能除罪」（来10:4），惟有那担当全人类过犯的大祭司基督，「只一次献上他的身体」（来10:10），才使赎罪与赔偿都得着终极的成全——祂不但担当了刑罚，也偿清了罪所亏欠神圣洁公义的一切。

回应

你我常常也像利未记里的百姓一样，在无心、疏忽中亏欠了神与人，甚至自己都未必察觉——但基督已经担当了这一切，不论是明知故犯或是误犯的罪，「他一次献祭，便叫那得以成圣的人永远完全」（来10:14）；你不需要先辨认清楚每一件亏欠、逐一献上对应等级的祭，才能坦然来到神面前，因为那使人成圣的祭，基督早已一次献上，且已完全。
content_en:
Book Background

Leviticus 1–3 dealt with offerings the people could give voluntarily; chapters 4–7 then deal with the mandatory offerings required once sin has already occurred and cannot be avoided — the sin offering and the guilt offering — along with supplementary details for the priests.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 4–7 still fall within the book’s first major section, “how to sacrifice,” echoing the voluntary offerings of chapters 1–3 to form a complete set of sacrificial regulations. The summary at the end of chapter 7 — “This is the law of the burnt offering, of the grain offering, of the sin offering, of the guilt offering, of the ordination offering, and of the peace offering” (Lev. 7:37) — brings this whole section to a close, and prepares for the ordination of the priests in the next section, chapters 8–10.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 4: The sin offering varies in specification according to the offender’s status — the anointed priest, the whole congregation, a leader, or a common person each have their own required animal. “If anyone sins unintentionally in any of the LORD’s commandments about things not to be done” (Lev. 4:2) — even an unintentional, unwitting sin still constitutes sin and still requires atonement. The higher the position and the greater the responsibility, the more costly the required sacrifice — showing that sin is measured not by how it feels, but by God’s standard of holiness.
  • Chapters 5–6: The guilt offering deals with sins involving a debt owed regarding holy things or a neighbor’s property; besides offering a sacrifice for atonement, the offender must also “add a fifth to it” (Lev. 6:5) and restore it to its owner — atonement and restitution go together; the sin offering cannot replace the human responsibility that is still owed.
  • Chapters 6–7: Supplementary details on the priests’ duties at the altar — “Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out” (Lev. 6:13); which parts of each animal belong to the priests, how they are to be eaten, and where, are all explicitly regulated, showing that even those who serve the holy things themselves live within holy boundaries, with no freedom to dispose of holy things as they please.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

The sin offering and the guilt offering clearly show: sin does not change in nature depending on whether it was intentional or whether anyone found out — anything that violates God’s command requires blood to cover it. The offering requirements that increase with rank and status also foreshadow that the greater the responsibility, the more serious the offense — until Hebrews points out that no matter how many times offered, or how detailed the specification of the sacrificial animal, none of it “can never take away sins” (Heb. 10:4); only Christ, the high priest who bore the guilt of the whole human race, “offered his body” once for all (Heb. 10:10), so that both atonement and restitution find their ultimate fulfillment — he not only bore the penalty, but also paid in full everything sin owed to God’s holy justice.

Response

You and I, too, often, like the people in Leviticus, owe God and others a debt through carelessness or oversight, sometimes without even realizing it ourselves — but Christ has already borne all of it, whether sins committed knowingly or unintentionally: “by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Heb. 10:14). You don’t need to first identify every single debt and offer the corresponding grade of sacrifice before you can come before God with confidence, because the sacrifice that sanctifies has already been offered once by Christ, and it is already complete.

title: 祭司的职任与限制
title_en: The Priests' Duty and Its Limits
verse: 利未记十章三节
content:
书卷背景

一至七章交代了各样祭的条例；八至十章接着记载这些条例首次付诸实行——祭司的按立、第一次献祭，以及祭司若不按神所吩咐的行事所带来的严重后果。

在全书结构中的位置

八至十章是全书第二大段的核心，处理「谁可以献祭」的问题：八章是亚伦父子承接圣职的按立礼，九章是他们第一次代替百姓献祭、神以荣光与烈火印证悦纳，十章却急转直下——拿答、亚比户擅自献上凡火，当场被神的烈火烧灭。这段记载把「圣洁」从抽象的原则，变成极其具体、甚至致命的现实。

主题与神学重点
  • 八章：摩西按神所吩咐，用水洗、穿圣衣、用膏油膏抹亚伦父子，又用祭牲的血抹在他们的耳垂、手指、脚趾上（利8:23-24），七天不可出会幕的门，「免得你们死亡」（利8:35）——承接圣职本身就是极其严肃的事。
  • 九章：亚伦按着条例第一次为自己与百姓献上赎罪祭、燔祭、平安祭；「有火从耶和华面前出来，在坛上烧尽燔祭和脂油；众民一见，就都欢呼，俯伏在地」（利9:24）——神亲自以烈火印证悦纳，百姓因此欢呼敬拜。
  • 十章：拿答、亚比户「各拿自己的香炉，盛上火，加上香，在耶和华面前献上凡火，是耶和华没有吩咐他们的」（利10:1），随即被神的火当场烧灭；耶和华借此宣告：「我在亲近我的人中要显为圣；在众民面前，我要得荣耀」（利10:3）。
救赎历史脉络

拿答、亚比户的死，不是因为他们比其他祭司更粗心，而是让全营立刻看见一个此前只在原则上宣告的事实：亲近这位圣洁的神，人不能按自己以为合宜的方式，而只能按神自己所定的道路。这也解释了为什么一整套如此精密繁复的祭司条例是必要的——不是神苛刻，而是人若靠自己的谨慎与创意来到神面前，随时可能像拿答、亚比户一样付上性命的代价。

回应

利未记要我们看见的，不是「要比拿答、亚比户更小心」，而是没有人能靠着自己足够小心、足够按规矩来亲近神——包括最资深的祭司在内。正因如此，基督的血才如此宝贵：「我们既因耶稣的血得以坦然进入至圣所，是藉着他给我们开了一条又新又活的路」（来10:19-20）。你今天来到神面前，不是靠自己把每个细节都做对，而是藉着基督已经用自己的血为你开通的这条又新又活的路——这条路不会像凡火那样惹神发怒，因为它本身就是神所悦纳、所亲自预备的道路。
content_en:
Book Background

Chapters 1–7 laid out the regulations for the various offerings; chapters 8–10 then record these regulations being carried out for the first time — the ordination of the priests, their first offering, and the severe consequences when a priest fails to act as God commanded.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 8–10 are the core of the book’s second major section, addressing the question of “who may offer sacrifices”: chapter 8 is the ordination ceremony of Aaron and his sons; chapter 9 is their first time offering sacrifices on the people’s behalf, with God confirming his acceptance by glory and fire; chapter 10 then takes a sudden, sharp turn — Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire on their own initiative, and are struck dead on the spot by God’s fire. This passage turns “holiness” from an abstract principle into an extremely concrete, even fatal, reality.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 8: Moses, following God’s instructions, washes Aaron and his sons with water, dresses them in the holy garments, and anoints them with oil, and puts the blood of the sacrifice on their earlobes, fingers, and toes (Lev. 8:23–24); they must not leave the entrance of the tent of meeting for seven days, “lest you die” (Lev. 8:35) — the ordination itself is an extremely solemn matter.
  • Chapter 9: Aaron, following the regulations, offers the sin offering, burnt offering, and peace offering for himself and the people for the first time. “Fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the pieces of fat on the altar, and when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces” (Lev. 9:24) — God himself confirms his acceptance with fire, and the people respond with shouts of worship.
  • Chapter 10: Nadab and Abihu “each took his censer and put fire in it and laid incense on it and offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them” (Lev. 10:1), and are immediately consumed by fire from the LORD. The LORD declares through this: “Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified” (Lev. 10:3).
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

The death of Nadab and Abihu was not because they were more careless than other priests, but to let the whole camp immediately see, in a way principle alone had not yet shown: no one can draw near this holy God on their own terms; only on the way God himself has appointed. This also explains why such a precise and elaborate system of priestly regulations was necessary — not because God is harsh, but because if people rely on their own caution and creativity to come before God, they risk paying with their lives, just as Nadab and Abihu did.

Response

What Leviticus wants us to see is not “be more careful than Nadab and Abihu,” but that no one — including the most senior priest — can draw near to God by being sufficiently careful or sufficiently by-the-book on their own. Precisely because of this, Christ’s blood is so precious: “we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us” (Heb. 10:19–20). You come before God today not by getting every detail right yourself, but through this new and living way Christ has already opened for you with his own blood — a way that will never provoke God’s anger the way unauthorized fire did, because it is itself the way God accepts, and himself prepared.

title: 家庭与卫生条例
verse: 利未记十一章四十四节至四十五节
content:
书卷背景

八至十章处理了祭司的问题；十一至十四章接着把「圣洁」的界线延伸到百姓日常生活的方方面面——吃什么、生育后如何洁净、身上或衣物房屋若染上大麻风怎样处理。

在全书结构中的位置

这四章与其后的十五章同属全书「日常洁净条例」的一段，穿插在祭司条例（八至十章）与赎罪日（十六章）之间；篇幅虽长，主旨却单一：让百姓在最琐碎的日常生活中，也时时被提醒洁净与不洁净的分别，为要预备他们能安全地亲近住在营中的神。

主题与神学重点
  • 十一章：可吃与不可吃的走兽、水族、雀鸟，条例末了道出理由——「我是耶和华－你们的神；所以你们要成为圣洁，因为我是圣洁的」（利11:44），又说「我是把你们从埃及地领出来的耶和华，要作你们的神；所以你们要圣洁，因为我是圣洁的」（利11:45）；饮食的分别，是圣洁的分别在日常餐桌上的具体操练。
  • 十二章：妇人生产后有一段不洁净、家居的日子，满了日期要献燔祭与赎罪祭，「为她赎罪，她的血源就洁净了」（利12:7）——连生命的诞生这样美好的事，也因人生在罪中而需要洁净。
  • 十三至十四章：大麻风的诊断与洁净条例极其详尽，患者要「独居营外」（利13:46），得洁净后要经过两阶段、长达七天以上的礼仪才能重新进入营中——用可见的隔离与漫长的洁净过程，具体演出罪与污秽如何使人与神的百姓、与神的同在隔绝。
救赎历史脉络

这些琐碎详尽的条例，若单看表面容易显得只是卫生规范，但它们真正要教导的是一件更深的事：罪与污秽会真实地隔绝人与神——不是比喻，而是活生生地演出来，让百姓在吃饭、生育、生病这些最平凡的日常里，无从遗忘自己需要被洁净才能亲近神。这套外在、身体层面的洁净礼仪本身无法使人的良心真正洁净，正如希伯来书所说：「所献的礼物和祭物，就着良心说，都不能叫礼拜的人得以完全」（来9:9），只是预表一个更深的、只有基督才能成就的洁净。

回应

利未记这些条例所指向的，不是「你要活得更卫生、更小心，才能被神接纳」，而是人靠着遵守条例、隔离、等候，始终无法一次性解决污秽的根本问题。基督却藉着祂的血，使我们「心中天良的亏欠已经洒去，身体用清水洗净了」（来10:22），这洁净不是外在礼仪式的、暂时的，而是深入良心、一次到底的。你今天无需再靠着自己隔离、洁身，才能被算为洁净——那洁净，基督早已藉着祂的血，一次为你成就了。
content_en:
Book Background

Chapters 8–10 dealt with the matter of the priesthood; chapters 11–14 then extend the boundary of “holiness” to every corner of the people’s daily life — what to eat, how to become clean after childbirth, and how to handle leprous disease on the body, clothing, or in a house.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

These four chapters, together with chapter 15 that follows, belong to the book’s section on “regulations for daily purity,” inserted between the priestly regulations (chapters 8–10) and the Day of Atonement (chapter 16). Though lengthy, their message is singular: to keep the people continually reminded, even in the most trivial matters of daily life, of the distinction between clean and unclean, so they would be prepared to safely draw near to the God who dwells in the camp.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 11: Clean and unclean land animals, water creatures, and birds — the regulations close with the reason: “I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy” (Lev. 11:44), and again, “I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy” (Lev. 11:45). The distinction in diet is a concrete, daily-table practice of the distinction of holiness.
  • Chapter 12: A woman, after childbirth, has a period of uncleanness and confinement; once it ends, she must offer a burnt offering and a sin offering, “and he shall make atonement for her, and she shall be clean from the flow of her blood” (Lev. 12:7) — even the birth of new life, so good a thing, requires cleansing, because human life itself is lived within sin.
  • Chapters 13–14: The diagnosis and cleansing regulations for leprous disease are extremely detailed; the afflicted must “live alone… outside the camp” (Lev. 13:46), and once cleansed, must go through a two-stage ceremony lasting over seven days before re-entering the camp — a visible isolation and a lengthy purification process concretely acting out how sin and impurity cut a person off from God’s people and from God’s presence.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

Taken at face value, these detailed regulations can easily look like mere hygiene codes, but what they truly teach is something far deeper: sin and impurity genuinely separate people from God — not as a metaphor, but acted out in living reality, so that the people, in the most ordinary events of eating, giving birth, and falling sick, could never forget that they need to be cleansed in order to draw near to God. This outward, bodily system of purification rites could never by itself truly cleanse the conscience, just as Hebrews says: “gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper” (Heb. 9:9) — they were only a foreshadowing of a deeper cleansing that only Christ could accomplish.

Response

What these regulations in Leviticus point to is not, “live more hygienically, more carefully, so you can be accepted by God,” but that relying on keeping rules, isolation, and waiting could never once and for all solve the underlying problem of impurity. But Christ, through his blood, has “our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water” (Heb. 10:22) — this cleansing is not an outward, ritual, temporary one, but reaches deep into the conscience, accomplished once and for all. You don’t need to isolate or purify yourself today in order to be counted clean — Christ has already, through his blood, accomplished that cleansing for you, once for all.
verse_text: 我是耶和华－你们的 神；所以你们要成为圣洁，因为我是圣洁的。你们也不可在地上的爬物污秽自己。我是把你们从 埃及 地领出来的耶和华，要作你们的 神；所以你们要圣洁，因为我是圣洁的。」

title: 漏症与赎罪日条例
title_en: Bodily Discharges and the Day of Atonement
verse: 利未记十七章十一节
content:
书卷背景

十一至十四章处理了饮食、生育、皮肤病的洁净问题；十五章接着处理身体分泌物带来的不洁，十六章则是全卷的高峰——一年一度的赎罪日，十七章再以血的圣洁作结，把前面所有献祭条例的根基讲明。

在全书结构中的位置

十六章的赎罪日，是利未记结构上的转折点：前面十一至十五章反复堆叠不洁净的清单，到这里由大祭司一年一次、代表全会众进入至圣所献血赎罪，一次处理百姓「诸般的污秽、过犯，就是他们一切的罪愆」（利16:16），把前十五章零散的洁净问题作一次总的了结；十七章则退后一步，宣告血为何能赎罪的根本原理，为十八章以后圣洁生活的条例奠定神学基础。

主题与神学重点
  • 十五章：身体的漏症、月经、遗精等分泌物都使人暂时不洁净，需要洗濯、等候，甚至献祭——目的是「使以色列人与他们的污秽隔绝，免得他们玷污我的帐幕」（利15:31）；连身体最私密、最不由自主的层面，也被纳入圣洁的界线之内。
  • 十六章：赎罪日，大祭司亚伦一年一次穿上细麻圣衣，先为自己、后为百姓献上赎罪祭，把血带入至圣所弹在施恩座上；又为两只山羊拈阄，一只献为赎罪祭，另一只由亚伦按手在其头上，「承认以色列人诸般的罪孽过犯」（利16:21），放入旷野，象征百姓的罪被担当、带走，永不再回来。
  • 十七章：条例讲明祭牲必须献到会幕门口，不可私自宰杀，又严禁吃血，理由只有一句：「因为活物的生命是在血中。我把这血赐给你们，可以在坛上为你们的生命赎罪；因血里有生命，所以能赎罪」（利17:11）——血能赎罪，不是因为它有魔力，而是因为血代表生命，一条生命代替另一条当死的生命。
救赎历史脉络

利未记十七章十一节这句「因血里有生命，所以能赎罪」，正是希伯来书论证的根基所在。希伯来书回顾利未记的献祭体系时说：「按着律法，凡物差不多都是用血洁净的；若不流血，罪就不得赦免了」（来9:22），直接呼应利未记的原理；又指出赎罪日一年一次的重复，恰恰证明它无法一次解决问题——「他从创世以来，就必多次受苦了。但如今在这末世显现一次，把自己献为祭，好除掉罪」（来9:26）。基督「并且不用山羊和牛犊的血，乃用自己的血，只一次进入圣所，成了永远赎罪的事」（来9:12）——利未记十六章那位每年都要重新进入至圣所的大祭司，与十七章「血里有生命」的原理，在基督身上一次性、永远地得着了成全：祂既是那完全的大祭司，又是那被献上、流出生命之血的羔羊。

回应

赎罪日那由大祭司一年一次、靠着牲畜的血才能进入的至圣所，如今因基督一次流出的血，向所有蒙召的人常开：「我们既因耶稣的血得以坦然进入至圣所」（来10:19）——这不是每年都要重新流一次的血，而是已经一次永远成就赎罪、且仍在为你说话的血；你此刻来到神面前，不必靠自己积累够资格，只需藉着这早已流出、且永不失效的血。
content_en:
Book Background

Chapters 11–14 dealt with purity concerning food, childbirth, and skin disease; chapter 15 goes on to deal with the impurity caused by bodily discharges, chapter 16 is the peak of the whole book — the annual Day of Atonement — and chapter 17 closes by explaining the fundamental holiness of blood, laying out the basis for all the preceding sacrificial regulations.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

The Day of Atonement in chapter 16 is the structural turning point of Leviticus: after chapters 11–15 pile up list after list of uncleanness, here the high priest, once a year, on behalf of the whole congregation, enters the Most Holy Place with blood to make atonement, dealing all at once with “all their uncleanness and their transgressions, all their sins” (Lev. 16:16) — bringing the scattered purity issues of the previous fifteen chapters to a single resolution. Chapter 17 then steps back to declare the fundamental principle of why blood can atone, laying the theological foundation for the regulations on holy living from chapter 18 onward.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 15: Bodily discharges, menstruation, and emissions all render a person temporarily unclean, requiring washing, waiting, and even sacrifice — the purpose being “to keep the people of Israel separate from their uncleanness, lest they die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle” (Lev. 15:31); even the most private, involuntary aspects of the body are drawn within the boundary of holiness.
  • Chapter 16: On the Day of Atonement, the high priest Aaron, once a year, puts on the holy linen garments, offers a sin offering first for himself and then for the people, and brings the blood into the Most Holy Place to sprinkle on the mercy seat. Lots are also cast for two goats — one offered as a sin offering, and the other, with Aaron laying his hands on its head, “confessing over it all the iniquities of the people of Israel” (Lev. 16:21), is sent into the wilderness, symbolizing the people’s sin being carried away, never to return.
  • Chapter 17: The regulations require that sacrificial animals must be brought to the entrance of the tent of meeting and not slaughtered privately, and strictly forbid eating blood, for one reason alone: “For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls, for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life” (Lev. 17:11) — blood atones not because it has some magical power, but because blood represents life, one life given in place of another life that was due to die.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

This statement in Leviticus 17:11 — “it is the blood that makes atonement by the life” — is exactly the foundation of Hebrews’s argument. Reviewing Leviticus’s sacrificial system, Hebrews says, “under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins” (Heb. 9:22), directly echoing Leviticus’s principle; it also points out that the yearly repetition of the Day of Atonement is precisely what proves it cannot solve the problem once for all: “he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Heb. 9:26). Christ, “not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, entered once for all into the holy places, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Heb. 9:12) — the high priest of Leviticus 16, who had to enter the Most Holy Place afresh every year, and the principle of chapter 17 that “the life is in the blood,” are both fulfilled once and eternally in Christ: he is both the perfect high priest, and the Lamb whose life-blood was poured out as the offering.

Response

The Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement, which the high priest could enter only once a year and only by the blood of animals, is now, because of the blood Christ shed once, always open to everyone who is called: “we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus” (Heb. 10:19) — this is not blood that must be shed anew every year, but blood that has already accomplished atonement once, forever, and still speaks on your behalf. You do not need to first accumulate enough merit to come before God; you need only come by means of this blood, already shed, and never losing its power.

title: 安息日：专注于神 (Focus on God)
content:
今天是安息日——出埃及记与利未记这一路读下来，条例繁多、细节庞杂，今天不读新经文，只是停下脚步，重新把焦点对准神自己。

这一周我们看着会幕终于建成、神的荣光亲自充满其中（出卅五至四十章），随后进入利未记，认识各样献祭的条例——甘心献上的燔祭、素祭、平安祭，为罪而献的赎罪祭、赎愆祭（利一至七章），祭司按立与拿答、亚比户擅自献祭而死的警戒（利八至十章），生活各样分别为圣的条例（利十一至十四章），最后来到赎罪日与血的意义（利十五至十七章）。这些条例初读枯燥，但若问一句「这一切究竟为了什么」，答案始终如一：为要让一位圣洁的神，能够与不圣洁的百姓同住，而不至因祂的圣洁毁灭他们。

建议你今天：①回顾这一周最难读、却也最有收获的一段经文；②默想利未记十七章11节「血里有生命，所以能赎罪」，感谢基督已一次永远地成就了这一切预表；③安静片刻，单单专注在神自己身上，而非条例本身。

应用：今天用一句话，把利未记这几章繁复的条例，浓缩成一句你自己的话：神为什么如此看重「圣洁」与「同住」？
content_en:
Today is a Sabbath day — after reading through so many regulations and so much detail in Exodus and Leviticus, today we read nothing new, just stop and refocus on God himself.

This week we watched the tabernacle finally completed, and the glory of the LORD filling it in person (Exodus 35–40), then moved into Leviticus, learning the various sacrificial regulations — the voluntary burnt offering, grain offering, and peace offering, and the sin offering and guilt offering given for sin (Leviticus 1–7); the ordination of the priests and the warning of Nadab and Abihu, who died for offering unauthorized fire (Leviticus 8–10); the regulations setting apart every area of daily life as holy (Leviticus 11–14); and finally the Day of Atonement and the meaning of blood (Leviticus 15–17). These regulations can feel dry at first read, but if you ask, “what is all this actually for,” the answer is always the same: so that a holy God could dwell with an unholy people, without his holiness destroying them.

Today, consider: (1) Look back over the passage this week you found hardest to read, yet also most rewarding. (2) Meditate on Leviticus 17:11, “it is the blood that makes atonement by the life,” and give thanks that Christ has once and eternally accomplished everything this foreshadowed. (3) Be still for a moment, focusing simply on God himself, rather than on the regulations themselves.

Application: Today, condense these dense chapters of Leviticus into one sentence of your own: why does God care so much about “holiness” and “dwelling together”?

title: 作圣洁的子民
verse: 利未记十九章十八节
content:
书卷背景

利未记是神在西奈山藉着摩西颁给以色列人的律法书，大致分为几个部分：献祭条例（1-7章）、祭司职分的设立（8-10章）、洁净条例（11-15章）、赎罪日（16章），以及贯穿十七至二十六章的「圣洁法典」。十八至二十章正处在这圣洁法典之中，把圣洁从祭坛延伸到婚姻、性关系、日常人际这些最普通的生活领域。

在全书结构中的位置

十七章已经确立了「一个祭坛、一位耶和华」的原则；十八至二十章紧接着把这原则应用在具体的伦理生活上：十八章禁止效法埃及、迦南的淫乱风俗，十九章展开为一套涵盖敬虔与公义的生活守则，二十章则为十八章所列的罪行订定刑罚，并以「你们要归我为圣」收束——圣洁不是抽象的宗教情操，而是具体可数算的生活样式。

主题与神学重点
  • 十八章：神吩咐以色列人不可效法埃及、迦南人的行为（利18:3），随后列出一连串禁止的乱伦、淫乱关系；本章末了警告，连迦南地本身也会因居民的污秽「把你们吐出」（利18:28），圣洁关乎的不只是个人得失，也关乎这地能否存留百姓。
  • 十九章：开篇道出圣洁法典的核心：「你们要圣洁，因为我耶和华－你们的神是圣洁的」（利19:2）；接着涉及孝敬父母、守安息日、为穷人留地角、诚实交易、不可怀恨、不可报仇，最后总结为「却要爱人如己」（利19:18），这命令后来直接被耶稣引用，成为律法中第二大的诫命。
  • 二十章：重申十八章所列罪行当受的刑罚，本章以「你们要归我为圣，因为我－耶和华是圣的，并叫你们与万民有分别，使你们作我的民」（利20:26）作结——圣洁的最终目的，不是划清界限本身，而是要成为神所拥有、有别于万民的子民。
救赎历史脉络

耶稣把利未记十九章十八节从众多律例中挑出来，直接引用：「其次也相仿，就是要爱人如己」（太22:39），与尽心尽性尽意爱主你的神一同被称为「律法和先知一切道理的总纲」（太22:40）——这提醒我们，圣洁法典从来不是一堆孤立的规条，而是有一条主线贯穿其中：全心爱神，并以此延伸出爱人如己。但十八至二十章同时也让人看见，这条主线的要求何等全面——没有一个罪人能凭自己完全活出这样的圣洁；正因如此，这套律法本身也在预备百姓，让他们看见自己需要一位能真正成就「爱人如己」的君王。

回应

耶稣正是那位在地上完全活出「爱人如己」的那一位——祂不但教导这诫命，更亲身在十字架上为祂所爱的人舍命，担当了我们无数次没有爱人如己的亏欠。你若知道自己远没有达到利未记十九章的标准，不必因此却步——正因祂已经替你担当了这亏欠的审判，「你们要归我为圣」（利20:26）这身份此刻已藉着祂赐给凡信靠祂的人，而不是等你先做到才配得。
content_en:
Book Background

Leviticus is the book of law God gave the Israelites at Sinai through Moses, falling broadly into several sections: the sacrificial regulations (chapters 1–7), the establishment of the priesthood (chapters 8–10), the purity regulations (chapters 11–15), the Day of Atonement (chapter 16), and the “Holiness Code” running through chapters 17–26. Chapters 18–20 fall within this Holiness Code, extending holiness from the altar to marriage, sexual relationships, and the most ordinary areas of everyday human relationships.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapter 17 has already established the principle of “one altar, one LORD”; chapters 18–20 immediately apply this principle to concrete ethical living: chapter 18 forbids imitating the sexually immoral customs of Egypt and Canaan; chapter 19 unfolds into a set of rules for living that spans piety and justice; chapter 20 sets the penalties for the sins listed in chapter 18, and closes with “you shall be holy to me” — holiness is not an abstract religious sentiment, but a concrete, countable way of life.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 18: God commands the Israelites not to follow the practices of Egypt or Canaan (Lev. 18:3), then lists a series of forbidden incestuous and immoral relationships. The chapter closes with a warning that even the land of Canaan itself will “vomit you out” (Lev. 18:28) because of the defilement of its inhabitants — holiness concerns not only personal gain or loss, but whether the land itself can continue to sustain a people.
  • Chapter 19: The chapter opens by stating the core of the Holiness Code: “You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy” (Lev. 19:2); it then covers honoring parents, keeping the Sabbath, leaving the corners of fields for the poor, honest dealing, not bearing hatred, and not taking revenge, closing with “you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. 19:18) — a command Jesus later quotes directly, making it the second greatest commandment in the law.
  • Chapter 20: The penalties for the sins listed in chapter 18 are reaffirmed, and the chapter closes: “You shall be holy to me, for I the LORD am holy and have separated you from the peoples, that you should be mine” (Lev. 20:26) — the ultimate purpose of holiness is not the drawing of boundaries for its own sake, but becoming a people who belong to God, distinct from all other peoples.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

Jesus singles out Leviticus 19:18 from among all these many statutes and quotes it directly: “And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:39), pairing it with loving the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and mind as the summary of “all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40) — reminding us that the Holiness Code was never a pile of isolated rules, but has one thread running through it all: wholehearted love for God, extending outward into love for one’s neighbor as oneself. Yet chapters 18–20 also let us see just how comprehensive this thread’s demand truly is — no sinner can, by their own effort, fully live out such holiness. This is precisely why this whole law also prepares the people to see that they need a king who can truly fulfill “love your neighbor as yourself.”

Response

Jesus is that very one who perfectly lived out “love your neighbor as yourself” on earth — he not only taught this commandment, but personally laid down his life on the cross for those he loved, bearing the debt of our countless failures to love our neighbor as ourselves. If you know you fall far short of the standard of Leviticus 19, don’t let that make you shrink back — precisely because he has already borne the judgment for that debt in your place, the identity “you shall be holy to me” (Lev. 20:26) is now given, through him, to everyone who trusts him — not something you must first achieve before you deserve it.

title: 作圣洁的领袖
verse: 利未记廿三章三节
content:
书卷背景

利未记的圣洁法典从十七章一路延伸至此：十八至二十章讲圣洁如何落实在百姓的日常伦理中，二十一至二十三章则转向两个更专门的领域——祭司的圣洁（21-22章），以及神为全体百姓所定的敬拜节期（23章）。

在全书结构中的位置

祭司是站在百姓与神之间的中保，他们若沾染污秽，受害的不只是自己，更是全会众敬拜的洁净；因此二十一至二十二章对祭司提出比一般百姓更严格的圣洁要求。二十三章紧接其后，把焦点从「谁可以事奉」转向「百姓一年中要如何按时聚集敬拜神」，为以色列全年的敬拜生活订出节奏。

主题与神学重点
  • 廿一章：祭司不可因死人沾染自己（近亲例外），大祭司的要求更严，甚至不可为父母的丧事离开圣所（利21:11-12）；有残疾的祭司后裔虽仍可吃圣物，却不可近前献祭——祭司职分本身的圣洁标准，高于个人的资格与恩赐。
  • 廿二章：祭司若身上有污秽，不可吃圣物，直到洁净；献给耶和华的祭牲必须毫无残疾（利22:20）——所献上的必须配得上那位接受敬拜者的完全。
  • 廿三章：神吩咐以色列人守每周的安息日：「六日要做工，第七日是圣安息日，当有圣会；你们什么工都不可做」（利23:3），随后展开全年的节期日历——逾越节与无酵节、初熟节、七七节（五旬节）、吹角节、赎罪日、住棚节。这份节期日历不是随意的节庆安排，而是神刻意把救赎的节奏，事先编织进以色列人的年历之中。
救赎历史脉络

这份节期日历后来在基督身上一一应验：逾越节的羊羔预表基督被钉十字架为百姓舍命，初熟节预表基督从死里复活、成为收成的头一份保证（已在哥林多前书十五章的复活论述中提过），七七节／五旬节所纪念的收割，也正是圣灵降临、教会诞生的那一天（已在使徒行传二章提过）。以色列人守节期，其实是在年复一年地演练一出尚未完全揭晓的救赎剧本，而这剧本的每一幕，都在基督里得到了成就。

回应

祭司需要毫无残疾的祭牲才能蒙悦纳，自己也需要谨守繁琐的洁净条例才能事奉；但你不需要等到自己毫无瑕疵才能亲近神——那一位毫无残疾的真羊羔已经代替我们献上，那使我们得享安息的真安息日主已经来到。利未记廿三章开头的安息日，最终在那句邀请里得着回应：「凡劳苦担重担的人可以到我这里来，我就使你们得安息」（太11:28）——这安息，不是靠你先活出祭司般的圣洁去挣得，而是白白赐给凡愿意来到祂面前的人。
content_en:
Book Background

Leviticus’s Holiness Code extends all the way from chapter 17 to here: chapters 18–20 addressed how holiness is lived out in the people’s daily ethics; chapters 21–23 then turn to two more specialized areas — the holiness of the priests (chapters 21–22), and the appointed feasts God set for the whole people’s worship (chapter 23).

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

The priests stand as mediators between the people and God; if they become defiled, the harm falls not only on themselves, but on the purity of the whole congregation’s worship. That is why chapters 21–22 hold the priests to a stricter standard of holiness than the ordinary people. Chapter 23 follows immediately after, shifting the focus from “who may serve” to “how the people are to gather and worship God throughout the year,” setting the rhythm for Israel’s entire calendar of worship.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 21: Priests may not defile themselves for the dead (except for close relatives); the requirements for the high priest are even stricter — he may not even leave the sanctuary to mourn his own father or mother (Lev. 21:11–12). A priest’s descendant with a physical defect may still eat the holy food, but may not come near to offer the sacrifices — the holiness standard of the priestly office itself outweighs personal qualification or gifting.
  • Chapter 22: If a priest has any uncleanness on him, he may not eat the holy food until he is clean; an animal offered to the LORD must have no defect whatsoever (Lev. 22:20) — what is offered must be worthy of the one who is perfect and receives the worship.
  • Chapter 23: God commands the Israelites to keep the weekly Sabbath: “Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, a holy convocation. You shall do no work” (Lev. 23:3), and then unfolds the calendar of feasts for the whole year — Passover and Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost), the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Booths. This calendar of feasts is not an arbitrary arrangement of holidays, but God deliberately weaving the rhythm of redemption ahead of time into the Israelites’ yearly calendar.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

This calendar of feasts is later fulfilled point by point in Christ: the Passover lamb foreshadows Christ crucified, laying down his life for his people; the Feast of Firstfruits foreshadows Christ rising from the dead as the first guarantee of the harvest (already touched on in the discussion of the resurrection in 1 Corinthians 15); and the harvest commemorated at the Feast of Weeks/Pentecost is the very day the Spirit descended and the church was born (already touched on in Acts 2). In keeping these feasts year after year, Israel was, in effect, rehearsing a redemption story not yet fully revealed — and every scene of that story has now been fulfilled in Christ.

Response

The priests needed a flawless sacrificial animal to be accepted, and had to keep elaborate purity regulations themselves in order to serve. But you don’t need to wait until you are without blemish yourself before you can draw near to God — the true, spotless Lamb has already been offered up in our place, and the true Lord of the Sabbath who gives us rest has already come. The Sabbath that opens Leviticus 23 finds its answer, in the end, in this invitation: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matt. 11:28) — this rest is not something you earn by first living out priest-like holiness, but is freely given to everyone willing to come to him.

title: 对神及大自然之回应
verse: 利未记廿六章十二节
content:
书卷背景

利未记廿四至廿七章是全书的收尾部分：廿四章处理圣所内的日常事奉与两个具体案例，廿五章订立安息年与禧年，廿六章是整卷书的高潮——立约的祝福与咒诅，廿七章则以许愿与十一奉献的条例作结。

在全书结构中的位置

十七至二十六章的「圣洁法典」在廿六章达到顶点：这一章以「若遵行……就……」「若不听从……就……」的格式，把整卷书所颁的律例典章，浓缩成一组立约的祝福与咒诅，正式为西奈之约画上句点；廿七章则作为附录，处理百姓向耶和华许愿、分别为圣的具体条例。

主题与神学重点
  • 廿四章：常燃的灯与常设的陈设饼，象征以色列在神面前不间断的敬拜；一名亵渎圣名者被治死，随之颁布同态报应原则：「以眼还眼，以牙还牙」（利24:20）——公义必须合乎比例，不容私自加重。
  • 廿五章：安息年（第七年）与禧年（第五十年）让土地歇息、让被卖的产业与为奴的弟兄得以归回：「这年必为你们的禧年，各人要归自己的产业，各归本家」（利25:10）；地与人终究都不属于以色列人自己，而属于耶和华，因此不能被永久占有或奴役。
  • 廿六至廿七章：遵行律例带来降雨丰收、平安无惧、神在他们中间行走的祝福；悖逆则招致疾病、饥荒、被掳、地土荒凉——但即使在被掳的咒诅中，神仍应许「我却要为他们的缘故记念我与他们先祖所立的约」（利26:45），刑罚不是神毁约，而是恢复百姓归向祂的管教；廿七章则以许愿、估价、十一奉献的条例，为全书划下句点。
救赎历史脉络

利未记从头到尾都在回答一个问题：一位圣洁的神，如何能与不洁净的百姓同住？献祭制度（1-7章）处理罪的代价，祭司职分（8-10章）设立中保，洁净条例（11-15章）划定界线，赎罪日（16章）一年一度遮盖全会众的罪，圣洁法典（17-26章）教百姓在日常生活中活出被分别为圣的身份——而这一切制度所指向的终极目标，正凝聚在廿六章十二节这一句立约的应许里：「我要在你们中间行走；我要作你们的神，你们要作我的子民」（利26:12）。这句「同住的应许」并非利未记独有，它在出埃及记廿九章、以西结书三十七章反复出现，而最终毫无保留地实现在启示录廿一章：「神的帐幕在人间，他要与人同住，他们要作他的子民」（启21:3）。利未记全书所建立的献祭与圣洁体系，从来不是目的本身，而是在旧约的限制之下，暂时维系这应许不至断绝的权宜之法——旧约百姓一次次因悖逆而几乎失去这同住的应许，正如廿六章所警告的，但神对这应许的心意从未改变，直到基督成就了永不废去的同住。

回应

利未记廿六章十二节所应许的同住，在旧约底下始终系于百姓能否遵行律例——而以色列人一次又一次证明自己做不到。但神对这应许的信实，不是靠着百姓的表现，而是靠着祂自己的约；基督的死正是要挪去那使我们与神隔绝的罪，好叫「我要作你们的神，你们要作我的子民」这句古老的应许，如今能毫无保留地、永远地临到凡信靠祂的人——你与神同住的资格，不在于你有没有活出利未记的标准，而在于那位已经替你成就了这一切的基督。
content_en:
Book Background

Leviticus 24–27 forms the closing section of the book: chapter 24 deals with daily service within the sanctuary and two specific cases; chapter 25 establishes the sabbatical year and the Year of Jubilee; chapter 26, the climax of the whole book, gives the covenant blessings and curses; and chapter 27 closes with regulations on vows and the tithe.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

The “Holiness Code” of chapters 17–26 reaches its peak in chapter 26: using the pattern “if you walk in my statutes… then…” and “if you will not listen to me… then…”, this chapter condenses all the statutes given in the whole book into a single set of covenant blessings and curses, formally bringing the Sinai covenant to its conclusion. Chapter 27 then serves as an appendix, dealing with the specific regulations for vows and consecration the people make to the LORD.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 24: The continually burning lamp and the continually set bread of the Presence symbolize Israel’s unceasing worship before God. One who blasphemes the Name is put to death, and this is followed by the principle of proportional retribution: “eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Lev. 24:20) — justice must be proportionate, never privately escalated.
  • Chapter 25: The sabbatical year (the seventh year) and the Year of Jubilee (the fiftieth year) let the land rest and let sold property and enslaved kinsmen return: “this fiftieth year shall be a jubilee for you… each of you shall return to his property and each of you shall return to his clan” (Lev. 25:10) — the land and the people ultimately belong not to Israel itself, but to the LORD, and so cannot be permanently seized or enslaved.
  • Chapters 26–27: Obedience to the statutes brings rain and abundant harvest, peace and freedom from fear, and God walking among them; rebellion brings disease, famine, exile, and a desolate land — yet even amid the curse of exile, God still promises, “I will remember for their sake the covenant with their forefathers” (Lev. 26:45); the punishment is not God breaking covenant, but discipline meant to restore the people back to him. Chapter 27 then closes the book with regulations on vows, valuations, and the tithe.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

From beginning to end, Leviticus answers one question: how can a holy God dwell with an unclean people? The sacrificial system (chapters 1–7) deals with the cost of sin, the priesthood (chapters 8–10) establishes a mediator, the purity regulations (chapters 11–15) draw boundaries, the Day of Atonement (chapter 16) covers the whole congregation’s sin once a year, and the Holiness Code (chapters 17–26) teaches the people to live out their set-apart identity in daily life — and the ultimate goal all these systems point to is condensed in this one covenant promise: “I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people” (Lev. 26:12). This “promise of dwelling together” is not unique to Leviticus; it recurs in Exodus 29 and Ezekiel 37, and is finally fulfilled without reservation in Revelation 21: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people” (Rev. 21:3). The sacrificial and holiness system Leviticus establishes was never an end in itself, but a temporary provision, under the limits of the Old Testament, to keep this promise from being lost — the Old Testament people, again and again, nearly forfeited this promise of dwelling together through their rebellion, exactly as chapter 26 warns, yet God’s resolve toward this promise never changed, until Christ accomplished a dwelling together that can never be undone.

Response

The dwelling together promised in Leviticus 26:12 always, under the Old Testament, hinged on whether the people could keep the statutes — and Israel proved again and again that they could not. But God’s faithfulness to this promise was never anchored in the people’s performance, but in his own covenant; Christ’s death was precisely to remove the sin that separated us from God, so that this ancient promise, “I will be your God, and you shall be my people,” could now come, without reservation, forever, to everyone who trusts him — your qualification to dwell with God rests not on whether you have lived up to Leviticus’s standard, but on Christ, who has already accomplished all of it for you.

title: 人口普查及职业分配
title_en: The Census and Assignment of Duties
verse: 民数记三章十二节至十三节
content:
书卷背景

民数记记载以色列人从西奈山出发、直到抵达摩押平原、准备进入迦南地之间大约四十年的旷野岁月。英文书名「Numbers」（数目）取自书中开头（一章）与末了（廿六章）两次人口普查，但希伯来文书名「Bemidbar」（意思是「在旷野」）其实更贴近全书的重点——这不只是一本记数的书，而是一卷记载蒙救赎的百姓，如何在旷野中学习与神同行的书。全书的核心悲剧发生在加低斯巴尼亚（十三至十四章）：探子回报的恶信使百姓因不信而拒绝进入迦南，那整个成年一代因此要在旷野飘流卅八年、直到死尽，只有他们的儿女，加上迦勒和约书亚，才能进入应许之地。因此，民数记从头到尾都在呈现一个张力：神信实不变的引导与供应，对照百姓一再的埋怨与不信——这张力如此深刻，以致保罗后来在哥林多前书十章直接把旷野一代当作警戒教会的反面教材。

在全书结构中的位置

一至四章正站在全书最开头——以色列人还未拔营离开西奈，神先吩咐摩西数点能打仗的男丁，把百姓编列成一支行军的队伍；再另外数点利未人，把他们从战斗编制中分别出来，专责服事会幕。这四章为即将展开的旷野之旅定下秩序：一个以神的居所为中心、层层环绕安营的百姓。

主题与神学重点
  • 一章：按支派数点二十岁以外能出去打仗的男丁，共计六十万零三千五百五十名（民1:45）；十二支派都被数点，惟独利未支派不算在其中（民1:47-49），因为他们另有职分——办理会幕的事。
  • 二章：十二支派按东、南、西、北四方安营，以会幕居中，利未人在最内层——整个营区本身就是一篇无声的信息：神的居所在百姓中间，百姓无论走到哪里，都环绕着祂安营。
  • 三至四章：利未人按革顺、哥辖、米拉利三个宗族分别数点，各自承担抬会幕不同部分的职责；神又吩咐利未人正式代替以色列人一切头生的男子归祂所有：「凡头生的是我的」（民3:13）——这要追溯到出埃及那夜，头生的因逾越节的羊羔而得以存活。
救赎历史脉络

三章利未人代替以色列头生男子的安排，直接连于埃及地那一夜的逾越节：头生的之所以存活，不是因为他们本身配得，而是因为一只羊羔代替他们死了；如今利未人代替头生的、归耶和华所有，延续的正是这「有一位代替」的逻辑，日后要一次又一次地在以色列的献祭制度里重演。而这卷刚刚才如此细致地把百姓、按着神的居所安营编排妥当的书，接下来要记载的却是这同一批百姓，如何在加低斯巴尼亚因不信而几乎断送了这一切秩序原本要带领他们进入的产业——神对祂计划的信实持续不变，纵使百姓的信心屡屡崩溃。

回应

以色列人还没有做什么配得纪念的事，神就已经把百姓环绕自己安营，并预备了利未人这「代替」的安排来保全头生的男子——这正是后来在基督身上完全成就的同一个模式：祂亲自代替那本该归于神审判的我们死了，好使我们不被驱赶、反倒能被带到祂近前。这不是靠我们先整队站好、先配得才蒙悦纳；乃是神先施恩，才使我们得以在祂面前有份。
content_en:
Book Background

Numbers records roughly forty years of wilderness wandering, from the Israelites leaving Mount Sinai to arriving at the plains of Moab, ready to enter Canaan. The English title “Numbers” comes from the two censuses that bookend the story (chapter 1 and chapter 26), but the Hebrew title, Bemidbar (“in the wilderness”), better captures the book’s real focus — this is not merely a book of counting, but a book about how a redeemed people learns to walk with God in the wilderness. The book’s central tragedy takes place at Kadesh-barnea (chapters 13–14): the spies’ bad report causes the people, in unbelief, to refuse to enter Canaan, so that entire generation must wander in the wilderness for thirty-eight years until they die out — only their children, plus Caleb and Joshua, would enter the promised land. So from beginning to end, Numbers presents a tension: God’s unchanging, faithful guidance and provision, set against the people’s repeated grumbling and unbelief — a tension so deep that Paul, in 1 Corinthians 10, later holds up the wilderness generation directly as a warning to the church.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 1–4 stand right at the beginning of the book — the Israelites have not yet broken camp from Sinai. God first commands Moses to count the men able to go to war, organizing the people into a marching army; he then separately counts the Levites, setting them apart from the fighting ranks to serve the tabernacle exclusively. These four chapters set the order for the wilderness journey about to unfold: a people encamped in layers, centered on God’s dwelling place.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 1: The men over twenty able to go to war are counted by tribe, totaling 603,550 (Num. 1:45); all twelve tribes are counted, except the tribe of Levi (Num. 1:47–49), because they have a different duty — caring for the tabernacle.
  • Chapter 2: The twelve tribes camp on the east, south, west, and north sides, with the tabernacle at the center and the Levites in the innermost ring — the whole camp itself is a silent sermon: God’s dwelling is in the midst of the people, and wherever they go, they camp around him.
  • Chapters 3–4: The Levites are counted separately by their three clans — Gershon, Kohath, and Merari — each responsible for carrying a different part of the tabernacle. God also commands that the Levites formally take the place of all Israel’s firstborn males as his own: “every firstborn is mine” (Num. 3:13) — tracing back to the night of the exodus, when the firstborn survived because of the Passover lamb.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

The arrangement in chapter 3, where the Levites take the place of Israel’s firstborn males, is directly connected to that night of Passover in Egypt: the firstborn survived not because they themselves deserved it, but because a lamb died in their place. Now the Levites take the place of the firstborn, belonging to the LORD — continuing exactly this logic of “one substituted for another,” a pattern that would replay again and again in Israel’s sacrificial system. And this book, having just so carefully arranged the people around God’s dwelling place, is about to record how this very same people, at Kadesh-barnea, through unbelief, nearly forfeited the very inheritance this whole order was meant to lead them into — God’s faithfulness to his plan remains unchanging, even though the people’s faith collapses again and again.

Response

Before Israel had done anything to deserve remembrance, God had already arranged the people to camp around himself, and prepared the Levites as this arrangement of “substitution” to preserve the firstborn males — this is exactly the same pattern later fully accomplished in Christ: he himself died in the place of us, who deserved God’s judgment, so that we would not be driven away, but instead brought near to him. This is not something we earn by first getting in formation or first becoming worthy of acceptance; it is God who shows grace first, so that we might have a share in his presence.

title: 洁净百姓
verse: 民数记六章廿四节至廿六节
content:
书卷背景

以色列人还未拔营出发，神在西奈继续为营地立下秩序——这次的焦点从「谁站在哪里」转向「营地如何保持洁净」，为要配得神在他们中间居住。

在全书结构中的位置

一至四章按支派与宗族把营地编排妥当之后，五至八章接续处理营内的洁净问题：谁必须被隔离在营外（五章）、百姓可以如何甘心乐意地额外分别自己归神（六章拿细耳人的愿）、众支派首领如何为会幕的启用献上供物（七章），以及利未人自己如何被洁净、正式就职（八章）。贯穿这四章的，是同一个逻辑：一位圣洁的神住在营的中心，营就必须被保持洁净——无论是藉着律例强制要求，还是藉着百姓甘心的奉献。

主题与神学重点
  • 五章：患大麻风、漏症，或因死尸不洁净的人要被迁到营外（民5:1-4）；亏负邻舍的要认罪赔还；疑恨的条例（民5:11-31）把丈夫心中的猜疑，交托给神自己审断，而不是任凭人私下报复。
  • 六章：拿细耳人的愿——无论男女，都可以自愿离俗归耶和华一段时间，戒酒、蓄发、避开死尸（民6:2-7），这是一幅图画：分别为圣归神，不是祭司的专利，普通百姓也能甘心如此奉献自己。本章末了记下亚伦要为百姓所祝的福：「愿耶和华赐福给你，保护你。愿耶和华使他的脸光照你，赐恩给你。愿耶和华向你仰脸，赐你平安」（民6:24-26）。
  • 七章：十二支派首领在会幕分别为圣的十二天里，逐日献上完全相同的供物——这重复本身就是信息：每个支派在神面前的敬拜权利，毫无差别。
  • 八章：金灯台常常点着；利未人受洁净礼，被百姓按手、当作摇祭献给耶和华，从此专职事奉，服事年龄定在廿五岁到五十岁。
救赎历史脉络

亚伦所颂的祝福，把神对百姓的心意说得清清楚楚——愿祂的脸向他们光照，而不是转脸不顾。可是这祝福是藉着还需要自己献祭赎罪的祭司之口说出来的，还不能担保百姓的心不再像后面十一、十二章所记的那样很快转向埋怨。这祝福所应许的平安与恩待，最终要等到一位不需要自己先献祭赎罪、就能把神完全的恩待带给百姓的大祭司才得以稳固地临到——那就是基督。

回应

亚伦口中的祝福「愿耶和华向你仰脸，赐你平安」（民6:26）不是靠百姓当天的表现赢得的，而是神主动定意要赐给他们的；如今这平安藉着基督成就得更加确实——祂不只是宣告这祝福，更亲自用自己的血买定了这平安，使凡投靠祂的人，不必等自己先配得，就可以领受神向你仰脸的恩待。
content_en:
Book Background

The Israelites have not yet broken camp; God continues, at Sinai, to establish order for the camp — this time shifting focus from “who stands where” to “how the camp stays pure,” so as to be worthy of God dwelling among them.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Having arranged the camp by tribe and clan in chapters 1–4, chapters 5–8 go on to address the matter of purity within the camp: who must be put outside the camp (chapter 5), how the people can voluntarily set themselves further apart to God (the Nazirite vow in chapter 6), how the tribal leaders present offerings for the dedication of the tabernacle (chapter 7), and how the Levites themselves are purified and formally installed (chapter 8). Running through all four chapters is the same logic: a holy God dwells at the center of the camp, so the camp must be kept pure — whether through required statutes or through the people’s willing offerings.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 5: Those with leprous disease, a discharge, or defiled by a corpse must be moved outside the camp (Num. 5:1–4); one who wrongs a neighbor must confess and make restitution; the regulation concerning jealousy (Num. 5:11–31) entrusts a husband’s suspicion to God’s own judgment, rather than leaving it to private revenge.
  • Chapter 6: The Nazirite vow — any man or woman may voluntarily set themselves apart to the LORD for a period, abstaining from wine, letting their hair grow, and avoiding contact with the dead (Num. 6:2–7); this pictures that being set apart to God is not the exclusive privilege of priests — ordinary people, too, can willingly consecrate themselves this way. The chapter closes with the blessing Aaron is to pronounce over the people: “The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace” (Num. 6:24–26).
  • Chapter 7: During the twelve days of the tabernacle’s dedication, the leaders of the twelve tribes each bring an identical offering, day after day — this very repetition is itself the message: every tribe’s right to worship before God is exactly the same, with no distinction.
  • Chapter 8: The golden lampstand is kept continually lit; the Levites undergo a purification rite, are presented by the people with the laying on of hands, and are offered to the LORD as a wave offering, from then on serving exclusively, with their years of service set between twenty-five and fifty.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

The blessing Aaron pronounces states God’s heart toward the people with total clarity — may his face shine upon them, rather than turn away. But this blessing is spoken through the mouth of a priest who still needs to offer sacrifices for his own sin, and cannot yet guarantee that the people’s hearts will not, as chapters 11 and 12 will soon record, quickly turn to grumbling again. The peace and favor this blessing promises would only be securely fulfilled once a high priest arose who needed no sacrifice of his own, and could bring God’s complete favor to the people fully and finally — that is Christ.

Response

The blessing from Aaron’s mouth, “the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace” (Num. 6:26), was not earned by the people’s performance that day, but something God took the initiative to determine to give them. Today this peace is made even more certain through Christ — he not only pronounces this blessing, but has himself purchased this peace with his own blood, so that everyone who takes refuge in him need not first prove themselves worthy before receiving the favor of God’s face turned toward them.

title: 旷野中的埋怨与温柔
title_en: Grumbling and Gentleness in the Wilderness
verse: 民数记十二章三节
content:
书卷背景

以色列人在西奈山下已经安营将近一年，接下来的几章记载他们如何终于拔营起行，以及旅程一开始便浮现的裂痕。

在全书结构中的位置

九至十章为西奈的日子画下句点：百姓在西奈守了出埃及后第一个逾越节，神赐下云柱火柱、银号，百姓终于拔营前行；十一至十二章则记录旅程刚开始不久，百姓的埋怨与领袖之间的嫉妒便相继爆发——这为十三至十四章加低斯巴尼亚那场决定整代人命运的不信埋下伏笔。

主题与神学重点
  • 九章：以色列人在西奈守出埃及后第一个逾越节，神也体恤那些因不洁净或出外远行不能按时守节的人，另定二月十四日补守（民9:10-11）；此后云彩昼夜引导百姓的脚步，云彩几时收上去，百姓就几时起行——神亲自定了行程的快慢。
  • 十章：银号吹响，以色列人终于离开西奈的旷野，约柜在前头为他们寻找安歇之处（民10:33）——这是一次满有盼望、井然有序的出发。
  • 十一章：气氛几乎立刻逆转——百姓埋怨路途的艰难，又因贪恋肉食而轻看每日所赐的吗哪，甚至怀念埃及（民11:4-6）；摩西被这重担压垮，神就分摩西身上的灵给七十位长老，与他分担（民11:16-17）；神虽赐下鹌鹑，却也在百姓贪欲之处降下灾殃，那地方因此得名基博罗·哈他瓦，意思是贪欲之人的坟墓（民11:34）。
  • 十二章：米利暗和亚伦因摩西所娶的古实女子毁谤他，实质是挑战摩西独特的领受地位；经文特意插入一句评语：「摩西为人极其谦和，胜过世上的众人」（民12:3）——神亲自出面，为摩西与祂面对面说话的独特地位辩护；米利暗虽然长了大麻风，却在摩西的代求下，七天后得洁净归回。
救赎历史脉络

九至十章满有盼望的出发，几章之内便滑落成埋怨、贪恋与嫉妒——这提醒我们，蒙救赎的百姓离弃悖逆的心，并不会因为神迹与供应而自动痊愈。摩西的谦和（民12:3）恰恰与百姓的强求、亲属的嫉妒成对比，也正是这份谦和，而不是权力手腕，使他配作那位神藉以向百姓说话、又为百姓代求的中保——这预表了后来那位「心里柔和谦卑」（太11:29）的更大中保，祂同样担当着一群不断埋怨、不断需要代求的百姓，却从不撇弃他们。

回应

摩西为米利暗的代求只维持了七天，而那位比摩西更谦和的中保，却为祂的百姓恒久代求，从不止息。你若看见自己心里也常像旷野中的百姓那样，对神已经赐下的心怀不满、觊觎着别处的东西——不要因此绝望：使我们得以存留的，从来不是我们比以色列人更懂得知足感恩，而是那位为我们代求、永不撇弃我们的基督。
content_en:
Book Background

The Israelites have camped at the foot of Sinai for nearly a year; the following chapters record how they finally break camp and set out, and the cracks that appear right at the start of the journey.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 9–10 bring the days at Sinai to a close: the people keep the first Passover since the exodus, God gives the pillar of cloud and fire and the silver trumpets, and the people finally break camp. Chapters 11–12 then record how, not long into the journey, the people’s grumbling and jealousy among the leaders erupt one after another — foreshadowing the unbelief at Kadesh-barnea in chapters 13–14 that would determine the whole generation’s fate.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 9: Israel keeps the first Passover since the exodus at Sinai; God also makes provision for those who cannot keep the feast on time due to uncleanness or a distant journey, setting a make-up date on the fourteenth of the second month (Num. 9:10–11); from then on, the cloud guides the people’s steps day and night — whenever the cloud lifted, the people set out — God himself set the pace of the journey.
  • Chapter 10: The trumpets sound, and the Israelites finally leave the wilderness of Sinai, with the ark going ahead of them to seek out a place to rest (Num. 10:33) — a hopeful, orderly departure.
  • Chapter 11: The mood almost immediately reverses — the people complain about the hardship of the journey, and, craving meat, despise the manna given daily, even longing for Egypt (Num. 11:4–6). Moses, crushed by the burden, has God’s Spirit distributed from him to seventy elders to share it (Num. 11:16–17). God sends quail, but also strikes the people with a plague at the very place of their craving, so that place is named Kibroth-hattaavah, meaning “graves of craving” (Num. 11:34).
  • Chapter 12: Miriam and Aaron slander Moses over the Cushite woman he married, but the real issue is a challenge to Moses’s unique standing before God. Scripture inserts a deliberate remark: “Now the man Moses was very meek, more than all people who were on the face of the earth” (Num. 12:3) — God himself steps in to defend Moses’s unique standing as the one who speaks with him face to face. Though Miriam is struck with leprosy, at Moses’s intercession she is cleansed and restored after seven days.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

The hopeful departure of chapters 9–10 collapses, within just a few chapters, into grumbling, craving, and jealousy — reminding us that a redeemed people’s rebellious heart is not automatically healed by miracles and provision. Moses’s meekness (Num. 12:3) stands in sharp contrast to the people’s demanding and his own family’s jealousy — and it is precisely this meekness, not any exercise of power, that qualifies him to be the mediator through whom God speaks to the people, and who intercedes on their behalf. This foreshadows the greater mediator later described as “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matt. 11:29), who likewise bears with a people who complain endlessly and constantly need intercession, yet never abandons them.

Response

Moses’s intercession for Miriam lasted only seven days, but the mediator gentler than Moses intercedes for his people continually, without ceasing. If you see in your own heart the same pattern as the people in the wilderness — dissatisfied with what God has already given, coveting something else — don’t despair over it: what preserves us has never been our being more content or grateful than Israel was, but Christ, who intercedes for us and never abandons us.

title: 安息日：安息与更新 (Rest and Renewal)
content:
今天是安息日——从利未记的圣洁法典，到民数记的启程与初期挫折，这一周份量厚重，今天停下脚步，回顾、安歇。

这一周我们读完了利未记（十八至廿七章）：性道德与「爱人如己」的圣洁准则、祭司更严格的要求、七大节期、安息年与禧年、顺服悖逆的祝福咒诅；随后进入民数记（一至十二章）：人口普查、十二支派安营、拿细耳人誓愿、祭司祝福词、百姓启程后不久便埋怨思念埃及、米利暗亚伦挑战摩西的权柄。从利未记严谨的圣洁条例，到民数记百姓迅速的软弱失败，形成鲜明的对比——神已经清楚吩咐了当行的道，百姓却仍然一再跌倒。

留意这一周经文里反复出现的画面：神愿意「在你们中间行走」（利26:12），愿意用云柱火柱亲自引路（民九至十章），却也一次次目睹祂的百姓埋怨、悖逆、彼此相争。这提醒我们：神的同在，从不保证百姓自动就会顺服；祂的信实，恰恰是在百姓一再软弱之中，仍然不离不弃。

建议你今天：①回顾这一周，挑一段你印象最深的经文重读一遍；②默想民数记六章24至26节的祭司祝福，把它当作神此刻对你的祝福；③安静反省：我这一周的信仰生活，是更像百姓的埋怨，还是摩西的谦和？

应用：今天用一句话，为自己写下这一周读经的收获——一句最触动你、也最想带着走的话。
content_en:
Today is a Sabbath day — from Leviticus’s Holiness Code to Numbers’s departure and early setbacks, this week has been dense; today we stop, look back, and rest.

This week we finished Leviticus (chapters 18–27): the holiness standards of sexual morality and “love your neighbor as yourself,” the stricter requirements for priests, the seven great feasts, the sabbatical year and Jubilee, and the blessings and curses of obedience and rebellion; then we moved into Numbers (chapters 1–12): the census, the twelve tribes camping, the Nazirite vow, the priestly blessing, and, not long after setting out, the people grumbling and longing for Egypt, and Miriam and Aaron challenging Moses’s authority. The contrast between Leviticus’s rigorous holiness code and Numbers’s swift human weakness and failure is stark — God has clearly commanded the way to walk, yet the people still stumble again and again.

Notice the image that recurs throughout this week’s reading: God is willing to “walk among you” (Lev. 26:12), willing to guide personally by pillar of cloud and fire (Numbers 9–10) — and yet he also, again and again, witnesses his people grumble, rebel, and quarrel with one another. This reminds us: God’s presence never guarantees the people will automatically obey; his faithfulness is precisely this — that even amid the people’s repeated weakness, he never lets go.

Today, consider: (1) Look back over this week and reread the passage that struck you most. (2) Meditate on the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:24–26, and receive it as God’s blessing over you right now. (3) Reflect quietly: has my faith life this week looked more like the people’s grumbling, or Moses’s meekness?

Application: Write down, in one sentence, what you’ve gained from this week’s reading — the one line that struck you most, and that you most want to carry with you.

title: 十二探子与旷野的悖逆
title_en: The Twelve Spies and Rebellion in the Wilderness
verse: 民数记十四章九节
content:
书卷背景

民数记记载以色列人从西奈山到摩押平原的旷野路程；此前的篇幅（一至十二章）安顿了会众的编制、利未人的服事，也记下了百姓一路的抱怨。十三至十六章要记的，是这段旅程的转折点——以色列站在应许之地的门口，却因不信而转身离弃。

在全书结构中的位置

十三至十四章是全书的枢纽：在此之前，以色列朝着迦南前进；从此以后，整整一代人要在旷野飘流四十年，直到消灭净尽。十五章紧接在这审判宣告之后，却记载了「你们到了我所赐给你们居住的地」（民15:2）的献祭条例——上主一面宣告这一代人不得进迦南，一面已经在为下一代人预备进地后的敬拜生活，暗示应许并未因人的不信而落空。十六章可拉一党的叛乱，则是对刚确立的摩西、亚伦领导权柄（及背后神所设立的秩序）的又一次挑战——从口头的怨言，升级为对神所立中保职分的公然反叛。

主题与神学重点
  • 十三章：摩西差十二支派首领窥探迦南，四十日后回报：那地「果然是流奶与蜜之地」（民13:27），但十位探子看见城邑坚固、居民身量高大，就在百姓中散布惧怕；唯有迦勒在摩西面前安抚百姓：「我们立刻上去得那地吧！我们足能得胜」（民13:30）——同一片土地，十人看见拦阻，两人看见应许。
  • 十四章：全会众因惧怕而彻夜哭号，甚至彼此说：「不如立一个首领回埃及去」（民14:4）；约书亚、迦勒撕裂衣服劝百姓：「但你们不可背叛耶和华，也不要怕那地的居民……有耶和华与我们同在，不要怕他们」（民14:9），百姓竟要用石头打死他们二人。摩西为百姓代求，倚靠的是神自己的性情：「耶和华不轻易发怒，并有丰盛的慈爱，赦免罪孽和过犯」（民14:18）；神应允赦免这罪孽本身，却仍宣告后果——凡二十岁以外曾发怨言的，「他们断不得看见我向他们的祖宗所起誓应许之地」（民14:23），唯独迦勒和约书亚因「另有一个心志，专一跟从我」（民14:24）得以进入。赦免与管教，在这一章里同时成立，并不互相取消。
  • 十五至十六章：十五章的条例——初熟的举祭、误犯的赎罪祭——都是写给「将来」进地的百姓，紧跟在「这一代人不得进地」的宣判之后，成了一种沉默却确实的应许延续。十六章可拉、大坍、亚比兰聚集攻击摩西、亚伦：「你们为什么自高，超过耶和华的会众呢」（民16:3）——地开口吞灭了叛党，又有火烧灭了献香的二百五十人；然而百姓次日竟向摩西、亚伦发怨言：「你们杀了耶和华的百姓了」（民16:41）——连亲眼见证的审判，也没有挪去他们心中的悖逆。
救赎历史脉络

这段加低斯巴尼亚的悖逆，后来被新约作者直接引用为警戒：「他们不能进入安息是因为不信的缘故了」（来3:19）——不是能力不够，也不是应许不够好，而是不信，拦阻了那一代人进入神所应许的安息。希伯来书接着指出，那安息至今仍向神的子民存留，通往这安息的路，惟独藉着信。十四章里唯二存活、得以进地的两个人中，「嫩的儿子约书亚」这个名字本身（与「耶稣」原是同一个希伯来名字）已经埋下伏笔：真正带领神的百姓进入安息的，最终要靠一位比约书亚更伟大的引路者。

回应

以色列在加低斯巴尼亚跌倒之处，正是耶稣在旷野受试探之处得胜——他没有像那一代人那样因所见的艰难而怀疑天父的信实，反而以顺服走完了通往十字架的路，为要使凡因不信而理当被拦在门外的人，得以「坦然无惧地来到施恩的宝座前」（来4:16）。你不必先证明自己的信心配得进入，因为使人进入安息的，从来不是信心本身的分量，而是信心所倚靠的那一位；他已亲自走完了不信之人本该走的死路，把安息的门为你敞开。
content_en:
Book Background

Numbers records Israel’s wilderness journey from Sinai to the plains of Moab; the preceding chapters (1–12) settled the organization of the congregation and the Levites’ service, and also recorded the people’s grumbling along the way. Chapters 13–16 record the turning point of this journey — Israel stands at the door of the promised land, yet turns away in unbelief.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 13–14 are the hinge of the whole book: before this, Israel was advancing toward Canaan; from here on, an entire generation would wander in the wilderness for forty years until it perished completely. Chapter 15 immediately follows this pronouncement of judgment, yet records sacrificial regulations for “when you come into the land I am giving you to live in” (Num. 15:2) — the LORD, even while declaring that this generation would not enter Canaan, is already preparing the worship life of the next generation after they enter the land, hinting that the promise had not failed because of human unbelief. Chapter 16’s rebellion of Korah’s company is then yet another challenge to the leadership authority of Moses and Aaron (and the order God had established behind it) that had just been reaffirmed — escalating from verbal complaint to open rebellion against the mediatorial office God had appointed.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 13: Moses sends the leaders of the twelve tribes to spy out Canaan; forty days later they report that the land “does flow with milk and honey” (Num. 13:27), but ten of the spies, seeing the fortified cities and the tall stature of the inhabitants, spread fear among the people. Only Caleb reassures the people before Moses: “Let us go up at once and occupy it, for we are well able to overcome it” (Num. 13:30) — the same land, ten see an obstacle, two see a promise.
  • Chapter 14: The whole congregation weeps aloud all night in fear, even saying to one another, “Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt” (Num. 14:4). Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes and urge the people: “Only do not rebel against the LORD, and do not fear the people of the land… the LORD is with us; do not fear them” (Num. 14:9), and the congregation nearly stones them both. Moses intercedes for the people, appealing to God’s own character: “The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity and transgression” (Num. 14:18); God agrees to forgive this very iniquity, yet still declares the consequence — everyone twenty years old and up who grumbled “shall by no means see the land that I swore to give to their fathers” (Num. 14:23), except Caleb and Joshua, who, having “a different spirit and have followed me fully” (Num. 14:24), would enter. Forgiveness and discipline both stand true in this chapter, neither canceling the other out.
  • Chapters 15–16: The regulations in chapter 15 — the firstfruits offering, the sin offering for unintentional sin — are written for the people who will enter the land “in the future,” following right on the heels of the judgment that “this generation shall not enter” — becoming a silent yet certain continuation of the promise. In chapter 16, Korah, Dathan, and Abiram gather to oppose Moses and Aaron: “Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?” (Num. 16:3); the ground opens and swallows the rebels, and fire consumes the two hundred and fifty men offering incense. Yet the very next day the people grumble against Moses and Aaron: “You have killed the people of the LORD” (Num. 16:41) — even witnessing the judgment with their own eyes did not remove the rebellion from their hearts.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

This rebellion at Kadesh-barnea is later cited directly by a New Testament author as a warning: “they were unable to enter because of unbelief” (Heb. 3:19) — it was not a lack of ability, nor was the promise not good enough; it was unbelief that kept that generation from entering the rest God had promised. Hebrews goes on to say that this rest still remains for God’s people today, and the only way into it is through faith. Of the only two people in chapter 14 who survive to enter the land, the very name of one of them — “Joshua the son of Nun” (the same Hebrew name as “Jesus”) — already plants a seed: the one who would truly lead God’s people into rest would, in the end, need a greater guide than Joshua.

Response

The very place Israel stumbled at Kadesh-barnea is the place Jesus overcame when tempted in the wilderness — he did not, like that generation, doubt the Father’s faithfulness because of the hardships he saw, but instead walked the road to the cross in obedience, so that everyone who, because of unbelief, deserved to be shut out, could “draw near with confidence to the throne of grace” (Heb. 4:16). You don’t need to first prove your faith worthy of entrance, because what brings a person into rest was never the weight of faith itself, but the one faith rests on; he has already walked, in our place, the road of death that unbelief deserved, and thrown open the door of rest for you.

title: 亚伦的杖与摩西的失误
verse: 民数记二十章十二节
content:
书卷背景

可拉一党的叛乱与随之而来的瘟疫（十六章）之后，十七至十九章处理的是两个问题：谁才是神真正拣选的祭司？百姓又当如何面对满营的死亡与污秽？二十章重新接续旅程的记事，却记下了旷野世代最年长的三位领袖——米利暗、摩西、亚伦——相继离场的一幕。

在全书结构中的位置

这四章像是叙事中的一次停顿：十七章用杖发芽的神迹确立亚伦祭司职分的合法性，十八章交代祭司与利未人的职责和供养，十九章设立红母牛的洁净礼，专门应对死尸带来的污秽——这在刚经历瘟疫的营地里，绝非题外话。到了二十章，故事重新往前走，却是以一连串的死亡与失败开场：米利暗死了，旷野最伟大的中保摩西在关键一刻失了准头，亚伦也死在何珥山上。带领这一代人出埃及的领袖，正随着这一代人一同凋零。

主题与神学重点
  • 十七章：耶和华吩咐十二支派首领各拿一根杖存在法柜前：「后来我所拣选的那人，他的杖必发芽」（民17:5）；次日，唯独亚伦的杖「已经发了芽，生了花苞，开了花，结了熟杏」（民17:8）——不是亚伦自己争来的地位，而是神以一根本已枯死的木杖亲自证明的拣选。
  • 十八章：神将祭司与利未人的供职、供养都详细定下，也划下一条不能挪移的界线：「凡挨近的外人必被治死」（民18:7）——亲近神的圣所从不是随意的事，唯有神所指定的中保才可以担当。
  • 十九章：红母牛焚烧成灰，调水用来洁净凡摸过死尸的人；这条例安放在十六章一万四千七百人死于瘟疫之后，绝非偶然——一个死亡如此频繁的营地，需要一条不断更新、使人得以重新亲近神的洁净之路。
  • 二十章：百姓在加低斯又因无水而向摩西、亚伦争闹，耶和华吩咐摩西：「你拿着杖去，和你的哥哥亚伦招聚会众，在他们眼前吩咐磐石发出水来」（民20:8）；摩西却举手「用杖击打磐石两下，就有许多水流出来」（民20:11）——水照样涌出，百姓照样喝了，但耶和华随即宣告：「因为你们不信我，不在以色列人眼前尊我为圣，所以你们必不得领这会众进我所赐给他们的地去」（民20:12）。不久，亚伦就死在何珥山上——审判几乎立刻应验。
救赎历史脉络

摩西是旧约中最伟大的中保，脸对脸与神说话，又一再为百姓的罪代求；然而就是这样一位摩西，也在磐石前失了准头——不是照神所吩咐的「说」，而是照自己的怒气去「击打」，把自己的情绪加进了神清清楚楚的话语里，结果就在百姓眼前歪曲了神的形象。保罗后来提醒哥林多教会，旷野中「所喝的，是出于随着他们的灵磐石；那磐石就是基督」（林前10:4）——那磐石早在出埃及记十七章已被击打过一次；这一次，神只要人「说」，不要再「打」。摩西的失误提醒我们：连以色列最伟大的中保也会在恩典的边界上跌倒；真正毫无瑕疵、永不失准的中保，还在后头。

回应

摩西的失误提醒我们，连以色列最伟大的中保也会在恩典的边界上跌倒——不是因为他能力不够，而是因为怒气使他偏离了神清楚吩咐的话。但这失误并没有拦住神的应许成就；神只是不再让摩西亲自带这百姓进去，应许本身仍然稳妥。那磐石「就是基督」（林前10:4），祂只被击打一次，如今向凡来就祂的人涌流不绝的恩典，不需要你先证明自己比摩西更能自持，只需要你像干渴的会众一样，来支取。
content_en:
Book Background

After the rebellion of Korah’s company and the plague that followed (chapter 16), chapters 17–19 deal with two questions: who is truly God’s chosen priest, and how should the people deal with the death and defilement now filling the camp? Chapter 20 picks the journey narrative back up, yet records the departure, one after another, of the wilderness generation’s three most senior leaders — Miriam, Moses, and Aaron.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

These four chapters form a kind of pause in the narrative: chapter 17 establishes the legitimacy of Aaron’s priesthood through the miracle of the budding staff; chapter 18 sets out the duties and provision of the priests and Levites; chapter 19 institutes the purification rite of the red heifer, specifically for dealing with the defilement caused by a corpse — hardly beside the point in a camp that has just been through a plague. By chapter 20, the story moves forward again, but opens with a series of deaths and failures: Miriam dies, Moses, the wilderness’s greatest mediator, loses his composure at a crucial moment, and Aaron dies on Mount Hor. The leaders who brought this generation out of Egypt are passing away along with that generation.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 17: The LORD commands the leaders of the twelve tribes each to place a staff before the ark: “the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout” (Num. 17:5); the next day, only Aaron’s staff “had sprouted and put forth buds and produced blossoms, and it bore ripe almonds” (Num. 17:8) — not a status Aaron won for himself, but an election God personally proved through an already-dead piece of wood.
  • Chapter 18: God sets out in detail the duties and provision of the priests and Levites, and draws an immovable boundary: “any outsider who comes near shall be put to death” (Num. 18:7) — drawing near to God’s sanctuary was never a casual matter; only the mediator God appoints may bear it.
  • Chapter 19: A red heifer is burned to ashes, and the ashes mixed with water are used to purify anyone who has touched a corpse; this regulation, placed right after fourteen thousand seven hundred died of plague in chapter 16, is no coincidence — a camp with death this frequent needs a continually renewable way of cleansing, so people can draw near to God again.
  • Chapter 20: The people, at Kadesh, again quarrel with Moses and Aaron for lack of water; the LORD commands Moses, “Take the staff, and assemble the congregation, you and Aaron your brother, and tell the rock before their eyes to yield its water” (Num. 20:8). But Moses raises his hand and “struck the rock with his staff twice, and water came out abundantly” (Num. 20:11) — the water flows just the same, and the people drink just the same, yet the LORD immediately declares: “Because you did not believe in me, to uphold me as holy in the eyes of the people of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them” (Num. 20:12). Not long after, Aaron dies on Mount Hor — the judgment is fulfilled almost immediately.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

Moses is the greatest mediator in the Old Testament, speaking with God face to face, interceding again and again for the people’s sin; yet even this Moses loses his composure before the rock — instead of “speaking” as God commanded, he “strikes” out of his own anger, mixing his own emotion into God’s clear word, and, in the sight of the people, distorting the image of God. Paul later reminds the Corinthian church that in the wilderness, “they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4) — that rock had already been struck once, back in Exodus 17; this time, God only wanted the people to “speak,” not to “strike” again. Moses’s failure reminds us: even Israel’s greatest mediator could stumble at the very edge of grace; the truly flawless mediator, who never once loses his composure, was still to come.

Response

Moses’s failure reminds us that even Israel’s greatest mediator could stumble at the very edge of grace — not because he lacked ability, but because anger led him away from God’s clear instruction. Yet this failure did not block God’s promise from being fulfilled; God simply no longer let Moses personally lead the people in, while the promise itself remained secure. That rock “was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4); he was struck only once, and now pours out grace without end to everyone who comes to him — you don’t need to first prove you can hold yourself together better than Moses; you need only, like the thirsty congregation, come and draw from it.

title: 铜蛇、巴兰与巴力毗珥
title_en: The Bronze Serpent, Balaam, and Baal-Peor
verse: 民数记廿一章八节至九节
content:
书卷背景

亚伦死后，以色列绕过以东，一路争战——先胜迦南人亚拉得王，又败亚摩利王西宏、巴珊王噩，逐步逼近摩押平原。这段进程被两次插曲打断：一次是百姓自己的悖逆招来火蛇（廿一章），一次是外邦先知巴兰几次三番想咒诅以色列却屡屡开口称颂（廿二至廿四章）；到了廿五章，威胁不再来自战场，而是来自以色列人自己与摩押女子的苟合。

在全书结构中的位置

廿一至廿五章合起来讲一件事：没有一个外来的敌人能真正拦倒以色列——不是亚拉得的刀剑，不是西宏、噩的重兵，甚至不是巴兰所掌握的一切法术，因为神藉巴兰的口自己宣告：「神非人，必不致说谎」（民23:19），后来更直言没有法术占卜能够伤害以色列。真正险些绊倒以色列的，不是外面的敌人，而是他们自己的心——先是在廿一章因缺粮缺水向神发怨言，后是在廿五章向巴力毗珥的偶像与淫乱屈膝。外患挡不住神所祝福的百姓，内里的悖逆却几乎办到。

主题与神学重点
  • 廿一章：百姓因绕道以东而心中烦躁，再次发怨言：「我们的心厌恶这淡薄的食物」（民21:5）；耶和华就打发火蛇进入营中，许多人被咬死。百姓认罪，求摩西代求，耶和华的回应并非除去所有的蛇，而是吩咐摩西「制造一条火蛇，挂在杆子上；凡被咬的，一望这蛇，就必得活」（民21:8-9）——医治不在于逃避审判的记号，而在于定睛仰望它。
  • 廿二至廿四章：摩押王巴勒重金聘请术士巴兰咒诅以色列，巴兰却四次开口，四次都成了祝福：「神非人，必不致说谎」（民23:19），甚至说出「有星要出于雅各，有杖要兴于以色列」（民24:17）这样指向以色列未来君王的预言——连一个被雇来咒诅的外邦术士，也无法不说出神要为以色列所成就的事。
  • 廿五章：然而在什亭，「以色列人与巴力‧毗珥连合」（民25:3），神的怒气因此发作，瘟疫夺去二万四千人的性命，直到祭司非尼哈以行动止住瘟疫——外邦的咒诅伤不了以色列，以色列自己向偶像的屈膝却几乎使他们全然败落。
救赎历史脉络

廿一章的铜蛇事件，是全旧约中被耶稣本人亲口引用、最明确指向自己的预表之一：「摩西在旷野怎样举蛇，人子也必照样被举起来，叫一切信他的都得永生」（约3:14-15）。铜蛇本身没有任何医治的能力——它甚至是审判的记号，是那使人丧命之物的形状；百姓要得活，不是靠功德、不是靠触摸，只是「一望」。耶稣被举起在十字架上，也不是荣耀的形象，而是担当咒诅、代罪而死的记号；然而正是这看似最不可能带来生命的记号，成了凡仰望的人得永生的凭据。

回应

你不需要先明白透彻，也不需要先做出什么弥补，才可以支取十字架的果效——以色列营中被蛇咬伤的人，唯一被要求的动作只是转脸仰望那挂在杆子上的铜蛇，而这正是耶稣自己解释十字架时所用的比喻。今天，凡因自己的悖逆、自己的罪毒而将死的人，同样只需要将目光转向那位被举起来的人子——「叫一切信他的都得永生」（约3:14-15），不是因为你配得，而是因为祂已经被举起，为要让仰望祂的人活。
content_en:
Book Background

After Aaron’s death, Israel goes around Edom, fighting battle after battle — first defeating the Canaanite king of Arad, then Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, gradually approaching the plains of Moab. This advance is interrupted twice: once by the people’s own rebellion, bringing fiery serpents (chapter 21), and once by the foreign prophet Balaam, who repeatedly tries to curse Israel but keeps opening his mouth to bless them instead (chapters 22–24). By chapter 25, the threat no longer comes from the battlefield, but from the Israelites’ own immorality with Moabite women.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

Chapters 21–25, taken together, make one point: no outside enemy could ever truly defeat Israel — not the sword of Arad, not the armies of Sihon and Og, not even the full weight of Balaam’s sorcery, for God himself declares through Balaam’s own mouth, “God is not man, that he should lie” (Num. 23:19), later stating outright that no divination or sorcery could harm Israel. What nearly tripped Israel up was never an external enemy, but their own heart — first grumbling against God for lack of food and water in chapter 21, then bowing before the idol of Baal of Peor and its immorality in chapter 25. External threats could not stop a people God had blessed; internal rebellion very nearly did.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 21: Impatient over the detour around Edom, the people grumble again: “our soul loathes this worthless food” (Num. 21:5); the LORD sends fiery serpents into the camp, and many are bitten and die. The people confess their sin and ask Moses to intercede; the LORD’s response is not to remove all the serpents, but to command Moses to “make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live” (Num. 21:8–9) — healing lay not in escaping the sign of judgment, but in fixing one’s eyes on it.
  • Chapters 22–24: Balak king of Moab hires the sorcerer Balaam at great cost to curse Israel, yet Balaam opens his mouth four times, and four times it becomes blessing: “God is not man, that he should lie” (Num. 23:19), even uttering a prophecy pointing to a future king of Israel: “a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel” (Num. 24:17) — even a foreign sorcerer hired to curse cannot help but speak the very things God intends to accomplish for Israel.
  • Chapter 25: Yet at Shittim, “the people began to whore with the daughters of Moab” and “Israel yoked himself to Baal of Peor” (Num. 25:1, 3), and the LORD’s anger burns; a plague takes twenty-four thousand lives, until the priest Phinehas’s action stops it — a foreign curse could not harm Israel, but Israel’s own bowing to idols very nearly destroyed them entirely.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

The bronze serpent incident in chapter 21 is one of the clearest Old Testament foreshadowings that Jesus himself quotes as pointing directly to himself: “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14–15). The bronze serpent itself had no healing power at all — it was even the very shape of the thing that had killed them, the sign of judgment; the people were saved to live not by merit, not by touching it, but simply by “looking.” Jesus lifted up on the cross was likewise not an image of glory, but the sign of one bearing a curse, dying in the place of the guilty — yet it is precisely this sign, which seemed the least likely to bring life, that became the guarantee of eternal life for everyone who looks to it.

Response

You don’t need to first fully understand, nor first make some amends, before you can draw on the cross’s effect — the only thing required of those bitten by serpents in Israel’s camp was to turn and look at the bronze serpent lifted on the pole, and this is the very picture Jesus himself uses to explain the cross. Today, everyone who is dying from their own rebellion, their own sin’s poison, likewise needs only to turn their eyes to the Son of Man who was lifted up — “that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14–15) — not because you deserve it, but because he has already been lifted up, so that everyone who looks to him may live.

title: 新一代的数点与交棒
title_en: A New Generation Numbered, and the Handoff of Leadership
verse: 民数记廿七章十八节
content:
书卷背景

巴力毗珥的瘟疫平息之后（廿五章），民数记转向一个几乎全新的会众——旷野飘流四十年，那一代蒙拯救出埃及、却因不信而倒毙的人，如今几乎无一存留。

在全书结构中的位置

廿六章的第二次数点，与全书开头（一章）在西奈山的数点遥相呼应，但名册上的名字几乎全部换新；本章结尾更直接点出十四章的审判已经彻底应验。廿七章由此处理两件顺理成章的事：西罗非哈女儿们的产业问题（律法在这里第一次为她们破例），以及摩西请求耶和华预备接班人——约书亚受命。廿八至廿九章接着列出整套节期献祭的历（日常、安息日、月朔，直到七个节期），在进地前先把敬拜的秩序安顿妥当——这提醒读者：进入迦南从来不是终点，在那里正确地敬拜神，才是。

主题与神学重点
  • 廿六章：这一次数点的结语毫不含糊：「除了耶孚尼的儿子迦勒和嫩的儿子约书亚以外，连一个人也没有存留」（民26:65）——十四章所宣告的审判，字字应验，没有一个二十岁以上曾发怨言的人活着看见迦南。
  • 廿七章：西罗非哈没有儿子，五个女儿求问：为什么因父亲没有儿子就要除掉他的名？耶和华的回应超出律法原先设想：「西罗非哈的女儿说得有理。你定要在她们父亲的弟兄中，把地分给她们为业」（民27:7）。紧接着，摩西求耶和华「立一个人治理会众」（民27:16），耶和华指明：「嫩的儿子约书亚是心中有圣灵的；你将他领来，按手在他头上」（民27:18）——继任者的资格，不是摩西挑选的，而是神先预备、后启示的。
  • 廿八至廿九章：常献的燔祭「要按日期献给我」（民28:2），从早晚常献之祭、安息日、月朔，到逾越节、七七节、吹角日、赎罪日、住棚节，逐一详细规定——这些条例被安放在进地之前，仿佛提醒新一代：迦南不是这一切的终点，在那里如何敬拜神，才是。
救赎历史脉络

这一整个单元记录了一件贯穿救赎历史的模式：人的不信断送了一代人的应许，神却总是兴起下一代人来承接祂的计划——应许的成就，从不真正倚靠人这一边的忠心，而是倚靠神自己持守到底的信实。约书亚的受命尤其意味深长：他「心中有圣灵」，按手受托，带领百姓进入那地——这与后来那位名字同为「约书亚」（希伯来文与「耶稣」同源）、受圣灵浇灌、要把神百姓真正带进安息的那一位，形成一条清晰的预表线索。

回应

你若因过去的失败而觉得自己配不上神继续使用你，请记得：民数记这一整卷所记的，正是神在一代人的不信之后，毫不迟疑地兴起下一代人来承接应许——祂的计划从来不是靠人的完全记录推进的。而那真正、完全带领神百姓进入安息之地的，不是约书亚，而是那位比约书亚更大的一位；祂「心中有圣灵」不是凭外加的恩赐，而是本来就有。你今天能进入祂所应许的产业，不是因为你比前一代人更配得，而是因为祂已经受托、已经带路，走在你前面。
content_en:
Book Background

After the plague of Baal of Peor subsides (chapter 25), Numbers turns to an almost entirely new congregation — of the generation redeemed out of Egypt but struck down for unbelief during forty years of wilderness wandering, almost no one now remains.

Its Place in the Book’s Structure

The second census in chapter 26 echoes the census at Sinai at the book’s opening (chapter 1), yet nearly every name on the roll has changed; the chapter’s close directly states that the judgment of chapter 14 has been utterly fulfilled. Chapter 27 then deals with two natural next matters: the inheritance question of Zelophehad’s daughters (the law makes its first exception for them here), and Moses’s request for the LORD to prepare a successor — Joshua is commissioned. Chapters 28–29 then lay out the entire calendar of festival offerings (daily, Sabbath, new moon, through the seven feasts), settling the order of worship before entering the land — reminding the reader that entering Canaan was never the destination; worshiping God rightly there was.

Themes and Theological Highlights
  • Chapter 26: This census closes with an unambiguous statement: “But among these there was not one of those listed by Moses and Aaron the priest… For the LORD had said of them, ‘They shall die in the wilderness.’ Not one man of them was left, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun” (Num. 26:64–65) — the judgment declared in chapter 14 is fulfilled to the letter; not one person over twenty who had grumbled lived to see Canaan.
  • Chapter 27: Zelophehad has no sons; his five daughters ask why their father’s name should be removed just because he had no son. The LORD’s response goes beyond what the law had originally provided for: “The daughters of Zelophehad are right… you shall give them a possession of an inheritance among their father’s brothers” (Num. 27:7). Immediately after, Moses asks the LORD to “appoint a man over the congregation” (Num. 27:16), and the LORD specifies: “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him” (Num. 27:18) — the successor’s qualification is not Moses’s own choice, but something God prepares first and reveals after.
  • Chapters 28–29: The regular burnt offering is “to be offered to me at its appointed time” (Num. 28:2), from the daily morning and evening offerings, the Sabbath, and the new moon, to Passover, the Feast of Weeks, the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Booths, each set out in detail — these regulations are placed right before entering the land, as if reminding the new generation: Canaan is not the end of all this; how to worship God there is.
The Redemptive-Historical Thread

This whole unit records a pattern that runs through redemptive history: human unbelief forfeits one generation’s promise, yet God always raises up the next generation to carry his plan forward — the fulfillment of the promise never truly depends on human faithfulness, but on God’s own faithfulness holding fast to the end. Joshua’s commissioning is especially significant: he is “a man in whom is the Spirit,” commissioned by the laying on of hands, to lead the people into the land — forming a clear line of foreshadowing toward the one whose name is likewise “Joshua” (the same root as “Jesus”), anointed with the Spirit, who would truly bring God’s people into rest.

Response

If past failures make you feel unworthy of God continuing to use you, remember: this whole book of Numbers records exactly this — God, without hesitation, raising up the next generation to carry the promise forward after one generation’s unbelief. His plan has never advanced on the strength of a flawless human record. And the one who truly and completely leads God’s people into the land of rest is not Joshua, but the one greater than Joshua; “a man in whom is the Spirit” was not an added gift for him, but who he already was. You can enter the inheritance he has promised today not because you are more deserving than the generation before you, but because he has already been commissioned, has already gone ahead, and walks before you.
